title: Putting It Together
text:
The final chapter steps back from individual methods. Strong evaluations rarely rely on a single design; strong evidence rarely comes from a single study.
We look at how the case studies in these notes combined designs, how to combine estimates across studies, what can go wrong at the level of the literature, and how to report an evaluation so that decision-makers can use it.
The generative AI studies from across the notes serve as a worked example of evidence synthesis.

Experimental and Observational Estimates






WarningChecking Designs Against Each Other




LaLonde’s benchmark: standard non-experimental estimates of a job-training program often missed the experimental answer (LaLonde 1986)
Within one paper: Cui et al. (2026) report both DiD and experimental (IV) estimates for each firm. The DiD estimates are sometimes larger and sometimes smaller: the direction of selection differs across firms
Across papers: an AI assistant raised support-agent productivity by about 15% in a staggered rollout (Brynjolfsson et al. 2025), and a coding assistant raised completed tasks by about 26% in randomized experiments (Cui et al. 2026). Different settings and estimands, but the same direction and similar size

Lesson: observational designs are most credible when their assumptions can be checked against an experiment, or against a design with different assumptions.

title: Putting It Together
text:
Accumulating Evidence

Combining Estimates Across Studies






NotePrecision Weighting



Given estimates \hat\tau_1, \dots, \hat\tau_K with standard errors s_1, \dots, s_K of the same estimand:
\hat\tau_{\text{pooled}} = \frac{\sum_k w_k \hat\tau_k}{\sum_k w_k}, \qquad w_k = \frac{1}{s_k^2}, \qquad SE(\hat\tau_{\text{pooled}}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\sum_k w_k}}

Precise studies get more weight
This is how Cui et al. (2026) combine their three noisy experiments into one informative estimate
If true effects differ across settings, a random-effects model adds a between-study variance \tau^2, which widens the pooled interval and shifts weight towards smaller studies





Pooling in R


Code
# Three hypothetical experiments estimating the same effect (in %)
est <- c(firm_A = 22, firm_B = 41, firm_C = 18)
se  <- c(firm_A = 12, firm_B = 25, firm_C = 15)

w <- 1 / se^2
pooled    <- sum(w * est) / sum(w)
pooled_se <- 1 / sqrt(sum(w))

# Test for heterogeneity across studies (Cochran's Q)
Q <- sum(w * (est - pooled)^2)

round(c(pooled = pooled, se = pooled_se,
        lower_95 = pooled - 1.96 * pooled_se, upper_95 = pooled + 1.96 * pooled_se,
        Q = Q, p_heterogeneity = pchisq(Q, df = length(est) - 1, lower.tail = FALSE)), 2)


         pooled              se        lower_95        upper_95               Q 
          22.97            8.77            5.77           40.17            0.64 
p_heterogeneity 
           0.73 




None of the three hypothetical experiments is significant on its own at the 5% level, but the pooled estimate is.
The heterogeneity test has little power with three studies; a non-significant Q does not prove effects are identical.




What Goes Wrong at the Level of a Literature






WarningSelective Reporting and Publication Bias




If studies with significant results are more likely to be published, the published literature overstates effects, even if every individual study is unbiased
Small studies that happen to find large effects are especially likely to be published
Symptoms: many estimates just past the significance threshold; small studies reporting larger effects (an asymmetric “funnel plot”)

Remedies: pre-registration (Chapter 4); registered reports; publishing null results; replication packages with data and code; reporting failed experiments (Cui et al. (2026) report the abandoned Accenture experiment).

title: Putting It Together
text:
From Evidence to Policy

External Validity






NoteWill It Work Here?



Questions to ask before applying a result elsewhere:

Population: are the people or firms similar? Compliers in an IV or experiment may differ from the target population
Setting: institutions, prices, and alternatives differ across countries and sectors
Scale: effects in a pilot may change when everyone is treated (market prices adjust; supply of trainers runs out; others respond)
Time: technologies change. An AI tool from 2021 is not the tool of 2026
Mechanism: if we know why something works, we can judge whether that reason holds elsewhere





Synthesis Example: Generative AI at Work






TipWhat Four Studies, Four Designs, Say Together











Study
Design
Finding




Cui et al. (2026)
Field experiments (Ch. 4–5)
Coding assistant raises completed tasks ~26%; larger gains and adoption for newer developers


Brynjolfsson et al. (2025)
Staggered rollout, FE/DiD (Ch. 8–9)
Support productivity +15%; +30% for less skilled and less experienced agents; small gains for the most experienced


Demirci et al. (2025)
DiD on ChatGPT’s release (Ch. 9)
Freelance job posts in writing and coding fall ~21% relative to manual work


Shaw and Nave (2026) (preprint)
Lab and online experiments (Ch. 4)
When they consult the AI, people follow its wrong answers ~80% of the time (Study 1)



Consistent pattern: within firms, AI complements less experienced workers; across markets, it substitutes for some outsourced tasks; and people over-rely on its output. A decision-maker needs all three.




Reporting an Evaluation






TipA Checklist for the Write-Up




Question and estimand: the effect of what, on what, for whom
Design: where the counterfactual comes from, stated in plain language
Assumptions and the evidence for them (balance, first stage, pre-trends, placebo tests)
Main estimate with uncertainty, in units a decision-maker understands
Robustness to alternative specifications and estimators
Heterogeneity: who gains and who loses
Limitations: what the design cannot rule out; external validity
Costs and benefits where possible
Replication materials: data access, code, pre-registration





Communicating to Decision-Makers






NoteTranslate Estimates into Decisions




Use meaningful units: “one fewer death for every 1,587 people sent a letter” (Goldin et al. 2021); “about 15,600 deaths averted had all states expanded Medicaid” (Miller et al. 2021)
Report uncertainty: a range as well as a point estimate
Say whose effect it is (compliers, treated units, units at a cutoff)
Separate what the evidence shows from what you recommend
Be explicit about what is not known

title: Putting It Together
text:
Summary

Summary


Every method in these notes finds a counterfactual in a different place, and rests on a different assumption
Strong studies combine designs whose weaknesses differ; strong conclusions rest on several studies
Pool comparable estimates with precision weights; check for heterogeneity
Guard against publication bias with pre-registration, replication, and reporting null and failed results
External validity needs as much attention as internal validity
Report evaluations so that a decision-maker can see the estimand, the assumptions, the uncertainty, and the limits




Final Exercise


Choose a policy question you care about (insurance, finance, technology, operations)
Identify the estimand and the assignment mechanism
Propose a primary design and a second design with different assumptions
Write the six questions from Chapter 1 for your own proposal
Draft a one-page summary for a decision-maker

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Difference-in-differences needs a comparison group whose trend stands in for the treated group’s counterfactual trend. With one treated region, country, or firm, there is often no single unit that does this well.
Synthetic control builds the comparison: a weighted combination of untreated units chosen to track the treated unit before the intervention.
Two case studies: the economic cost of terrorism in the Basque Country (the paper that introduced the method), and the stock-market value of connections to Timothy Geithner when he was nominated US Treasury Secretary in 2008.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Motivation

When Only One Unit Is Treated






NoteComparative Case Studies



Many policies and events affect a single large unit:

A region suffers decades of political violence
A state passes a tobacco-control law
A country joins a currency union or leaves a trading bloc
A firm’s well-connected former adviser becomes a regulator

We observe the treated unit before and after, and many untreated units over the same period.








WarningWhy DiD Struggles Here




Which comparison? Choosing “the most similar region” by hand is subjective and easy to dispute
The average of all untreated units may follow a very different path from the treated unit, so parallel trends fails
With one treated unit, the usual standard errors for DiD do not apply

title: Synthetic Control
text:
The Method

The Synthetic Control Idea






TipChoosing the Comparison from the Data



Build a synthetic version of the treated unit as a weighted average of untreated units (the donor pool), with weights chosen so the synthetic unit matches the treated unit before treatment:

in the path of the outcome over the pre-treatment period, and
in predictors of the outcome (income, industry mix, population, education)

After treatment, the synthetic unit’s outcome is the estimate of what would have happened without treatment. The gap between the two paths is the estimated effect.




The Estimator






NoteNotation



Unit 1 is treated from period T_0 + 1; units 2, \dots, J+1 are never treated.
Weights: W = (w_2, \dots, w_{J+1}) with w_j \geq 0 and \sum_j w_j = 1, chosen to minimize
(X_1 - X_0 W)' \, V \, (X_1 - X_0 W)
where X_1 holds pre-treatment predictors for the treated unit, X_0 the same for donors, and V weights the importance of each predictor.
Effect in each post-treatment period t > T_0:
\hat\tau_t = Y_{1t} - \sum_{j=2}^{J+1} w_j^* \, Y_{jt}








TipWhy Non-Negative Weights That Sum to One?



They prevent extrapolation: the synthetic unit must lie inside the range (the convex hull) of the donors. The method shows plainly when it cannot match the treated unit. If the treated unit is more extreme than every donor on some characteristic, no synthetic control can reproduce it. Even inside that range, averaging very different donors can cause interpolation bias, so the donor pool should be restricted to units similar to the treated one (Abadie 2021).




When Synthetic Control Beats DiD






NoteAllowing for Different Trends



DiD assumes the treated unit and the comparison group would have moved in parallel. Synthetic control allows units to respond differently to common shocks (for example, an industrial region is hit harder by an oil crisis), as long as a weighted mix of donors responds the same way as the treated unit.
A good fit over a long pre-treatment period is the evidence for this: it is unlikely that a mix of donors tracks the treated unit for many years by chance, unless it shares the treated unit’s exposure to the forces driving the outcome (Abadie et al. 2010).




Requirements and Limits






WarningWhen the Method Is Credible




Long pre-treatment period with a close fit; a poor fit means the counterfactual is not credible
Donor pool of units that were not affected by the treatment or by other large shocks in the same period
No spillovers from the treated unit to donors (otherwise the gap is biased)
No anticipation: if behaviour changed before the formal treatment date (for example, once a policy was announced), backdate the treatment to that point
Not too extreme: the treated unit must be within the range of donors on the characteristics that matter
Inference cannot rely on large-sample standard errors with one treated unit; use placebo tests (Abadie 2021)

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Inference

Placebo Tests






TipIs the Gap Unusual?



In-space placebos: pretend each donor was treated instead, and re-run synthetic control for it (excluding the real treated unit from its donor pool). If the treated unit’s gap is larger than almost all placebo gaps, the effect is unlikely to be chance.

Compare the ratio of post- to pre-treatment fit error (root mean squared prediction error, RMSPE), which penalizes placebos with poor pre-treatment fit
p-value = rank of the treated unit’s ratio among all J + 1 units, divided by J + 1. With 20 donors the smallest possible p-value is 1/21 \approx 0.048

In-time placebos: pretend treatment happened at an earlier date. A large “effect” before the real treatment signals a poor design.
Leave-one-out: drop each donor with positive weight in turn; results should not hinge on one donor.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Simulation

Synthetic Control vs. DiD


Code
set.seed(2026)
J <- 20; T0 <- 20; T1 <- 10; TT <- T0 + T1
pre <- 1:T0; post <- (T0 + 1):TT

# Units load differently on a common upward trend (e.g., a growing industry)
lambda <- c(1.8, runif(J, 0, 2))          # unit 1 is treated and strongly exposed
trend  <- seq(0, 3, length.out = TT)
alpha  <- c(10, rnorm(J, 10, 1))
Y <- sapply(1:TT, function(t) alpha + lambda * trend[t] + rnorm(J + 1, 0, 0.15))
effect <- c(rep(0, T0), -seq(0.5, 2.5, length.out = T1))
Y[1, ] <- Y[1, ] + effect                 # true effect: a growing loss

# Weights: non-negative, sum to one (softmax), chosen to fit the pre-period path
sc_weights <- function(y1, Y0) {
  loss <- function(a) { w <- exp(a) / sum(exp(a)); sum((y1 - colSums(w * Y0))^2) }
  a <- optim(rep(0, nrow(Y0)), loss, method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 2000))$par
  exp(a) / sum(exp(a))
}
w <- sc_weights(Y[1, pre], Y[-1, pre])
synth <- colSums(w * Y[-1, ])

did <- (mean(Y[1, post]) - mean(Y[1, pre])) -
       (mean(colMeans(Y[-1, post])) - mean(colMeans(Y[-1, pre])))

round(c(true_effect = mean(effect[post]),
        synthetic_control = mean((Y[1, ] - synth)[post]),
        DiD_all_donors = did,
        largest_weight = max(w)), 2)


      true_effect synthetic_control    DiD_all_donors    largest_weight 
            -1.50             -1.39              0.06              0.84 




The treated unit is more exposed to the common trend than the average donor. DiD against all donors assumes they share the trend, and misses the loss almost entirely.
Synthetic control puts most weight on the donors with similar exposure and recovers most of the effect.




Seeing the Fit and the Gap


Code
par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(1:TT, Y[1, ], type = "l", lwd = 3, ylim = range(Y[1, ], synth, colMeans(Y[-1, ])),
     xlab = "Period", ylab = "Outcome", main = "Treated unit, synthetic control, and donor average")
lines(1:TT, synth, lwd = 3, lty = 2, col = "#1565c0")
lines(1:TT, colMeans(Y[-1, ]), lwd = 2, lty = 3, col = "grey50")
abline(v = T0 + 0.5, col = "#c2410c")
legend("topleft", c("Treated", "Synthetic control", "Average of all donors"),
       lty = c(1, 2, 3), lwd = c(3, 3, 2), col = c("black", "#1565c0", "grey50"), bty = "n")











Placebo Inference


Code
# Ratio of post- to pre-treatment RMSPE for every unit, treating it as if treated
rmspe_ratio <- function(i) {
  donors <- setdiff(2:(J + 1), i)          # never use the real treated unit as a donor
  w_i <- sc_weights(Y[i, pre], Y[donors, pre])
  gap <- Y[i, ] - colSums(w_i * Y[donors, ])
  sqrt(mean(gap[post]^2)) / sqrt(mean(gap[pre]^2))
}
ratios <- sapply(1:(J + 1), rmspe_ratio)

c(treated_rank = rank(-ratios)[1],
  units = J + 1,
  p_value = round(rank(-ratios)[1] / (J + 1), 3))


treated_rank        units      p_value 
       1.000       21.000        0.048 




If the treated unit’s ratio is the largest of all 21, the p-value is 1/21. This is the smallest p-value achievable with 20 donors: synthetic control inference is limited by the size of the donor pool.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 1: The Basque Country

Case Study 1: The Economic Cost of Conflict






NoteAbadie & Gardeazabal (2003), American Economic Review (Abadie and Gardeazabal 2003)



Question: What did decades of terrorism cost the economy of the Basque Country?
Context: at the start of ETA’s terrorist campaign in the late 1960s, the Basque Country was the third-richest of Spain’s 17 regions; by the late 1990s it had fallen to sixth. Nearly 800 people were killed, and businesses were targets of extortion and kidnapping.
Why it is hard:

A before–after comparison mixes terrorism with Spain’s deep recession of the late 1970s and early 1980s
A comparison with the rest of Spain is misleading: the Basque Country was richer, more industrial, more densely populated, and better educated





Case Study 1: Building the Synthetic Basque Country






TipDonors, Predictors, and Weights




Donor pool: the 16 other Spanish regions
Predictors (1960s): GDP per head, investment ratio, population density, sectoral shares of production, and human capital
Choice of V: predictor weights chosen so that the synthetic region best reproduces Basque GDP per head in the 1960s
Result: Catalonia (0.85) and Madrid (0.15); all other regions receive zero weight
What cannot be matched: the Basque Country had the highest industrial share in Spain, so no weighted average of other regions reproduces it exactly





Catalonia and Madrid are not surprising: they were the other rich, industrial, densely populated regions. The method makes the choice explicit and reproducible.




Case Study 1: Results






TipMain Findings




The Basque Country and its synthetic control track each other closely until about 1975
Then they diverge as terrorism becomes large-scale: Basque GDP per head falls up to about 12% below the synthetic region, and about 10% on average over the 1980s and 1990s
The gap tracks terrorist activity: spikes in killings are followed by a widening gap two to three years later
The Basque population also fell relative to the synthetic region, so the loss in total output was larger still









NoteA Second Test: The 1998–99 Ceasefire



The authors also study stock returns during ETA’s ceasefire. Shares of firms with a large part of their business in the Basque Country outperformed other firms by about 10% as the truce became credible, and underperformed by about 11% when it ended.




Case Study 1: Threats and Checks






WarningCould the Gap Be Something Other Than Terrorism?




Placebo study: applied to Catalonia (similar, industrial, no comparable terrorism), the method reproduces its GDP path closely until the late 1980s; Catalonia then pulls about 4% ahead of its synthetic control (the 1992 Barcelona Olympics). Because Catalonia is the main donor for the Basque Country, this suggests the Basque gap in the 1990s may be overstated somewhat
Industrial decline: the Basque Country was more industrial, and industry collapsed after the oil crises. The authors argue this cannot explain why the gap moves with terrorist activity, and controlling for oil prices leaves the link unchanged
Spillovers to donors: if terrorism also hurt Catalonia or Madrid, the gap understates the effect; if it diverted investment to them, the gap overstates it. The synthetic region’s economy is much larger than the Basque economy, which limits the second concern





Case Study 1: What to Copy






TipPractices to Reuse




Fit a long pre-period and show it. Twenty years of close tracking (1955–1975) is what makes the later gap credible.
Report what you cannot match (the industrial share) instead of hiding it.
Look for a second, independent test: stock returns during the ceasefire.





Case Study 1: Discussion Questions


Why not simply compare the Basque Country with the average of all other Spanish regions?
The synthetic control cannot match the Basque industrial share. Why does that matter, and how do the authors respond?
Why does the close fit until 1975 make the post-1975 gap more convincing?
How does the ceasefire stock-market analysis strengthen the case, given that it uses a completely different design?
What spillovers from Basque terrorism to Catalonia could bias the estimate, and in which direction?








NoteSuggested Answers (click to expand)






The other regions were on average poorer, less industrial, and less densely populated, and followed different paths before terrorism. Their average is a poor guide to what the Basque economy would have done.
The Basque Country was more industrial, and industry declined after the oil crises, so part of the gap could reflect industrial decline. The authors note that the industrial share fell by similar amounts in both (17 vs. 15 points), that the gap follows terrorist activity, and that oil prices do not explain it.
A weighted mix of regions is unlikely to track the Basque economy for two decades unless it responds to the same economic forces. A long close fit makes it a credible guide to the path without terrorism.
It uses different data (share prices) and a different design (an event study around the truce), with different assumptions. Two methods with different weaknesses giving consistent answers are harder to explain away.
If terrorism also hurt Catalonia, through fear, trade, or tourism, the synthetic region is lower and the gap understates the effect. If investment moved from the Basque Country to Catalonia, the synthetic region is higher and the gap overstates it.

title: Synthetic Control
section: Case Study 2: Connections in a Crisis
text:
Case Study 2: Connections in a Crisis

Case Study 2: The Value of Connections to Policymakers






NoteAcemoglu, Johnson, Kermani, Kwak & Mitton (2016), Journal of Financial Economics (Acemoglu et al. 2016)



Question: When policymakers have wide discretion, as in a financial crisis, are firms connected to them worth more?
The event: on 21 November 2008, news leaked that Timothy Geithner, then president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, would be nominated US Treasury Secretary.
Treatment: financial firms connected to Geithner, using three alternative measures: meetings on his official schedule in 2007–08, shared board and non-profit memberships, and headquarters in New York City.
Outcome: daily stock returns of financial firms around the announcement.




Case Study 2: The Design






TipAn Event Study, Backed Up by Synthetic Matching



Main approach: abnormal returns relative to a market model estimated over 250 trading days ending 30 days before the event; compare connected and non-connected firms, controlling for size, profitability, and leverage.
The concern: connected firms may differ from non-connected ones in ways that move their returns on the same days.
Synthetic matching: for each connected firm, build a synthetic firm from non-connected financial firms, with weights chosen so the synthetic firm’s daily returns track the connected firm’s returns over the 250-day pre-event window.

The effect averages each firm’s gap, giving more weight to better matches
Inference: draw 5,000 placebo treatment groups of the same size from non-connected firms; the real effect is significant if it lies outside the middle 95% of placebo effects





Case Study 2: Results and Checks






TipMain Findings




Geithner-connected firms earned a cumulative abnormal return of about 6% after the first full trading day, and about 12% after ten trading days, relative to other financial firms
When news broke in January 2009 that his confirmation might be derailed by tax issues, connected firms had negative abnormal returns
Synthetic matching gives about 6.0% after the first full trading day and 12.4% after ten days, both significant; for the one-hour window on the leak day itself the estimate is smaller and not significant









WarningThreats the Authors Address




A simultaneous bailout: Citigroup, Geithner’s most connected firm, received additional government support between the leak and the next trading day. The authors drop firms whose returns were highly correlated with Citigroup’s
False positives: they run the same test on 100 ordinary trading days to check how often “significant” effects appear by chance





Case Study 2: What to Copy






TipPractices to Reuse




With many treated units, build a synthetic match for each one, weighted by how well it fits before the event.
Get p-values from placebo groups drawn from the controls (5,000 draws).
Check the false-positive rate on ordinary days, and deal openly with events at the same time (the Citigroup rescue).





Case Study 2: Discussion Questions


Why does synthetic matching on pre-event daily returns address concerns that controlling for size and leverage does not?
Why build a separate synthetic firm for each connected firm, rather than one synthetic portfolio?
How is the placebo-group inference similar to in-space placebos for a single treated region?
Why are the tax-issue returns a useful second test, like the Basque ceasefire?








NoteSuggested Answers (click to expand)






Matching the actual co-movement of returns captures each firm’s exposure to all common risks (sector, funding, credit), whether measured or not. Size and leverage capture only a few observed characteristics.
Connected firms differ a lot, so each needs its own comparison. Separate matches also let the authors weight firms by how well they are matched; one portfolio would mix good and bad matches.
Both ask how unusual the real effect is compared with effects for units that were not treated. Here, random groups of unconnected firms play the role of placebo regions.
News that lowered the chance of Geithner’s confirmation should reverse the earlier gain. A reversal for the same firms is hard to explain with a confounder that happened to coincide with the first announcement.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Best Practices

Synthetic Control Checklist






TipBefore and After Estimating




Choose the donor pool on substantive grounds: similar units, unaffected by the treatment or other large shocks
Use a long pre-treatment period and show the fit graphically
Report the weights and the predictor balance; explain what cannot be matched
Run placebo tests in space and in time, and report the rank-based p-value
Run leave-one-out checks on donors with positive weight
Look for a second, independent test of the same effect





Common Pitfalls






WarningMistakes to Avoid




Reporting an effect despite a poor pre-treatment fit
Including donors affected by the treatment (spillovers) or by their own large shocks
Searching over donor pools and predictors until the result “looks right”
Treating the gap as precise: inference is limited by the number of donors
Ignoring that the treated unit may be outside the range of the donors





Summary


With one or a few treated units, synthetic control builds the comparison as a weighted average of untreated donors
Weights are non-negative and sum to one, so the method interpolates rather than extrapolates
Credibility comes from a long, close pre-treatment fit and a clean donor pool
Inference uses placebo tests, not standard errors
Strong applications pair synthetic control with a second, independent test




Next Steps


Read: Abadie and Gardeazabal (2003) Sections I–II; Abadie (2021)
Practice: In the simulation, set the treated unit’s exposure (lambda[1]) to 2.5, outside the donors’ range. What happens to the pre-treatment fit and the estimate?
Next Class: Regression and matching, when units are observed only once (Chapter 11)

Abadie, Alberto, Alexis Diamond, and Jens Hainmueller. 2010. “Synthetic Control Methods for Comparative Case Studies: Estimating the Effect of California’s Tobacco Control Program.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 105 (490): 493–505.


Abadie, Alberto, and Javier Gardeazabal. 2003. “The Economic Costs of Conflict: A Case Study of the Basque Country.” American Economic Review 93 (1): 113–32. https://doi.org/10.1257/000282803321455188.


Acemoglu, Daron, Simon Johnson, Amir Kermani, James Kwak, and Todd Mitton. 2016. “The Value of Connections in Turbulent Times: Evidence from the United States.” Journal of Financial Economics 121 (2): 368–91. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2015.10.001.


Arkhangelsky, Dmitry, Susan Athey, David A Hirshberg, Guido W Imbens, and Stefan Wager. 2021. “Synthetic Difference-in-Differences.” American Economic Review 111 (12): 4088–118. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20190159.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Where This Chapter Fits






Step 4: Do you observe the same units before and after treatment?



You arrive here when: Only one or a few units are treated (a country, a state, a firm), and parallel trends with any single comparison group are hard to defend.
This chapter: Building a comparison unit as a weighted combination of untreated units.
Next: Chapter 11: when units are observed only once, and we must rely on observed characteristics.

See the design flowchart in Chapter 1.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
In Practice: Synthetic Control






Practitioner Summary



Use it when: one or a few units are treated and no single untreated unit is a convincing comparison
What you need: the outcome for the treated unit and many untreated units over a long pre-treatment period, plus predictors
What must hold: the weighted donors would have tracked the treated unit without treatment; no spillovers to donors; no anticipation (or backdate the treatment)
Checks to run: pre-treatment fit; the weights and predictor balance; in-space and in-time placebos; leave-one-out
In R: Synth::dataprep() and synth(), tidysynth, synthdid for synthetic DiD
Telling a manager: “We built a stand-in from regions that tracked ours closely for 15 years. After the event, ours fell about 10% below its stand-in.”

title: Synthetic Control
section: When Only One Unit Is Treated
text:
When Only One Unit Is Treated






Comparative Case Studies


Many policies and events affect a single large unit:

A region suffers decades of political violence
A state passes a tobacco-control law
A country joins a currency union or leaves a trading bloc
A firm’s well-connected former adviser becomes a regulator

We observe the treated unit before and after, and many untreated units over the same period.









Why DiD Struggles Here



Which comparison? Choosing “the most similar region” by hand is subjective and easy to dispute
The average of all untreated units may follow a very different path from the treated unit, so parallel trends fails
With one treated unit, the usual standard errors for DiD do not apply

title: Synthetic Control
text:
The Synthetic Control Idea






Choosing the Comparison from the Data


Build a synthetic version of the treated unit as a weighted average of untreated units (the donor pool), with weights chosen so the synthetic unit matches the treated unit before treatment:

in the path of the outcome over the pre-treatment period, and
in predictors of the outcome (income, industry mix, population, education)

After treatment, the synthetic unit’s outcome is the estimate of what would have happened without treatment. The gap between the two paths is the estimated effect.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
The Estimator






Notation


Unit 1 is treated from period T_0 + 1; units 2, \dots, J+1 are never treated.
Weights: W = (w_2, \dots, w_{J+1}) with w_j \geq 0 and \sum_j w_j = 1, chosen to minimize
(X_1 - X_0 W)' \, V \, (X_1 - X_0 W)
where X_1 holds pre-treatment predictors for the treated unit, X_0 the same for donors, and V weights the importance of each predictor.
Effect in each post-treatment period t > T_0:
\hat\tau_t = Y_{1t} - \sum_{j=2}^{J+1} w_j^* \, Y_{jt}









Why Non-Negative Weights That Sum to One?


They prevent extrapolation: the synthetic unit must lie inside the range (the convex hull) of the donors. The method shows plainly when it cannot match the treated unit. If the treated unit is more extreme than every donor on some characteristic, no synthetic control can reproduce it. Even inside that range, averaging very different donors can cause interpolation bias, so the donor pool should be restricted to units similar to the treated one (Abadie 2021).

title: Synthetic Control
text:
When Synthetic Control Beats DiD






Allowing for Different Trends


DiD assumes the treated unit and the comparison group would have moved in parallel. Synthetic control allows units to respond differently to common shocks (for example, an industrial region is hit harder by an oil crisis), as long as a weighted mix of donors responds the same way as the treated unit.
A good fit over a long pre-treatment period is the evidence for this: it is unlikely that a mix of donors tracks the treated unit for many years by chance, unless it shares the treated unit’s exposure to the forces driving the outcome (Abadie et al. 2010).

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Requirements and Limits






When the Method Is Credible



Long pre-treatment period with a close fit; a poor fit means the counterfactual is not credible
Donor pool of units that were not affected by the treatment or by other large shocks in the same period
No spillovers from the treated unit to donors (otherwise the gap is biased)
No anticipation: if behaviour changed before the formal treatment date (for example, once a policy was announced), backdate the treatment to that point
Not too extreme: the treated unit must be within the range of donors on the characteristics that matter
Inference cannot rely on large-sample standard errors with one treated unit; use placebo tests (Abadie 2021)

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Placebo Tests






Is the Gap Unusual?


In-space placebos: pretend each donor was treated instead, and re-run synthetic control for it (excluding the real treated unit from its donor pool). If the treated unit’s gap is larger than almost all placebo gaps, the effect is unlikely to be chance.

Compare the ratio of post- to pre-treatment fit error (root mean squared prediction error, RMSPE), which penalizes placebos with poor pre-treatment fit
p-value = rank of the treated unit’s ratio among all J + 1 units, divided by J + 1. With 20 donors the smallest possible p-value is 1/21 \approx 0.048

In-time placebos: pretend treatment happened at an earlier date. A large “effect” before the real treatment signals a poor design.
Leave-one-out: drop each donor with positive weight in turn; results should not hinge on one donor.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Synthetic Control vs. DiD


Code
set.seed(2026)
J <- 20; T0 <- 20; T1 <- 10; TT <- T0 + T1
pre <- 1:T0; post <- (T0 + 1):TT

# Units load differently on a common upward trend (e.g., a growing industry)
lambda <- c(1.8, runif(J, 0, 2))          # unit 1 is treated and strongly exposed
trend  <- seq(0, 3, length.out = TT)
alpha  <- c(10, rnorm(J, 10, 1))
Y <- sapply(1:TT, function(t) alpha + lambda * trend[t] + rnorm(J + 1, 0, 0.15))
effect <- c(rep(0, T0), -seq(0.5, 2.5, length.out = T1))
Y[1, ] <- Y[1, ] + effect                 # true effect: a growing loss

# Weights: non-negative, sum to one (softmax), chosen to fit the pre-period path
sc_weights <- function(y1, Y0) {
  loss <- function(a) { w <- exp(a) / sum(exp(a)); sum((y1 - colSums(w * Y0))^2) }
  a <- optim(rep(0, nrow(Y0)), loss, method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 2000))$par
  exp(a) / sum(exp(a))
}
w <- sc_weights(Y[1, pre], Y[-1, pre])
synth <- colSums(w * Y[-1, ])

did <- (mean(Y[1, post]) - mean(Y[1, pre])) -
       (mean(colMeans(Y[-1, post])) - mean(colMeans(Y[-1, pre])))

round(c(true_effect = mean(effect[post]),
        synthetic_control = mean((Y[1, ] - synth)[post]),
        DiD_all_donors = did,
        largest_weight = max(w)), 2)


      true_effect synthetic_control    DiD_all_donors    largest_weight 
            -1.50             -1.39              0.06              0.84 




The treated unit is more exposed to the common trend than the average donor. DiD against all donors assumes they share the trend, and misses the loss almost entirely.
Synthetic control puts most weight on the donors with similar exposure and recovers most of the effect.

text:
Case Study 1: The Economic Cost of Conflict






Abadie & Gardeazabal (2003), American Economic Review (Abadie and Gardeazabal 2003)


Question: What did decades of terrorism cost the economy of the Basque Country?
Context: at the start of ETA’s terrorist campaign in the late 1960s, the Basque Country was the third-richest of Spain’s 17 regions; by the late 1990s it had fallen to sixth. Nearly 800 people were killed, and businesses were targets of extortion and kidnapping.
Why it is hard:

A before–after comparison mixes terrorism with Spain’s deep recession of the late 1970s and early 1980s
A comparison with the rest of Spain is misleading: the Basque Country was richer, more industrial, more densely populated, and better educated

title: Synthetic Control
section: Case Study 1: Building the Synthetic Basque Country
text:
Case Study 1: Building the Synthetic Basque Country






Donors, Predictors, and Weights



Donor pool: the 16 other Spanish regions
Predictors (1960s): GDP per head, investment ratio, population density, sectoral shares of production, and human capital
Choice of V: predictor weights chosen so that the synthetic region best reproduces Basque GDP per head in the 1960s
Result: Catalonia (0.85) and Madrid (0.15); all other regions receive zero weight
What cannot be matched: the Basque Country had the highest industrial share in Spain, so no weighted average of other regions reproduces it exactly






Catalonia and Madrid are not surprising: they were the other rich, industrial, densely populated regions. The method makes the choice explicit and reproducible.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 1: Results






Main Findings



The Basque Country and its synthetic control track each other closely until about 1975
Then they diverge as terrorism becomes large-scale: Basque GDP per head falls up to about 12% below the synthetic region, and about 10% on average over the 1980s and 1990s
The gap tracks terrorist activity: spikes in killings are followed by a widening gap two to three years later
The Basque population also fell relative to the synthetic region, so the loss in total output was larger still










A Second Test: The 1998–99 Ceasefire


The authors also study stock returns during ETA’s ceasefire. Shares of firms with a large part of their business in the Basque Country outperformed other firms by about 10% as the truce became credible, and underperformed by about 11% when it ended.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 1: Threats and Checks






Could the Gap Be Something Other Than Terrorism?



Placebo study: applied to Catalonia (similar, industrial, no comparable terrorism), the method reproduces its GDP path closely until the late 1980s; Catalonia then pulls about 4% ahead of its synthetic control (the 1992 Barcelona Olympics). Because Catalonia is the main donor for the Basque Country, this suggests the Basque gap in the 1990s may be overstated somewhat
Industrial decline: the Basque Country was more industrial, and industry collapsed after the oil crises. The authors argue this cannot explain why the gap moves with terrorist activity, and controlling for oil prices leaves the link unchanged
Spillovers to donors: if terrorism also hurt Catalonia or Madrid, the gap understates the effect; if it diverted investment to them, the gap overstates it. The synthetic region’s economy is much larger than the Basque economy, which limits the second concern

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 1: What to Copy






Practices to Reuse



Fit a long pre-period and show it. Twenty years of close tracking (1955–1975) is what makes the later gap credible.
Report what you cannot match (the industrial share) instead of hiding it.
Look for a second, independent test: stock returns during the ceasefire.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 1: Discussion Questions

Why not simply compare the Basque Country with the average of all other Spanish regions?
The synthetic control cannot match the Basque industrial share. Why does that matter, and how do the authors respond?
Why does the close fit until 1975 make the post-1975 gap more convincing?
How does the ceasefire stock-market analysis strengthen the case, given that it uses a completely different design?
What spillovers from Basque terrorism to Catalonia could bias the estimate, and in which direction?

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 1: Suggested Answers (1–2)

The other regions were on average poorer, less industrial, and less densely populated, and followed different paths before terrorism. Their average is a poor guide to what the Basque economy would have done.
The Basque Country was more industrial, and industry declined after the oil crises, so part of the gap could reflect industrial decline. The authors note that the industrial share fell by similar amounts in both (17 vs. 15 points), that the gap follows terrorist activity, and that oil prices do not explain it.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 1: Suggested Answers (3–4)

A weighted mix of regions is unlikely to track the Basque economy for two decades unless it responds to the same economic forces. A long close fit makes it a credible guide to the path without terrorism.
It uses different data (share prices) and a different design (an event study around the truce), with different assumptions. Two methods with different weaknesses giving consistent answers are harder to explain away.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 1: Suggested Answers (5)

If terrorism also hurt Catalonia, through fear, trade, or tourism, the synthetic region is lower and the gap understates the effect. If investment moved from the Basque Country to Catalonia, the synthetic region is higher and the gap overstates it.

title: Synthetic Control
section: Case Study 2: The Value of Connections to Policymakers
text:
Case Study 2: The Value of Connections to Policymakers






Acemoglu, Johnson, Kermani, Kwak & Mitton (2016), Journal of Financial Economics (Acemoglu et al. 2016)


Question: When policymakers have wide discretion, as in a financial crisis, are firms connected to them worth more?
The event: on 21 November 2008, news leaked that Timothy Geithner, then president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, would be nominated US Treasury Secretary.
Treatment: financial firms connected to Geithner, using three alternative measures: meetings on his official schedule in 2007–08, shared board and non-profit memberships, and headquarters in New York City.
Outcome: daily stock returns of financial firms around the announcement.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 2: The Design






An Event Study, Backed Up by Synthetic Matching


Main approach: abnormal returns relative to a market model estimated over 250 trading days ending 30 days before the event; compare connected and non-connected firms, controlling for size, profitability, and leverage.
The concern: connected firms may differ from non-connected ones in ways that move their returns on the same days.
Synthetic matching: for each connected firm, build a synthetic firm from non-connected financial firms, with weights chosen so the synthetic firm’s daily returns track the connected firm’s returns over the 250-day pre-event window.

The effect averages each firm’s gap, giving more weight to better matches
Inference: draw 5,000 placebo treatment groups of the same size from non-connected firms; the real effect is significant if it lies outside the middle 95% of placebo effects

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 2: Results and Checks






Main Findings



Geithner-connected firms earned a cumulative abnormal return of about 6% after the first full trading day, and about 12% after ten trading days, relative to other financial firms
When news broke in January 2009 that his confirmation might be derailed by tax issues, connected firms had negative abnormal returns
Synthetic matching gives about 6.0% after the first full trading day and 12.4% after ten days, both significant; for the one-hour window on the leak day itself the estimate is smaller and not significant










Threats the Authors Address



A simultaneous bailout: Citigroup, Geithner’s most connected firm, received additional government support between the leak and the next trading day. The authors drop firms whose returns were highly correlated with Citigroup’s
False positives: they run the same test on 100 ordinary trading days to check how often “significant” effects appear by chance

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 2: What to Copy






Practices to Reuse



With many treated units, build a synthetic match for each one, weighted by how well it fits before the event.
Get p-values from placebo groups drawn from the controls (5,000 draws).
Check the false-positive rate on ordinary days, and deal openly with events at the same time (the Citigroup rescue).

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 2: Discussion Questions

Why does synthetic matching on pre-event daily returns address concerns that controlling for size and leverage does not?
Why build a separate synthetic firm for each connected firm, rather than one synthetic portfolio?
How is the placebo-group inference similar to in-space placebos for a single treated region?
Why are the tax-issue returns a useful second test, like the Basque ceasefire?

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 2: Suggested Answers (1–3)

Matching the actual co-movement of returns captures each firm’s exposure to all common risks (sector, funding, credit), whether measured or not. Size and leverage capture only a few observed characteristics.
Connected firms differ a lot, so each needs its own comparison. Separate matches also let the authors weight firms by how well they are matched; one portfolio would mix good and bad matches.
Both ask how unusual the real effect is compared with effects for units that were not treated. Here, random groups of unconnected firms play the role of placebo regions.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Case Study 2: Suggested Answers (4)

News that lowered the chance of Geithner’s confirmation should reverse the earlier gain. A reversal for the same firms is hard to explain with a confounder that happened to coincide with the first announcement.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Two Applications Compared






Comparing the Two Applications











Abadie & Gardeazabal (2003)
Acemoglu et al. (2016)




Treated
One region
Many connected firms


Donor pool

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Synthetic Control Checklist






Before and After Estimating



Choose the donor pool on substantive grounds: similar units, unaffected by the treatment or other large shocks
Use a long pre-treatment period and show the fit graphically
Report the weights and the predictor balance; explain what cannot be matched
Run placebo tests in space and in time, and report the rank-based p-value
Run leave-one-out checks on donors with positive weight
Look for a second, independent test of the same effect

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Common Pitfalls






Mistakes to Avoid



Reporting an effect despite a poor pre-treatment fit
Including donors affected by the treatment (spillovers) or by their own large shocks
Searching over donor pools and predictors until the result “looks right”
Treating the gap as precise: inference is limited by the number of donors
Ignoring that the treated unit may be outside the range of the donors

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Summary

With one or a few treated units, synthetic control builds the comparison as a weighted average of untreated donors
Weights are non-negative and sum to one, so the method interpolates rather than extrapolates
Credibility comes from a long, close pre-treatment fit and a clean donor pool
Inference uses placebo tests, not standard errors
Strong applications pair synthetic control with a second, independent test

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Next Steps

Read: Abadie and Gardeazabal (2003) Sections I–II; Abadie (2021)
Practice: In the simulation, set the treated unit’s exposure (lambda[1]) to 2.5, outside the donors’ range. What happens to the pre-treatment fit and the estimate?
Next Class: Regression and matching, when units are observed only once (Chapter 11)

title: Panel Data and Fixed Effects
text:
Today we move from cross-sectional designs to panel data: the same units observed repeatedly over time.
The core idea: compare each unit to itself. This removes every confounder that does not change over time, whether or not we can measure it.
We’ll build the method, state what it does and does not identify, and then work through four recent papers that use fixed effects to study climate, environment, and decision-making.
This lecture is the bridge to difference-in-differences, which is a special case of the two-way fixed effects model.
crumbs: Chapter 8: Panel Data and Fixed Effects

title: Panel Data and Fixed Effects
text:
Motivation

Do Hot Places Learn Less?






NoteA Cross-Sectional Puzzle (Park et al. 2020)



Across countries: a 1°F increase in average annual temperature is associated with 0.02 SD lower PISA math scores.
Across US counties: students in the hottest decile score about 0.12 SD lower on grades 3–8 math tests.
Question: Is this relationship causal?








WarningWhy We Cannot Trust the Cross Section



Hot places differ from cool places in many ways:

Income, poverty, and school funding
Racial and ethnic composition (and historical discrimination)
Institutions, industry mix, urbanization
Disease burden, agricultural dependence

All of these affect test scores and are correlated with climate. A regression of scores on temperature across places mixes the effect of heat with the effect of everything else that differs across places.




The Panel Data Idea






TipCompare Units to Themselves



If we observe the same unit at multiple points in time, we can ask:

Does a student score lower after an unusually hot school year than the same student scored after an unusually cool school year?


The student’s ability, family background, neighborhood, and the region’s climate are the same in both comparisons.
Anything that is fixed over time, and affects the outcome the same way in every period, cancels out, even if we never measure it.

This is the logic of fixed effects (FE).




Connect to the RCT lectures: randomization balances all confounders, observed and unobserved. Matching and propensity scores balance only observed confounders.
Fixed effects sit in between: they handle unobserved confounders, but only the time-invariant ones.




Where Fixed Effects Fit in the Toolkit









Method
Handles observed confounders
Handles unobserved confounders
Key assumption




RCT
✓
✓
Random assignment


Matching / PSM
✓
✗
Selection on observables

✓
✓
Exclusion restriction

✓
✓ (near cutoff)
Continuity at the cutoff


Fixed effects
✓
Only time-invariant
Strict exogeneity

Time-invariant + common shocks
Parallel trends

title: Panel Data and Fixed Effects
text:
Panel Data Basics

What Is Panel Data?






NoteDefinition



A panel (longitudinal) dataset observes the same units i = 1, \dots, N at multiple times t = 1, \dots, T.

Units: individuals, students, workers, firms, postcodes, counties, countries
Time: days, test sittings, tournament rounds, years
Balanced panel: every unit observed in every period
Unbalanced panel: some units missing in some periods (very common)

Not a panel: repeated cross sections, where different individuals are sampled each period (e.g., an annual survey that draws a new sample each year). These support group-level FE (e.g., state FE) but not individual FE.




Data Structure: Long Format


Code
# Panel data should be stored in "long" format: one row per unit-period
# Example: students who took the PSAT more than once
#
#  student_id  school  take  test_year  heat_prior_yr  score
#  1001        A       1     2008       71.2           -0.10
#  1001        A       2     2009       74.8           -0.05
#  1002        A       1     2008       71.2            0.35
#  1002        A       2     2009       74.8            0.31
#  2001        B       1     2010       63.5            0.62
#  2001        B       2     2011       62.1            0.97

library(tidyr)
# Converting from wide to long
panel_long <- pivot_longer(
  wide_data,
  cols = starts_with("score_"),
  names_to = "take",
  names_prefix = "score_",
  values_to = "score"
)




Emphasize that the “time” index need not be calendar time. In Park et al. it is the test sitting; in Künn et al. it is the move within a game within a round.




Sources of Variation in a Panel






TipDecomposing Variation



Any variable D_{it} can be split into:
D_{it} = \underbrace{\bar{D}_i}_{\text{between (across units)}} + \underbrace{(D_{it} - \bar{D}_i)}_{\text{within (over time, for one unit)}}

Between variation: Miami is hotter than Boston (on average)
Within variation: Boston had a hotter year in 2012 than in 2011

Cross-sectional regressions use mainly between variation. Fixed effects regressions use only within variation.
The causal question becomes: Is the within variation as good as random?

title: Panel Data and Fixed Effects
text:
The Fixed Effects Model

The Model






NoteUnobserved Effects Model



Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \tau D_{it} + X_{it}'\beta + \varepsilon_{it}

Y_{it}: outcome for unit i at time t
D_{it}: treatment or exposure (binary or continuous, e.g., temperature)
X_{it}: observed time-varying controls
\alpha_i: unit fixed effect: everything about unit i that does not change over time (ability, location, climate, management quality…)
\varepsilon_{it}: idiosyncratic shocks

The problem: \alpha_i is unobserved and likely correlated with D_{it}.




Why Pooled OLS Fails






WarningOmitted Variable Bias



If we ignore \alpha_i and run pooled OLS of Y_{it} on D_{it}, the error term is (\alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it}):
\text{plim}\ \hat{\tau}_{\text{pooled}} = \tau + \frac{\text{Cov}(D_{it}, \alpha_i)}{\text{Var}(D_{it})}
Example (heat and learning):

\alpha_i = family and school resources
Hotter places have, on average, fewer resources: \text{Cov}(D_{it}, \alpha_i) < 0
Pooled OLS overstates the harm from heat

The bias does not shrink with more data. A larger cross section only gives a more precise estimate of the wrong number.




Removing \alpha_i: The Within Transformation






TipDemeaning Removes Anything Fixed



Average the model over time for each unit: \bar{Y}_i = \alpha_i + \tau \bar{D}_i + \bar{X}_i'\beta + \bar{\varepsilon}_i
Subtract from the original:
\underbrace{(Y_{it} - \bar{Y}_i)}_{\ddot{Y}_{it}} = \tau \underbrace{(D_{it} - \bar{D}_i)}_{\ddot{D}_{it}} + \ddot{X}_{it}'\beta + \ddot{\varepsilon}_{it}
\alpha_i is gone. Run OLS on demeaned data.


In practice, software does this for you (feols(y ~ d | unit, data)). Adding a dummy for every unit, or taking first differences, gives the same or closely related answers; see Going Deeper at the end of the chapter.


Whose Effect Does Fixed Effects Estimate?






NoteOnly Units That Change Treatment Count




Units whose treatment never changes (always or never treated) contribute nothing to the estimate; with time fixed effects they still help estimate the common time shocks
Units whose treatment varies more over time get more weight
So if effects differ across units, fixed effects give a weighted average that leans towards the units with the most variation, not the simple average effect (formula in Going Deeper)

Always ask: whose effect is the estimate weighting most heavily?




Example: in Park et al., only students who took the PSAT at least twice identify the effect. Single takers are absorbed by the student FE. The authors show retakers are more advantaged than the general pool, which matters for external validity.




Two-Way Fixed Effects (TWFE)






NoteAdding Time Fixed Effects



Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \tau D_{it} + X_{it}'\beta + \varepsilon_{it}

\lambda_t: time fixed effects absorb shocks common to all units in period t

Recessions, national policy changes, test difficulty in a given year, secular warming trends

Identifying variation: deviations of D_{it} from both the unit mean and the period mean

Example: Without year FE, a nationwide warming trend combined with a nationwide trend in test scores would be attributed to heat. Year FE remove this.








ImportantTWFE and Difference-in-Differences



When D_{it} is a binary policy that switches on at a given date, TWFE is the regression form of difference-in-differences. With staggered adoption and heterogeneous effects, TWFE can produce badly weighted averages, in which some treatment effects even receive negative weights (Goodman-Bacon 2021; Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2020). We cover this in detail in the DiD lecture.




A Worked Example: State and Year Fixed Effects






NoteDoes Raising the Minimum Wage Reduce Employment?



A panel of states s observed over years t:
\text{Employment}_{st} = \alpha_s + \lambda_t + \beta \,\text{MinWage}_{st} + \varepsilon_{st}







Term
Absorbs




Year FE \lambda_t
Anything hitting all states in year t: national recessions, interest rates, federal policy, nationwide trends


State FE \alpha_s
Persistent state differences: industry mix, cost of living, unionization, politics


\beta
Identified from states changing their minimum wage at different times, relative to their own average and to the national year average











WarningWhat It Still Assumes



No state-specific, time-varying shocks correlated with minimum-wage changes. If a state raises its minimum wage because its labour market is booming, strict exogeneity fails. Chapter 9 develops the event-study and DiD tools built for this setting.




Richer Fixed Effects: Interactions






TipFE Do Not Have to Be “Unit” and “Year”



Modern applications often use interacted fixed effects to make comparisons more local:







Fixed effect
Comparison it forces




Student
Same student, different test sittings


Postcode × month-year
Same postcode, different days of the same month


Cohort × test date × take number
Students taking the same test on the same date for the same time


Player + round + move number
Same player, at the same stage of the game


Firm
Same firm, different trading days



Rule of thumb: each additional FE removes a potential confounder and removes identifying variation. Choose them by asking what comparison do I believe is as good as random?

title: Panel Data and Fixed Effects
text:
Identification

The Key Assumption: Strict Exogeneity






ImportantStrict Exogeneity



E[\varepsilon_{it} \mid D_{i1}, \dots, D_{iT}, X_{i1}, \dots, X_{iT}, \alpha_i] = 0 \quad \text{for all } t
In words: after removing the unit’s permanent characteristics (and common time shocks), the shocks to the outcome are unrelated to the treatment in any period, past, present, or future.
Equivalent intuition: the within-unit variation in treatment is as good as randomly assigned.




What Strict Exogeneity Rules Out






WarningThreats to FE Identification



1. Time-varying confounders Something changes over time for unit i and affects both D_{it} and Y_{it}. Example: a local recession reduces both school AC maintenance and family resources. A fixed trait whose effect changes over time acts the same way. Example: a student’s ability is fixed, but if it counts for more on later tests, its contribution to scores changes from year to year.
2. Feedback / reverse causality Past outcomes affect future treatment: Y_{i,t-1} \rightarrow D_{it}. Example: a firm whose stock price fell cuts emissions. A worker who was injured changes jobs.
3. Anticipation and dynamic effects Future treatment affects current outcomes, or past treatment still matters today.
4. Lagged dependent variables Including Y_{i,t-1} as a regressor with unit FE violates strict exogeneity mechanically. This is the Nickell bias, of order 1/T (Nickell 1981).
5. Selection into the panel Whether unit i appears in period t depends on the treatment. Example: hot weather discourages students from retaking the test.




Choosing Time-Varying Controls






TipWhich X_{it} to Include




Only time-varying variables matter. Anything fixed within a unit is already absorbed by \alpha_i, so adding it changes nothing.
Include variables that change within units and affect both treatment and the outcome (time-varying confounders). Example: rain is related to both temperature and injury risk (Case Study 5).
Exclude anything the treatment can change. Hours worked respond to AI access, and pollution may respond to heat. Controlling for them removes part of the effect.
Watch for feedback. A control affected by past outcomes, or a lagged outcome, breaks strict exogeneity (Nickell bias).
Variables that only predict the outcome are optional. They can improve precision but do not remove bias.
Report results with and without debatable controls. Example: Case Study 5 reports 0.24% per 1°C without a pollution control and 0.20% with it.





Why Weather Is the Ideal FE Treatment






TipThe “Weather Design” (Dell et al. 2014; Hsiang 2016)



Three of this chapter’s case studies (Künn et al. 2023; Park et al. 2020; Ireland et al. 2023) use weather or air quality fluctuations as the treatment.

Climate (long-run averages) is correlated with everything: income, institutions, culture
Weather (deviations from the local norm) is plausibly random: no one chooses whether next Tuesday is 35°C

Unit (location) fixed effects remove climate. Time fixed effects remove seasonality and trends. What remains is weather, which is as close to a natural experiment as observational data get.
Caveat: weather effects ≠ climate effects. People adapt to persistent changes (AC, schedules, migration) in ways they cannot adapt to a single hot day.




Checking the Assumption






NoteDiagnostic Toolkit











Check
What it tests
Used in




Placebo leads: future treatment should not predict current outcomes
Reverse causality, spurious trends
Park et al. (2020)


Selection tests: regress panel entry/attrition on treatment
Selection into the sample
Park et al. (2020)


Unit-specific trends: add \alpha_i \times t or region × t
Smooth time-varying confounders
Park et al. (2020)


Alternative FE structures: results stable?
Sensitivity to the comparison
Ireland et al. (2023)


Add potential confounders: pollution, precipitation, traffic
Correlated time-varying shocks
All four


Placebo outcomes or periods: heat on weekends, in summer
Mechanism and specificity
Park et al. (2020)


IV using a different source of variation
Remaining endogeneity
Künn et al. (2023)







Dynamic Effects: Leads and Lags






TipTreatment Need Not Act Only in the Same Period



Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \sum_{k=-K}^{L} \beta_k \, D_{i,t-k} + \varepsilon_{it}

Lags (k > 0): effects can persist or accumulate. Park et al. (2020) find that hot school days two to four years before the test also lower scores, so the cumulative effect of a warmer climate is larger than the one-year estimate
Leads (k < 0): future treatment cannot cause today’s outcome. A significant lead signals reverse causality, anticipation, or a spurious trend. Park et al.’s (2020) future-temperature placebo is this test
When the treatment is a policy that switches on once and stays on, this becomes an event study, the central tool of Chapter 9

title: Panel Data and Fixed Effects
text:
Practical Issues

How Much Variation Is Left?






WarningFixed Effects Can Absorb Most of Your Variation



Always report the residual standard deviation of the treatment after partialling out the fixed effects.
Park et al. (2020): after student and cohort × test date × take FE, a 1 SD change in average school-day temperature is only about 1°F, and 1 SD in days above 90°F is about 3 days.
Why it matters:

Effects are identified from small, local fluctuations
Extrapolating to large climate change scenarios requires assuming linearity and no adaptation
Precision depends on residual variation, not raw variation





Measurement Error Is Amplified by FE






WarningAttenuation Bias Gets Worse



If treatment is measured with error, D^{obs}_{it} = D_{it} + u_{it}, OLS is attenuated by the factor
\frac{\text{Var}(\ddot{D}_{it})}{\text{Var}(\ddot{D}_{it}) + \text{Var}(\ddot{u}_{it})}
Demeaning removes much of the true signal (which is persistent) but little of the noise (which is not). The signal-to-noise ratio falls, so FE estimates are more attenuated than cross-sectional ones.
Park et al. (2020) evidence: restricting to schools within 5 miles of a weather station (less measurement error) raises the estimated effect by about 25%.




What You Cannot Estimate with Unit FE






WarningTime-Invariant Variables Are Absorbed



With unit FE you cannot estimate the effect of anything that does not vary within unit:

Gender, race, birthplace (individual FE)
Long-run climate, geography (location FE)
Industry (firm FE, if firms do not switch)

But you can estimate interactions between a time-invariant characteristic and a time-varying treatment:
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \tau D_{it} + \delta (D_{it} \times \text{Black}_i) + \varepsilon_{it}
This is how Park et al. (2020) show heat harms Black and Hispanic students’ learning about three times as much as white students’.




Inference: Clustering Standard Errors






ImportantErrors Are Correlated Within Units and Within Shocks




The same student’s scores are correlated over time → cluster by unit
All students near the same weather station receive the same heat shock → cluster by level of treatment variation (Abadie et al. 2023)
Nearby stations have correlated weather → consider spatial correlation (Conley 1999) or cluster at a coarser level (e.g., state)









Paper
Clustering level
Why




Park et al. (2020)
Weather station
Treatment assigned at station level


Ireland et al. (2023)
Postcode
Unit of observation and treatment


Künn et al. (2023)
Round × year (21 clusters)
All players in a round share the same air



Few clusters (fewer than ~40–50): cluster-robust SEs are biased downward. Use the wild cluster bootstrap (Cameron et al. 2008).




Nonlinear Effects: Temperature Bins






TipFlexible Treatment: Bins



Rather than a linear term in temperature, count the days in each temperature bin:
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \sum_{b \neq \text{ref}} \beta_b \cdot \text{Days}^{(b)}_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
Each \beta_b is the effect of replacing one day in the reference bin with one day in bin b. Both Park et al. (2020) and Ireland et al. (2023) use this to show damages that rise steeply at high temperatures.




Count Outcomes






TipCount Outcomes: Poisson Fixed Effects



For counts with many zeros (e.g., injury claims per postcode-day), use Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood with FE:
E[Y_{it} \mid \cdot] = \exp(\alpha_i + \tau D_{it} + X_{it}'\beta)

\tau is a semi-elasticity: 100 \cdot \tau ≈ percent change in Y per unit of D
Consistent even if the data are not Poisson, as long as the mean is correctly specified (Wooldridge 1999)
Groups with all-zero outcomes carry no information and are dropped automatically

title: Panel Data and Fixed Effects
text:
Simulation

Simulating the Bias and the Fix


Code
library(fixest)
setFixest_notes(FALSE)
set.seed(2026)

# Helper: "estimate (SE)" for the heat coefficient
heat_est <- function(m) {
  b <- coef(m)[grep("heat", names(coef(m)))][1]
  sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)", b, se(m)[names(b)])
}

N <- 1000   # students
n_t <- 4    # test sittings

# Long-run climate of each student's location (°F)
climate <- rnorm(N, mean = 65, sd = 5)

# Unobserved resources: lower in hotter places (the confounder)
alpha <- -0.05 * (climate - 65) + rnorm(N, 0, 0.3)

panel <- expand.grid(id = 1:N, t = 1:n_t)
year_shock <- c(0, 1.5, -1, 0.5)   # nationwide hot/cool years

panel$heat  <- climate[panel$id] + year_shock[panel$t] + rnorm(nrow(panel), 0, 1)
true_tau    <- -0.02
panel$score <- alpha[panel$id] + 0.1 * panel$t + true_tau * panel$heat +
               rnorm(nrow(panel), 0, 0.1)

# 1. Pooled OLS: confounded by alpha
m_pooled <- feols(score ~ heat + i(t), data = panel, cluster = ~id)

# 2. Unit fixed effects only
m_fe     <- feols(score ~ heat | id, data = panel, cluster = ~id)

# 3. Two-way fixed effects
m_twfe   <- feols(score ~ heat | id + t, data = panel, cluster = ~id)

# 4. First differences
panel    <- panel[order(panel$id, panel$t), ]
m_fd     <- feols(d(score) ~ d(heat), data = panel,
                  panel.id = ~id + t, cluster = ~id)

# Pooled OLS is over 3x too large. TWFE and FD recover the truth.
# Unit FE alone is slightly off: the year shocks happen to correlate with the score trend.
data.frame(
  model    = c("Pooled OLS", "Unit FE", "Two-way FE", "First differences"),
  estimate = sapply(list(m_pooled, m_fe, m_twfe, m_fd), heat_est),
  truth    = true_tau
)


              model         estimate truth
1        Pooled OLS -0.0693 (0.0018) -0.02
2           Unit FE -0.0256 (0.0016) -0.02
3        Two-way FE -0.0185 (0.0019) -0.02
4 First differences -0.0198 (0.0014) -0.02




Ask students to predict the sign of the pooled OLS bias before running it.
Note why the unit-FE-only model (m_fe) is also biased here: the nationwide year shocks are correlated with the time trend in scores. Adding year FE fixes this.
Then compare sd(panel$heat) (about 5°F) with the SD of heat after demeaning (about 0.9°F). This mirrors Park et al.’s point about residual variation.




Simulation: When FE Fails


Code
# Add a TIME-VARYING confounder: local economic shocks
# Bad economic years -> schools defer AC maintenance (more heat exposure)
#                    -> families have fewer resources (lower scores)
panel$econ_shock <- rnorm(nrow(panel), 0, 1)
panel$heat_ec    <- panel$heat - 0.8 * panel$econ_shock
panel$score_ec   <- alpha[panel$id] + 0.1 * panel$t + true_tau * panel$heat_ec +
                    0.05 * panel$econ_shock + rnorm(nrow(panel), 0, 0.1)

m_twfe_bad  <- feols(score_ec ~ heat_ec | id + t, data = panel, cluster = ~id)
m_twfe_ctrl <- feols(score_ec ~ heat_ec + econ_shock | id + t, data = panel,
                     cluster = ~id)

# FE cannot remove a confounder that varies within unit over time.
# Only measuring and controlling for it (or a better design) helps.
# This is why Park et al. control for county payroll in weather-exposed industries.
data.frame(
  model    = c("TWFE", "TWFE + econ_shock control"),
  estimate = sapply(list(m_twfe_bad, m_twfe_ctrl), heat_est),
  truth    = true_tau
)


                      model         estimate truth
1                      TWFE -0.0435 (0.0015) -0.02
2 TWFE + econ_shock control -0.0192 (0.0018) -0.02
