text:
Case Study 2: Experiments Inside Firms

Case Study 2: Generative AI and Software Developers






NoteCui, Demirer, Jaffe, Musolff, Peng & Salz (2026), Management Science (Cui et al. 2026)



Question: Does an AI coding assistant (GitHub Copilot) make professional software developers more productive?
The opportunity: three companies randomized access to Copilot “in the ordinary course of business”, to decide whether to adopt it, and shared the data.
Outcomes: from the companies’ version-control systems (GitHub): completed pull requests (units of finished work), commits, builds, and build success.




Case Study 2: Three Experiments, Three Designs






TipThe Same Question, Different Business Constraints













Microsoft
Accenture
Anonymous Fortune 100 firm




When
Sept 2022 – Apr 2023
Jul – Dec 2023
Sept – Oct 2023


Developers
1,746 (mainly US)
320 (Southeast Asia)
3,054


Randomized
Individuals and teams
Individuals
Teams


Design
Treatment vs. control
Treatment vs. control
Staggered: random order of access over six weeks


Encouragement
Email
Email, training, manager nudges
None







The designs differ across firms: Microsoft mixed individual and team randomization; at the anonymous firm every team was invited within about six weeks, and only the order of invitation was randomized.




Case Study 2: Results and Lessons






TipMain Findings




Pooling the three experiments (4,867 developers), using Copilot raises completed pull requests by 26.1% (standard error 10.3%); commits +13.6% and builds +38.4%
Each experiment on its own is noisy: many developer-weeks have zero pull requests
Newer developers were more likely to adopt the tool (82% vs. 72% for longer-tenured developers) and gained more









WarningLessons for Business Experiments




Firms’ decisions shape the design: encouragement rather than mandates; control groups that get access when the decision is made
Pooling several imperfect experiments can deliver a precise answer that none provides alone
Only about 60–70% of developers ever tried the tool, so the effect of access is much smaller than the effect of use. Chapter 5 shows how the authors handle this





Case Study 2: What to Copy






TipPractices to Reuse




Turn a business rollout into an experiment. When a permanent control group is unacceptable, randomize the order of access.
Use outcomes the systems already log. Pull requests, commits, and builds came straight from version control.
Run several experiments and pool them. Each was noisy; pooled, they give +26.1% (SE 10.3%).





Case Study 2: Discussion Questions


Why might a firm prefer a staggered rollout (everyone eventually treated, in random order) over a permanent control group?
Microsoft randomized some developers by team. What spillovers within teams might that design be guarding against?
“Pull requests completed” is the primary outcome. What could make it a misleading measure of productivity?
The lab study (Case 1) finds people follow faulty AI answers; the field study finds productivity gains. How can both be true?








NoteSuggested Answers (click to expand)






Everyone gets the tool within weeks, which is easier to justify to managers and staff, while the random order still creates a valid comparison between early and late groups during the rollout.
Developers in a team share code, review each other’s work, and divide tasks. A treated developer could pass on prompts or AI-written code, or take on different tasks, so untreated teammates would not be a clean control.
Pull requests vary in size and difficulty. AI could encourage more, smaller requests, or lower quality that shows up later as bugs or rework. Counts also ignore design, review, and mentoring work.
They measure different things in different settings. The lab study isolates reliance when the AI is wrong on reasoning puzzles; in real coding, suggestions are often right and errors can be caught by tests and review. Average gains can coexist with over-reliance on bad suggestions.

text:
Summary

Summary

text:

Practitioner Summary



Use it when: you have agreement to randomize and must decide where to run it, what to measure, and how to analyze it

Telling a manager: “We fixed the measure and the analysis before seeing any results, so this finding was not fished for.”

text:
Chapter 1 introduced the fundamental problem: we never see both potential outcomes for the same unit.
This chapter builds the language used in the rest of the notes: potential outcomes, estimands, the assumptions about treatments (SUTVA), assignment mechanisms, and causal diagrams for deciding what to control for.
The running example is a firm giving some customer-support agents access to a generative AI assistant.

title: Causal Inference Framework
text:
Potential Outcomes

The Running Example






NoteAn AI Assistant for Customer-Support Agents




Setting: the customer-support centre from the Chapter 1 case study. Agents answer customers’ questions in live chats.
Treatment: access to a generative AI assistant that reads each chat and suggests replies. Agents can accept, edit, or ignore the suggestions.
Outcome: tickets (customer issues) resolved per hour.
Question: how many more tickets per hour does an agent resolve with the assistant than without it?

We follow eight agents, from new to expert, through this chapter. Real studies of such tools find the largest gains for less experienced agents (Chapters 8 and 9), and the made-up numbers here follow that pattern.




Units, Treatments, Outcomes






NoteThe Ingredients of a Causal Question




Units i = 1, \dots, N: the entities affected (workers, households, firms, postcodes)
Treatment D_i: the intervention whose effect we want, e.g., access to an AI assistant (D_i = 1) or not (D_i = 0)
Outcome Y_i: what the intervention might change, e.g., tickets resolved per hour
Potential outcomes Y_i(1) and Y_i(0): the outcome unit i would have under each treatment
Unit-level effect \tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)









TipA Treatment Must Be Something We Could Change



“What is the effect of a worker’s experience?” is vague. “What is the effect of giving a worker six months of on-the-job training?” is a well-defined intervention with two clear potential outcomes. Precise policy questions start with a treatment that someone could actually manipulate.




A Potential Outcomes Table






NoteEight Support Agents (Made-Up Numbers)






Agent

Y_i(1): with AI
\tau_i

Average effect: \frac{1}{8}\sum_i \tau_i = +0.25 tickets per hour. Effects differ across agents, and in reality we only ever see one of the two outcome columns for each agent.




The pattern (larger gains for newer workers) mirrors the findings of Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond (2025), studied in Chapters 8 and 9.




What Happens When Managers Choose
The table shows both outcomes for every agent, which real data never do. We use it to see what an observed comparison would report under two ways of handing out the tool: managers give it to their four strongest agents (E–H), or a lottery picks four agents. Because we know the true average effect (0.25), we can check which comparison gets it right.


Code
po <- data.frame(
  worker = LETTERS[1:8],
  y0 = c(1.0, 1.2, 1.4, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2, 2.6, 2.8),
  y1 = c(1.6, 1.7, 1.8, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.6, 2.7)
)
ate <- mean(po$y1 - po$y0)

# Scenario 1: managers give AI to their four strongest agents
d_mgr <- as.integer(po$worker %in% c("E", "F", "G", "H"))
naive_mgr <- mean(po$y1[d_mgr == 1]) - mean(po$y0[d_mgr == 0])

# Scenario 2: AI assigned by lottery, repeated many times
set.seed(2026)
lottery <- replicate(10000, {
  d <- sample(rep(0:1, 4))
  mean(po$y1[d == 1]) - mean(po$y0[d == 0])
})

round(c(true_ATE = ate,
        managers_choose = naive_mgr,
        lottery_average = mean(lottery),
        lottery_sd = sd(lottery)), 3)


       true_ATE managers_choose lottery_average      lottery_sd 
          0.250           1.100           0.249           0.375 








TipReading the Result




Managers choose: agents E–H with the tool against agents A–D without it gives 1.10, more than four times the true 0.25. Most of the gap is the strong agents’ higher output even without AI, and they are the agents who gain least from it.
Lottery: averaged over 10,000 lotteries, the comparison gives 0.25, the true effect. With only eight agents, a single lottery can still miss by about 0.37 (the standard deviation). Chapter 3 deals with this chance variation.

title: Causal Inference Framework
text:
Estimands

Which Average Effect?






NoteCommon Estimands











Estimand
Definition
Policy question it answers




ATE (average treatment effect)
E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]
What if everyone got the treatment?


ATT (average treatment effect on the treated)
E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1]
Did the program help the people who actually received it?


ATC (average treatment effect on the controls, i.e. the untreated)
E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0]
What if we extended it to those not yet covered?


CATE (conditional average treatment effect)
E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid X_i = x]
Who benefits most? How should we target?











TipIn the AI Example



If managers give the tool to the experts (E–H), the ATT is +0.05, while the ATC (new and mid-level agents) is +0.45. Both are “the effect of AI”, and they differ by a factor of nine. Always say whose effect you are estimating.




Effects When Take-Up or Rules Matter






NoteThree More Estimands











Estimand
Definition
Policy question it answers




ITT (intent-to-treat effect)
E[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - E[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]
What happens if we offer the treatment, knowing not everyone will take it?


LATE (local average treatment effect)
E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid \text{complier}]
What does it do for people who take it only because they were offered it?


Effect at the cutoff
E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid X_i = c]
What would happen if we moved an eligibility threshold slightly?



Z_i is a random offer or assignment, which people may decline. Compliers are units that take the treatment if offered and not otherwise. X_i is a score, such as income or a test result, and c is the cutoff that decides eligibility.








TipIn the AI Example



The firm emails a random half of agents inviting them to use the tool, and some do not. The ITT is the effect of the email on resolutions per hour. The LATE is the effect of using the tool for agents who use it only because they got the email.




Estimands in Later Chapters






NoteMany Designs Recover a Specific, Local Effect











Design
What it recovers
Chapter




Randomized experiment
ATE; the ITT if not everyone takes up the treatment
3–5


Experiment with imperfect take-up, or an instrument
LATE
5–6

Effect at the cutoff
7


Panel fixed effects
A weighted average of unit-level effects, weighted towards units whose treatment varies most (a by-product of the estimator, not a chosen target)
8


Difference-in-differences
ATT, after treatment
9


Synthetic control
Effect for the treated unit (or few units), period by period
10


Regression, matching
ATE or ATT, depending on the method
11



A credible local effect is often more useful than a non-credible global one. But it should be described as what it is.

title: Causal Inference Framework
text:
Assumptions About the Treatment

SUTVA: No Interference






WarningOne Unit’s Treatment Must Not Change Another’s Outcome



The Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) has two parts. The first is no interference: Y_i depends only on D_i, not on D_j.
When it fails:

Vaccines: my vaccination protects you
Platforms and markets: an incentive that makes some ride-hail drivers work more lowers earnings for other drivers
Teams: if half a support team gets an AI assistant, the untreated half may receive harder tickets, or learn from treated colleagues
Information: treated households tell untreated neighbours about a program

Interference biases simple comparisons and changes what the estimand means. Designs that randomize whole clusters (teams, villages, markets) are one response (Chapter 5).




SUTVA: No Hidden Versions of Treatment






Warning“The Treatment” Must Mean One Thing



The second part: there is only one version of each treatment level.

“Health insurance” may mean Medicaid or a private plan with a high deductible
“An AI assistant” in 2021 (GPT-3) is not the same treatment as in 2025
“Training” delivered by an expert and by a novice trainer may have different effects

If versions differ, define the treatment more narrowly, or measure and analyze versions separately.








NoteAssignment Is Not Receipt



Being offered a treatment is not the same as taking it. Many evaluations randomize or study the offer (a letter, an invitation, eligibility). The effect of the offer is the intent-to-treat effect; the effect of actually taking the treatment requires extra assumptions (Chapters 5–6).

title: Causal Inference Framework
text:
The Assignment Mechanism

Why Assignment Is Everything






TipRecall the Decomposition from Chapter 1



E[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - E[Y_i \mid D_i = 0] = \text{ATT} + \underbrace{E[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] - E[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0]}_{\text{selection bias}}
Selection bias is zero when treatment is unrelated to untreated potential outcomes. Whether that holds depends entirely on how units came to be treated: the assignment mechanism.




Five Assignment Mechanisms






NoteHow Treatment Was Assigned Determines the Method











Assignment mechanism
Key condition
Methods




The researcher randomizes
(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp D_i
Experiments (Ch. 3–5)


An outside shock shifts treatment
The shock is as good as random and affects outcomes only through treatment
Instrumental variables (Ch. 6)


A rule based on a score
Treatment switches at a known cutoff c of a running variable
Regression discontinuity (Ch. 7)


Units choose, observed over time
Untreated outcomes evolve similarly, or confounders are fixed within units
Fixed effects, DiD, synthetic control (Ch. 8–10)


Units choose, observed once
(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp D_i \mid X_i, with overlap
Regression, matching (Ch. 11)

title: Causal Inference Framework
text:
Causal Diagrams

Drawing Your Assumptions






NoteThree Basic Structures



A causal diagram draws variables as nodes and causal effects as arrows. Three patterns matter most for deciding what to control for:









Structure
Picture
Example
Control for it?




Confounder
D \leftarrow X \rightarrow Y
Firm size drives both AI adoption and productivity
Yes: controlling for it blocks a non-causal (back-door) path


Mediator
D \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y
Insurance → doctor visits → health
No if you want the total effect


Collider
D \rightarrow C \leftarrow Y
AI adoption and productivity both make a firm “featured” in the press
No: conditioning on it creates bias







Good and Bad Controls






WarningControlling for More Is Not Always Better




Confounders measured before treatment: good controls
Mediators (affected by treatment): controlling for them removes part of the effect you want to measure
Colliders, including sample selection on an outcome-related variable: conditioning on them creates spurious associations
Pre-treatment variables that only predict the outcome: harmless, and they improve precision
Pre-treatment variables that only predict treatment (instrument-like): they add no bias protection, reduce precision, and can amplify bias from any remaining unmeasured confounder

The rule of thumb “only control for variables determined before treatment” avoids most mistakes, but not all: some pre-treatment variables are also bad controls (the instrument-like case above, and pre-treatment colliders, known as M-bias). Causal diagrams handle these cases (Cinelli et al. 2024).




Simulation: Collider Bias
A business magazine features firms that adopted AI or that are highly productive. Being featured is therefore a collider: AI adoption → featured ← productivity. In this simulation AI has no effect on productivity at all. We estimate its effect twice: across all firms, and only among featured firms, as a researcher would if the data came from magazine stories.


Code
set.seed(2026)
n <- 5000
ai_adoption  <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)          # randomly adopted: NO effect on productivity
productivity <- rnorm(n)

# A firm is "featured" in a business magazine if it adopted AI or is highly productive
featured <- (ai_adoption == 1 & runif(n) < 0.3) | productivity > 1

est_all      <- unname(coef(lm(productivity ~ ai_adoption))["ai_adoption"])
est_featured <- unname(coef(lm(productivity ~ ai_adoption, subset = featured))["ai_adoption"])
round(c(all_firms = est_all, featured_firms = est_featured), 2)


     all_firms featured_firms 
          0.01          -1.11 








TipReading the Result




All firms: 0.01, close to the true effect of zero.
Featured firms only: −1.11. A featured firm that did not adopt AI must have got in by being highly productive, while many adopters got in through AI alone with ordinary productivity. Among featured firms, AI therefore looks harmful, although it does nothing.
Lesson: do not control for, or select the sample on, a variable that both the treatment and the outcome affect. Firms in the news, firms that survived a crisis, and firms that published a case study are all selected this way.

title: Causal Inference Framework
text:
Identification, Estimation, Inference

Three Separate Questions
Every causal study has to get three things right, and each can fail on its own. Separating them tells you what kind of problem a study has, and whether more data would help.






TipKeep Them Apart












Question
What it asks
In the support-centre example
More data helps?




Identification
With unlimited data, would our comparison reveal the estimand?
When managers choose, comparing agents with and without the tool gives 1.10, not 0.25, however many agents we have. A lottery fixes this
No


Estimation
Which formula do we apply to the sample we have?
With lottery data, a difference in means, or a regression that adds baseline productivity to sharpen the estimate
Partly


Inference
How uncertain is the estimate?
With eight agents, one lottery can miss the true effect by about 0.37; a confidence interval reports this
Yes



Most disagreements about a study are about identification, and so are most of these notes. Estimation is the R code in each chapter. Inference covers standard errors, clustering, and randomization inference (Chapters 3 and 8).




Summary


A causal effect compares potential outcomes for the same unit; only one is ever observed
Estimands (ATE, ATT, ATC, CATE, LATE, local effects) answer different policy questions; say which one you target
SUTVA requires no interference and a single, well-defined version of treatment
The assignment mechanism determines whether a comparison is biased, and which method fits
Causal diagrams clarify which variables to control for: confounders yes; mediators and colliders no
Separate identification from estimation and inference




Next Steps


Read: Holland (1986); Cinelli et al. (2024)
Practice: In the eight-agent simulation, let managers give AI to the four newest agents. Is the naive comparison now too high or too low? Why?
Think: For a policy you know well, write down the treatment, the outcome, the estimand, and the assignment mechanism
Next Class: Randomized experiments: design and inference (Chapter 3)




References


Cinelli, Carlos, Andrew Forney, and Judea Pearl. 2024. “A Crash Course in Good and Bad Controls.” Sociological Methods & Research 53 (3): 1071–104. https://doi.org/10.1177/00491241221099552.


Holland, Paul W. 1986. “Statistics and Causal Inference.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 81 (396): 945–60. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1986.10478354.

All firms: 0.01, close to the true effect of zero.
Featured firms only: −1.11. A featured firm that did not adopt AI must have got in by being highly productive, while many adopters got in through AI alone with ordinary productivity. Among featured firms, AI therefore looks harmful, although it does nothing.
Lesson: do not control for, or select the sample on, a variable that both the treatment and the outcome affect. Firms in the news, firms that survived a crisis, and firms that published a case study are all selected this way.

title: Causal Inference Framework
text:
Three Separate Questions
Every causal study has to get three things right, and each can fail on its own. Separating them tells you what kind of problem a study has, and whether more data would help.






Keep Them Apart











Question
What it asks
In the support-centre example
More data helps?




Identification
With unlimited data, would our comparison reveal the estimand?
When managers choose, comparing agents with and without the tool gives 1.10, not 0.25, however many agents we have. A lottery fixes this
No


Estimation
Which formula do we apply to the sample we have?
With lottery data, a difference in means, or a regression that adds baseline productivity to sharpen the estimate
Partly


Inference
How uncertain is the estimate?
With eight agents, one lottery can miss the true effect by about 0.37; a confidence interval reports this
Yes



Most disagreements about a study are about identification, and so are most of these notes. Estimation is the R code in each chapter. Inference covers standard errors, clustering, and randomization inference (Chapters 3 and 8).

title: Causal Inference Framework
text:
Summary

A causal effect compares potential outcomes for the same unit; only one is ever observed
Estimands (ATE, ATT, ATC, CATE, LATE, local effects) answer different policy questions; say which one you target
SUTVA requires no interference and a single, well-defined version of treatment
The assignment mechanism determines whether a comparison is biased, and which method fits
Causal diagrams clarify which variables to control for: confounders yes; mediators and colliders no
Separate identification from estimation and inference

title: Causal Inference for Policy Evaluation
text:
Policy evaluation asks whether a program, regulation, or intervention actually changed the outcomes it was designed to change, and by how much. Answering that question means comparing what happened with what would have happened without the policy: a counterfactual we never observe directly.
These open lecture notes cover the modern toolkit for that comparison. It starts from the potential outcomes framework and randomized experiments, including what goes wrong in real experiments (non-compliance, attrition, spillovers). It then works through designs in which the researcher does not control assignment: instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, panel methods (fixed effects, difference-in-differences, synthetic control), and regression and matching, before closing with how to combine designs and evidence. Each chapter is available as a web page and as in-class slides, with worked R code and case studies from published research.

title: Causal Inference for Policy Evaluation
text:
Who These Notes Are For
These notes are for analysts who evaluate policies and business decisions in government, insurance, banking, and industry, and for graduate students in business and economics who are learning to do so.
The chapters follow the way an evaluation is planned. Each part starts from how treatment was assigned, and the flowchart below points to the relevant chapter. Each method chapter opens with a one-page summary for practitioners: when the method applies, the data it needs, the assumption it rests on, the checks to run, the R code, and how to explain the result to a manager. The methods are then applied to recent studies from leading journals in economics, finance, insurance, information systems, and operations management, several of them on generative AI at work, and each case study ends with the practices worth reusing. Simulations with a known true effect show what each method recovers, and three chapters repeat the analysis on real public data. Derivations are kept short in the main text, with fuller versions in optional sections.

title: Causal Inference for Policy Evaluation
text:
How the Notes Are Organized
The notes are organized around one question: who or what decided who was treated? Each part covers a different answer, moving from designs where the researcher controls assignment, through designs that exploit a known source of variation (a shock, a rule, timing), to designs that rely only on measured characteristics.

title: Causal Inference for Policy Evaluation
text:
Methods at a Glance
Every method below answers the same question: what would have happened without the policy? They differ in which assumption does the work, and in whose effect they recover.
For a worked example, the case study in Chapter 1 applies every method to one simulated customer-support centre, with plots, and compares each estimate with the true effect.


Main methods for causal policy evaluation










Method
Core idea
Key identifying assumption
What it estimates
Main limitations
Chapters




Randomized controlled trial (RCT)
Researcher randomly assigns treatment, so treated and control groups are comparable on everything, observed or not
Random assignment; excludability; no interference between units
Average treatment effect (ATE), or intent-to-treat (ITT) effect
Costly, sometimes unethical or infeasible; external validity; non-compliance, attrition and spillovers can break the design
3–5


Instrumental variables (IV)
Use a variable that shifts treatment but affects the outcome only through treatment
Instrument relevance; exclusion restriction; independence; monotonicity (no defiers)
Local average treatment effect (LATE) for compliers
Exclusion restriction is untestable; weak instruments; LATE may not generalize beyond compliers
6


Regression discontinuity (RDD)
Compare units just above and just below a cutoff that determines treatment
Potential outcomes continuous at the cutoff; no precise manipulation of the running variable
Effect for units at the cutoff
Local to the cutoff; needs many observations near it; sensitive to bandwidth and functional form
7


Panel data / fixed effects
Compare each unit with itself over time
Strict exogeneity: no time-varying confounders and no feedback from past outcomes
Variance-weighted average of within-unit effects
Time-varying confounders remain; measurement error amplified; needs within-unit variation; cannot estimate effects of time-invariant traits
8


Difference-in-differences (DiD)
Compare the change over time in treated units with the change in untreated units
Parallel trends in the absence of treatment; no anticipation
Average treatment effect on the treated (ATT)
Parallel trends untestable after treatment; two-way FE biased with staggered adoption and heterogeneous effects; serially correlated errors
9


Synthetic control
Build a weighted combination of untreated units that tracks the treated unit before treatment
Pre-treatment fit carries over to the post-treatment counterfactual; no spillovers to donor units
Effect for one or a few treated units, over time
Needs a long pre-treatment period and good fit; few treated units; inference relies on placebo/permutation tests
10


Regression / covariate adjustment
Compare treated and untreated units with the same observed characteristics
Selection on observables (no unmeasured confounders); correct functional form
A weighted average of effects across covariate values (the ATE if effects are constant or the model is fully interacted)
Cannot handle unobserved confounders; extrapolates where groups do not overlap
3, 11


Matching / propensity scores
Pair each treated unit with similar untreated units, or reweight by the probability of treatment
Selection on observables; overlap (common support)
ATT or ATE
Same blind spot for unobservables as regression; poor overlap; results sensitive to specification
11

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Policies Rest on Causal Claims






Every Policy Embeds a Causal Claim



Expanding public health insurance will reduce deaths among low-income adults
Giving workers a generative AI assistant will raise productivity
Subsidizing insurance premiums will increase take-up
Higher credit limits will increase borrowing and stimulate spending

Each claim is about what would happen with the policy compared with what would happen without it.









What Policy Evaluation Asks



Did it work? Is there an effect at all?
How much? Is the effect large enough to matter relative to cost?
For whom? Who gains, who loses, and who is unaffected?
Why? Through which mechanism?
Would it work elsewhere? At a larger scale, in another country, for another population?

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Three Kinds of Questions






Data Can Answer Different Questions










Type
Example (insurance)
What it needs




Description
What share of adults have no health insurance?
Good measurement and sampling


Prediction
Which policyholders are likely to lodge a claim next year?
Patterns that hold in new data


Causation
Would a premium subsidy make uninsured people buy cover?
A counterfactual: what happens with vs. without the subsidy












Prediction Is Not Causation


A model can predict claims very well using variables that do not cause claims (postcode, car colour, the time of day a quote is requested). Machine learning models and LLMs are excellent prediction engines. A policy question, however, asks what would happen if we changed something. That is a causal question, and good prediction does not answer it.
These notes are about causal questions.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Potential Outcomes






Two Outcomes, Only One Observed


For each person i and a treatment D_i \in \{0, 1\} (e.g., having health insurance):

Y_i(1): the outcome if person i is treated
Y_i(0): the outcome if person i is not treated
The causal effect for person i is Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)

We observe only one of the two: Y_i = D_i \, Y_i(1) + (1 - D_i) \, Y_i(0).
The other one, the counterfactual, is missing for everyone. This is the fundamental problem of causal inference (Holland 1986).









The Way Forward: Averages


We cannot learn individual effects, but we can learn average effects, such as the average treatment effect (ATE) E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)], if we can find a group whose outcomes stand in for the missing counterfactual. Every method in these notes is a different way of finding that group. Chapter 2 develops the framework formally.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Estimand, Estimator, Estimate






Three Words Worth Keeping Apart



Estimand: the quantity we want to know, defined with potential outcomes. Example: the average effect of being sent a letter encouraging insurance enrollment on two-year mortality, among previously uninsured adults aged 45–64: E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)] in that population, where treatment is receiving the letter
Estimator: the recipe we apply to data. Example: the difference in mean two-year mortality between people randomly sent and not sent the letter
Estimate: the number the recipe produces in our sample. Example: a fall of about 0.06 percentage points (Chapter 3)

A design is credible when its estimator recovers the estimand under assumptions we can defend. A precise estimate of the wrong estimand is still wrong.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Why Naive Comparisons Fail






Comparing the Insured with the Uninsured


The naive comparison of mortality between insured and uninsured people decomposes into two terms:
\underbrace{E[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - E[Y_i \mid D_i = 0]}_{\text{observed difference}} = \underbrace{E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1]}_{\text{effect on the treated}} + \underbrace{E[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] - E[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0]}_{\text{selection bias}}
Selection bias is the difference the two groups would have had even without insurance.

People who expect high medical costs are more likely to buy insurance (adverse selection): selection bias pushes towards insurance looking harmful
People with higher income and education are more likely to be insured and are healthier anyway: selection bias pushes towards insurance looking helpful

Without a design, we cannot know which force dominates, or by how much.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Simulation Design






Insurance and Mortality in Two Worlds



People: 100,000 adults, each with an underlying health risk. The researcher does not observe it.
Without insurance: a person’s annual chance of dying (in percent) is 1.5 + 0.8 × risk, so sicker people die more often.
With insurance: that chance falls by 0.3 percentage points, or less for the few people already close to zero. The true average effect is therefore about −0.29.
Observational world: the sicker a person is, the more likely they are to buy insurance (adverse selection).
Experimental world: a coin flip decides who is insured.

In each world we compare the death rates of the insured and the uninsured.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
section: Simulation: Selection Bias Can Flip the Sign
text:
Simulation: Selection Bias Can Flip the Sign


Code
set.seed(2026)
n <- 100000

# Underlying health risk (higher = sicker); unobserved by the researcher
risk <- rnorm(n)

# Potential outcomes: annual probability of death (in percent)
y0 <- pmax(0, 1.5 + 0.8 * risk)          # without insurance
y1 <- pmax(0, y0 - 0.3)                  # insurance lowers mortality by up to 0.3 pp

# Observational world: sicker people are more likely to buy insurance
d_obs <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(1.5 * risk))
naive <- mean(ifelse(d_obs == 1, y1, y0)[d_obs == 1]) -
         mean(ifelse(d_obs == 1, y1, y0)[d_obs == 0])

# Experimental world: a coin flip decides who is insured
d_rct <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
y_rct <- ifelse(d_rct == 1, y1, y0)
rct <- mean(y_rct[d_rct == 1]) - mean(y_rct[d_rct == 0])

# The two terms from the previous slide
att <- mean((y1 - y0)[d_obs == 1])                          # effect on the insured
selection <- mean(y0[d_obs == 1]) - mean(y0[d_obs == 0])    # selection bias

round(c(true_ATE = mean(y1 - y0), naive_comparison = naive, ATT = att,
        selection_bias = selection, randomized = rct), 3)


        true_ATE naive_comparison              ATT   selection_bias 
          -0.286            0.536           -0.299            0.835 
      randomized 
          -0.287 








Reading the Result


In the observational world the insured die more often, so insurance looks harmful (+0.54 percentage points). That gap is the effect on the insured (−0.30) plus selection bias (+0.83), because sicker people bought insurance. The coin flip balances risk across the two groups, and the comparison recovers the true effect (−0.29).





The naive comparison says insurance raises mortality, because the insured are sicker to begin with. Randomization removes the selection term and recovers the true protective effect.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Other Ways Correlations Mislead






Six Traps










Trap
What it means
Example




Confounding
A third factor drives both the treatment and the outcome, so the two move together even if the treatment does nothing
Larger, better-managed firms are more likely to adopt AI tools and are more productive anyway


Reverse causality
The outcome, or what predicts it, causes the treatment
Struggling workers are given AI tools because they are struggling, so AI users look less productive


Controlling for a mechanism
Adjusting for something the treatment itself changes removes part of the effect you want to measure
Insurance improves health partly through more doctor visits; holding visits fixed hides that channel


Reversion to the mean
Units picked for an extreme value tend to move back towards average next time, with or without any intervention
Drivers enrolled in a safety program after an unusually bad year file fewer claims the next year anyway


Selection into the sample
The data contain only units that passed a filter related to the outcome
Studying only firms that survived a crisis hides the ones the crisis destroyed


Searching and selective reporting
Trying many analyses and reporting only the significant ones produces chance findings
With 20 outcomes tested, about one will be “significant” at 5% by chance alone

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Internal and External Validity






Two Kinds of Validity



Internal validity: is the estimate right for the people, place, and time studied?
External validity: does it carry over to other populations, places, or scales?

Strong designs often buy internal validity with a narrow setting (one firm, one state, units near a cutoff). Keep both in view.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Who Decided Who Was Treated?






The Question That Organizes These Notes


Every method finds a counterfactual by exploiting how treatment was assigned. The notes move from designs where the researcher controls assignment, through designs that exploit a known source of variation (a shock, a rule, timing), to designs that rely only on measured characteristics:









Who or what decided treatment?
Where the counterfactual comes from
Method
Part · Ch.




The researcher
A lottery
Randomized experiment
II · 3–5


An outside shock
Units nudged into treatment by something unrelated to outcomes
Instrumental variables
III · 6


A rule
Units just on the other side of the cutoff
Regression discontinuity
IV · 7


The units, observed over time
The same units before treatment, or the change in untreated units
Fixed effects, DiD, synthetic control
V · 8–10


The units, observed once
Similar units, compared on observed characteristics
Regression, matching
VI · 11

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Choosing a Design



Walk through the five questions left to right. Each “no” moves to a design with less control over assignment; the final step relies on the strongest untestable assumption, that every confounder is measured.
This is a starting point, not a rule. Strong evaluations often combine designs (Chapter 12).

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Moving Between Methods






When One Design Runs Into Trouble










Situation
Move to
Why




An experiment where not everyone takes up the treatment
IV (Ch. 5–6)
Random assignment is an instrument for take-up


A cutoff rule that is not followed exactly
Fuzzy RDD = IV at the cutoff (Ch. 6–7)
Crossing the cutoff shifts the probability of treatment


An instrument that is weak or hard to defend, but you have panel data
Fixed effects or DiD (Ch. 8–9)
Use changes within units instead


Treated and comparison groups differ in levels
Fixed effects or DiD (Ch. 8–9)
Fixed differences cancel out


Policy adopted at different times by different units
Heterogeneity-robust DiD (Ch. 9)
Static two-way fixed effects can mislead


Only one or a few treated units, no single good comparison
Synthetic control (Ch. 10)
Build a comparison from a weighted mix


Parallel trends plausible only for similar units
DiD with matching or reweighting (Ch. 9, 11)
Compare like with like, then difference

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
The Credibility Revolution






Design Before Estimation


Over the past three decades, empirical economics and management research shifted from “control for everything and hope” to research design: a clear source of variation in treatment that is plausibly as good as random (Angrist and Pischke 2010).
What that means in practice:

State the comparison that identifies the effect, in plain language
Make the identifying assumption explicit
Show evidence for it (balance, pre-trends, placebo tests, first stages)
Report robustness, and state what the design cannot rule out

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
The Setting






A Customer-Support Centre


A software firm runs a customer-support centre. Its agents resolve about two customer issues per hour. The firm wants to know whether a generative AI assistant raises that number.
The data on the next slides are simulated, so we know the true answer: the assistant adds 0.3 resolutions per hour for every agent.
Each slide tells a different story about who got the assistant. The question stays the same. The assignment changes, and so does the method that can answer the question.
In every story, a simple comparison gives the wrong answer. By a simple (or naive) comparison we mean the obvious one: agents with the tool against agents without it, or output after against output before, ignoring how the tool was assigned.





This is an illustrative case with simulated data. The method chapters use published studies; this one keeps the setting fixed so that only the assignment mechanism changes.
The setting echoes the generative AI study of customer-support agents in Chapters 8 and 9, but every number here is made up.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 1: Randomized Experiment
The firm considers two ways to roll out the tool. Plan A: managers choose who gets it, and they tend to pick their strongest agents. Plan B: a lottery decides. The plot compares the two plans.


Code
suppressMessages(library(fixest))
f2 <- function(x) sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", x))   # format estimates
blue <- "#1565c0"; orange <- "#c2410c"; grey <- "grey55"
tau <- 0.3                                                # true effect

set.seed(11)
n <- 2000
skill <- rnorm(n)                                         # unobserved by the analyst
y0 <- 2.0 + 0.3 * skill + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)                # resolutions per hour without AI
pick <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(1.5 * skill))                 # managers pick stronger agents
y_pick <- y0 + tau * pick
naive_pick <- mean(y_pick[pick == 1]) - mean(y_pick[pick == 0])

lottery <- sample(rep(0:1, n / 2))                        # the alternative: a lottery
y_rct <- y0 + tau * lottery
rct <- mean(y_rct[lottery == 1]) - mean(y_rct[lottery == 0])

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(skill[pick == 0], breaks = 30, col = adjustcolor(grey, 0.5), border = NA, xlim = c(-3.5, 3.5),
     main = "Plan A: who got the tool, by skill", xlab = "Skill (unobserved)")
hist(skill[pick == 1], breaks = 30, col = adjustcolor(blue, 0.5), border = NA, add = TRUE)
legend("topleft", c("No tool", "Tool"), fill = adjustcolor(c(grey, blue), 0.5), border = NA, bty = "n")
barplot(c("Plan A (managers)" = naive_pick, "Plan B (lottery)" = rct), col = c(grey, blue), border = NA, ylim = c(0, 0.7),
        main = "Estimated effect", ylab = "Resolutions per hour")
abline(h = tau, col = orange, lty = 2, lwd = 2)

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 1: Randomized Experiment (continued)






How the Method Fits the Story



Plan A, managers choose (simple comparison): comparing agents with the tool against agents without it gives 0.61. Too high, because the chosen agents were stronger to begin with (left panel).
Plan B, a lottery (randomized experiment): chance decides who gets the tool, so both groups have the same mix of skill, measured or not. Their difference is the effect: 0.31.
The lottery is the better design. It needs no assumption beyond the randomization being carried out as planned, and treated agents not affecting untreated ones.
Timing matters: a lottery is only possible before the rollout. If managers have already chosen, see Designs 4 and 7.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 2: Instrumental Variables
Use of the tool is voluntary. The firm emails a random half of agents encouraging them to try it. Motivated agents use it more, with or without the email.


Code
set.seed(12)
n_iv <- 8000
email <- rbinom(n_iv, 1, 0.5)                             # randomized encouragement
motiv <- rnorm(n_iv)                                      # unobserved motivation
use <- rbinom(n_iv, 1, plogis(qlogis(0.2) + (qlogis(0.6) - qlogis(0.2)) * email + 1.2 * motiv))
y_iv <- 2.0 + 0.25 * motiv + rnorm(n_iv, 0, 0.3) + tau * use
first <- mean(use[email == 1]) - mean(use[email == 0])    # first stage
itt <- mean(y_iv[email == 1]) - mean(y_iv[email == 0])    # reduced form
as_treated <- mean(y_iv[use == 1]) - mean(y_iv[use == 0])
iv <- itt / first

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
barplot(tapply(use, email, mean), names.arg = c("No email", "Email"), col = c(grey, blue), border = NA,
        ylim = c(0, 0.8), main = "Share using the tool", ylab = "Share")
barplot(tapply(y_iv, email, mean), names.arg = c("No email", "Email"), col = c(grey, blue), border = NA,
        ylim = c(1.8, 2.3), xpd = FALSE, main = "Resolutions per hour", ylab = "Mean")

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 2: Instrumental Variables (continued)






How the Method Fits the Story



Simple comparison: agents who used the tool against those who did not: 0.51. Too high, because motivated agents both use it more and resolve more.
Instrumental variables: the email is random, so compare agents who got it with those who did not. It raised use by 0.33 and output by 0.10. Output rose only because use rose, so the effect of using the tool is 0.10 ÷ 0.33 = 0.31.
Relies on: the email changing output only through use of the tool.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 3: Regression Discontinuity
The firm gives the tool to agents who scored below 70 on a skills test.


Code
set.seed(13)
score <- runif(n, 40, 100)
below <- as.integer(score < 70)                           # the rule
y_rd <- 1.0 + 0.015 * score + tau * below + rnorm(n, 0, 0.15)
naive_rd <- mean(y_rd[below == 1]) - mean(y_rd[below == 0])
near <- abs(score - 70) < 10                              # local linear fit within 10 points
rdd <- unname(coef(lm(y_rd ~ below * I(score - 70), subset = near))["below"])

bins <- cut(score, seq(40, 100, 2.5))
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(tapply(score, bins, mean), tapply(y_rd, bins, mean), pch = 19,
     col = ifelse(tapply(score, bins, mean) < 70, blue, grey),
     xlab = "Test score", ylab = "Resolutions per hour")
for (side in 0:1) {
  s <- if (side == 1) score < 70 & near else score >= 70 & near
  fit <- lm(y_rd[s] ~ score[s]); xs <- range(score[s])
  lines(xs, coef(fit)[1] + coef(fit)[2] * xs, lwd = 3, col = if (side == 1) blue else grey)
}
abline(v = 70, col = orange, lty = 2)

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 3: Regression Discontinuity (continued)






How the Method Fits the Story



Simple comparison: everyone below 70 against everyone above: −0.14, the wrong sign, because low scorers are weaker agents.
Regression discontinuity: agents scoring 69 and 71 are almost equally skilled; only the tool differs. The jump in output at 70 is the effect: 0.33.
Relies on: nothing else changing at 70, and agents being unable to game their score.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 4: Panel Fixed Effects
Managers again give the tool to their strongest agents, at different months. We see every agent’s monthly output for a year.


Code
set.seed(14)
na <- 300
sk <- rnorm(na)
gets <- rbinom(na, 1, plogis(1.5 * sk))                   # stronger agents get the tool
start <- ifelse(gets == 1, sample(4:9, na, replace = TRUE), Inf)
fe <- expand.grid(agent = 1:na, month = 1:12)
fe$tool <- as.integer(fe$month >= start[fe$agent])
fe$y <- 2.0 + 0.3 * sk[fe$agent] + tau * fe$tool + rnorm(nrow(fe), 0, 0.2)
pooled <- unname(coef(lm(y ~ tool, fe))["tool"])
fe_est <- unname(coef(feols(y ~ tool | agent + month, fe))["tool"])

treated <- which(gets == 1)[1:30]
before <- sapply(treated, function(a) mean(fe$y[fe$agent == a & fe$tool == 0]))
after <- sapply(treated, function(a) mean(fe$y[fe$agent == a & fe$tool == 1]))
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0.8, 2.2), ylim = range(before, after), xaxt = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "Resolutions per hour")
axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = c("Before the tool", "After the tool"))
segments(1, before, 2, after, col = adjustcolor(blue, 0.5), lwd = 2)
points(rep(1, 30), before, pch = 19, col = grey); points(rep(2, 30), after, pch = 19, col = blue)

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 4: Panel Fixed Effects (continued)






How the Method Fits the Story



Simple comparison: months with the tool against months without, pooling all agents: 0.52. Too high, because the agents with the tool are the stronger ones.
Fixed effects: compare each agent with themselves before and after getting the tool (each line in the plot), so permanent skill differences cancel. The average change is 0.29.
Relies on: nothing else changing for an agent at the time they got the tool.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 5: Difference-in-Differences
Office A switches the tool on in month 7; office B never does. Output is rising in both offices for other reasons.


Code
set.seed(15)
did <- expand.grid(office = c("A", "B"), month = 1:12, agent = 1:400)
did$tool <- as.integer(did$office == "A" & did$month >= 7)
did$y <- ifelse(did$office == "A", 2.0, 1.8) + 0.03 * did$month + tau * did$tool + rnorm(nrow(did), 0, 0.25)
m <- tapply(did$y, list(did$office, did$month >= 7), mean)
before_after <- m["A", "TRUE"] - m["A", "FALSE"]
did_est <- before_after - (m["B", "TRUE"] - m["B", "FALSE"])

path <- tapply(did$y, list(did$office, did$month), mean)
counterfactual <- path["A", 6] + (path["B", ] - path["B", 6])
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
matplot(1:12, t(path), type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 3, col = c(blue, grey), xlab = "Month", ylab = "Resolutions per hour")
lines(6:12, counterfactual[6:12], lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = blue)
abline(v = 6.5, col = orange, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("Office A", "Office B", "Office A without the tool (implied)"),
       col = c(blue, grey, blue), lty = c(1, 1, 2), lwd = c(3, 3, 2), bty = "n")

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 5: Difference-in-Differences (continued)






How the Method Fits the Story



Simple comparison: office A after against before: 0.49. Too high, because it includes the rise that would have happened anyway.
Difference-in-differences: office B’s change over the same months (0.16) shows that rise. Subtracting it leaves the effect: 0.33. The dashed line is office A without the tool.
Relies on: office A following office B’s trend had it not adopted (parallel trends).

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 6: Synthetic Control
Only the Manila office adopts, in month 13. Offices differ in how fast their output grows.


Code
set.seed(16)
J <- 12; T0 <- 12; TT <- 24
load <- c(1.6, runif(J, 0.2, 2))                          # exposure to a growing trend; Manila first
trend <- seq(0, 1, length.out = TT)
Y <- t(sapply(1:(J + 1), function(i) 2.0 + rnorm(1, 0, 0.08) * (i > 1) + load[i] * trend + rnorm(TT, 0, 0.02)))
Y[1, (T0 + 1):TT] <- Y[1, (T0 + 1):TT] + tau               # Manila gets the tool in month 13

sc_weights <- function(y1, Y0) {                          # non-negative weights that sum to one
  loss <- function(a) { w <- exp(a) / sum(exp(a)); sum((y1 - colSums(w * Y0))^2) }
  a <- optim(rep(0, nrow(Y0)), loss, method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 2000))$par
  exp(a) / sum(exp(a))
}
w <- sc_weights(Y[1, 1:T0], Y[-1, 1:T0])
synth <- colSums(w * Y[-1, ])
post <- (T0 + 1):TT
sc_est <- mean(Y[1, post] - synth[post])
did_avg <- (mean(Y[1, post]) - mean(Y[1, 1:T0])) - (mean(colMeans(Y[-1, post])) - mean(colMeans(Y[-1, 1:T0])))

par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(1:TT, Y[1, ], type = "l", lwd = 3, col = blue, ylim = range(Y[1, ], synth, colMeans(Y[-1, ])),
     xlab = "Month", ylab = "Resolutions per hour")
lines(1:TT, synth, lwd = 3, lty = 2, col = blue)
lines(1:TT, colMeans(Y[-1, ]), lwd = 2, lty = 3, col = grey)
abline(v = T0 + 0.5, col = orange, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("Manila", "Synthetic Manila", "Average of other offices"),
       col = c(blue, blue, grey), lty = c(1, 2, 3), lwd = c(3, 3, 2), bty = "n")

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 6: Synthetic Control (continued)






How the Method Fits the Story



Simple comparison: difference-in-differences against the average of the other offices: 0.59. Too high, because Manila was growing faster than the average office.
Synthetic control: build a “synthetic Manila”: a weighted mix of offices chosen to match Manila’s path in months 1–12. After month 13, the gap between Manila and its synthetic version is the effect: 0.30.
Relies on: the mix that tracked Manila before month 13 continuing to track it.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 7: Regression and Matching
Managers give the tool mostly to experienced agents, and experience raises output. We observe each agent’s tenure.


Code
set.seed(17)
tenure <- sample(1:4, n, replace = TRUE)                  # years on the job (observed)
tool_t <- rbinom(n, 1, c(0.15, 0.35, 0.65, 0.85)[tenure]) # more experienced, more likely to get it
y_t <- 1.6 + 0.2 * tenure + tau * tool_t + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)
naive_t <- mean(y_t[tool_t == 1]) - mean(y_t[tool_t == 0])
reg_t <- unname(coef(lm(y_t ~ tool_t + factor(tenure)))["tool_t"])
gaps <- sapply(1:4, function(k) mean(y_t[tool_t == 1 & tenure == k]) - mean(y_t[tool_t == 0 & tenure == k]))
match_t <- sum(gaps * tabulate(tenure[tool_t == 1], 4)) / sum(tool_t)   # exact matching on tenure

mt <- tapply(y_t, list(tool_t, tenure), mean)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
matplot(1:4, t(mt), type = "b", pch = 19, lty = 1, lwd = 3, col = c(grey, blue), xaxt = "n",
        xlab = "Years of tenure", ylab = "Resolutions per hour")
axis(1, at = 1:4)
legend("topleft", c("No tool", "Tool"), col = c(grey, blue), lwd = 3, pch = 19, bty = "n")

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Design 7: Regression and Matching (continued)






How the Method Fits the Story



Simple comparison: agents with the tool against agents without it: 0.53. Too high, because experienced agents resolve more anyway.
Regression and matching: compare agents with the same tenure (the gap within each tenure group in the plot), then average: 0.29 by regression, 0.28 by matching.
Relies on: tenure being the only thing managers used. If they also used something unobserved, such as skill in Design 1, this would fail.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Comparing the Estimates


Code
res <- data.frame(
  design = c("1 Randomized experiment", "2 Instrumental variables", "3 Regression discontinuity",
             "4 Fixed effects", "5 Difference-in-differences", "6 Synthetic control", "7 Regression / matching"),
  naive  = c(naive_pick, as_treated, naive_rd, pooled, before_after, did_avg, naive_t),
  design_est = c(rct, iv, rdd, fe_est, did_est, sc_est, reg_t))
par(mar = c(4, 13, 1, 1))
plot(res$naive, 7:1, xlim = c(-0.2, 0.7), pch = 1, cex = 1.6, col = grey, yaxt = "n", ylab = "",
     xlab = "Estimated effect (resolutions per hour)")
points(res$design_est, 7:1, pch = 19, cex = 1.6, col = blue)
axis(2, at = 7:1, labels = res$design, las = 1)
abline(v = tau, col = orange, lty = 2, lwd = 2); abline(v = 0, col = "grey85")
legend("topleft", c("Simple comparison", "Design-based estimate", "Truth"),
       pch = c(1, 19, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, 2), col = c(grey, blue, orange), bty = "n")









Why the Estimates Agree Here


The tool has the same effect for every agent, so every design recovers 0.3. With real data, effects differ across people, and each design recovers the effect for a different group: everyone (experiment), agents who use the tool because of the email (IV), agents near the cutoff (RDD), or the offices and agents that were treated (DiD, synthetic control). The chapters return to this point.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
The Plan of These Notes
Part I: Foundations: what a causal effect is, and how treatment gets assigned
Part II: Randomized Experiments: the researcher assigns treatment; design, practice, and what goes wrong
Part III: Instrumental Variables: an outside shock shifts treatment; from randomized offers to natural instruments
Part IV: Regression Discontinuity: a rule assigns treatment at a cutoff
Part V: Panel Methods: units choose, but we see them over time; fixed effects, DiD, synthetic control
Part VI: Selection on Observables: units choose, and we observe them once; regression and matching
Part VII: Synthesis: combining designs, accumulating evidence, and reporting

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
LLMs as Research Tools






Measuring Variables with LLMs


LLMs are also increasingly used to measure variables, such as classifying text or rating job tasks. A measured variable is only as good as its validation: measurement error in a treatment variable biases estimates (Chapter 8 shows how fixed effects make this worse).

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Six Questions for Any Evaluation






Use These for Any Evaluation You Read or Design



Question: What is the causal effect of what, on what, for whom?
Estimand: Is the target an ATE, an effect on the treated, or a local effect (compliers, units at a cutoff)?
Identification: What comparison identifies the effect, and what assumption makes it valid?
Threats: What would break that assumption in this setting?
Evidence: How do the authors test or defend the assumption?
External validity: Would the result hold in another place, time, or population?

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Ethics in Policy Evaluation






Evaluations Involve Real People



Informed consent and institutional review: ethics board approval, and registration in a public trial registry
Equipoise: randomizing is easier to justify when we genuinely do not know whether the policy helps, or when resources are limited and must be rationed anyway
Privacy: linking survey, tax, health, and death records requires secure facilities and disclosure review
Distribution: average effects can hide harm to specific groups; check heterogeneity
Complete reporting: pre-registration, pre-analysis plans, and reporting null results

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Software and Code






Working with the Code in These Notes



All examples use R; the packages used are fixest (fixed effects, IV, DiD, event studies), rdrobust and rddensity (regression discontinuity), did (staggered DiD), Synth (synthetic control), and MatchIt (matching)
Simulations with made-up data and a known true effect show whether each method recovers it; real datasets that ship with these packages (minimum wages, the Basque Country, the LaLonde (1986) job-training data) show the methods at work
Code is folded by default in both the lecture notes and the slides; click “Code” to expand it

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Summary

Policy evaluation asks what would have happened without the policy
Individual causal effects are never observed; we estimate averages using a comparison group
Naive comparisons mix the causal effect with selection bias, which can even flip the sign
Each method in these notes finds the counterfactual in a different place: chance, an outside shock, a cutoff, time, a synthetic unit, or observed characteristics
Credible evaluation is about design: a clear comparison, an explicit assumption, and evidence for it

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Next Steps

Read: Angrist and Pischke (2010); Holland (1986)
Practice: In the selection-bias simulation, change the strength of selection (1.5 * risk) to 0 and to −1.5. When is the naive comparison right? When does it overstate the benefit of insurance?
Think: Pick one policy you care about. What comparison would identify its effect?
