title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
This chapter sets up the rest of the notes: what policy evaluation is, why it is hard, and how each method in these notes solves the same core problem in a different way.
The running example is health insurance and mortality, a question where naive comparisons give the wrong sign.
We finish with a roadmap of the methods and how to choose between them.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Why Policy Evaluation

Policies Rest on Causal Claims






NoteEvery Policy Embeds a Causal Claim




Expanding public health insurance will reduce deaths among low-income adults
Giving workers a generative AI assistant will raise productivity
Subsidizing insurance premiums will increase take-up
Higher credit limits will increase borrowing and stimulate spending

Each claim is about what would happen with the policy compared with what would happen without it.








TipWhat Policy Evaluation Asks




Did it work? Is there an effect at all?
How much? Is the effect large enough to matter relative to cost?
For whom? Who gains, who loses, and who is unaffected?
Why? Through which mechanism?
Would it work elsewhere? At a larger scale, in another country, for another population?





Three Kinds of Questions






NoteData Can Answer Different Questions











Type
Example (insurance)
What it needs




Description
What share of adults have no health insurance?
Good measurement and sampling


Prediction
Which policyholders are likely to lodge a claim next year?
Patterns that hold in new data


Causation
Would a premium subsidy make uninsured people buy cover?
A counterfactual: what happens with vs. without the subsidy











WarningPrediction Is Not Causation



A model can predict claims very well using variables that do not cause claims (postcode, car colour, the time of day a quote is requested). Machine learning models and LLMs are excellent prediction engines. A policy question, however, asks what would happen if we changed something. That is a causal question, and good prediction does not answer it.
These notes are about causal questions.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
The Fundamental Problem

Potential Outcomes






NoteTwo Outcomes, Only One Observed



For each person i and a treatment D_i \in \{0, 1\} (e.g., having health insurance):

Y_i(1): the outcome if person i is treated
Y_i(0): the outcome if person i is not treated
The causal effect for person i is Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)

We observe only one of the two: Y_i = D_i \, Y_i(1) + (1 - D_i) \, Y_i(0).
The other one, the counterfactual, is missing for everyone. This is the fundamental problem of causal inference (Holland 1986).








TipThe Way Forward: Averages



We cannot learn individual effects, but we can learn average effects, such as the average treatment effect (ATE) E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)], if we can find a group whose outcomes stand in for the missing counterfactual. Every method in these notes is a different way of finding that group. Chapter 2 develops the framework formally.




Estimand, Estimator, Estimate






TipThree Words Worth Keeping Apart




Estimand: the quantity we want to know, defined with potential outcomes. Example: the average effect of being sent a letter encouraging insurance enrollment on two-year mortality, among previously uninsured adults aged 45–64: E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)] in that population, where treatment is receiving the letter
Estimator: the recipe we apply to data. Example: the difference in mean two-year mortality between people randomly sent and not sent the letter
Estimate: the number the recipe produces in our sample. Example: a fall of about 0.06 percentage points (Chapter 3)

A design is credible when its estimator recovers the estimand under assumptions we can defend. A precise estimate of the wrong estimand is still wrong.




Why Naive Comparisons Fail






WarningComparing the Insured with the Uninsured



The naive comparison of mortality between insured and uninsured people decomposes into two terms:
\underbrace{E[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - E[Y_i \mid D_i = 0]}_{\text{observed difference}} = \underbrace{E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1]}_{\text{effect on the treated}} + \underbrace{E[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] - E[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0]}_{\text{selection bias}}
Selection bias is the difference the two groups would have had even without insurance.

People who expect high medical costs are more likely to buy insurance (adverse selection): selection bias pushes towards insurance looking harmful
People with higher income and education are more likely to be insured and are healthier anyway: selection bias pushes towards insurance looking helpful

Without a design, we cannot know which force dominates, or by how much.




Simulation Design






NoteInsurance and Mortality in Two Worlds




People: 100,000 adults, each with an underlying health risk. The researcher does not observe it.
Without insurance: a person’s annual chance of dying (in percent) is 1.5 + 0.8 × risk, so sicker people die more often.
With insurance: that chance falls by 0.3 percentage points, or less for the few people already close to zero. The true average effect is therefore about −0.29.
Observational world: the sicker a person is, the more likely they are to buy insurance (adverse selection).
Experimental world: a coin flip decides who is insured.

In each world we compare the death rates of the insured and the uninsured.




Simulation: Selection Bias Can Flip the Sign


Code
set.seed(2026)
n <- 100000

# Underlying health risk (higher = sicker); unobserved by the researcher
risk <- rnorm(n)

# Potential outcomes: annual probability of death (in percent)
y0 <- pmax(0, 1.5 + 0.8 * risk)          # without insurance
y1 <- pmax(0, y0 - 0.3)                  # insurance lowers mortality by up to 0.3 pp

# Observational world: sicker people are more likely to buy insurance
d_obs <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(1.5 * risk))
naive <- mean(ifelse(d_obs == 1, y1, y0)[d_obs == 1]) -
         mean(ifelse(d_obs == 1, y1, y0)[d_obs == 0])

# Experimental world: a coin flip decides who is insured
d_rct <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
y_rct <- ifelse(d_rct == 1, y1, y0)
rct <- mean(y_rct[d_rct == 1]) - mean(y_rct[d_rct == 0])

# The two terms from the previous slide
att <- mean((y1 - y0)[d_obs == 1])                          # effect on the insured
selection <- mean(y0[d_obs == 1]) - mean(y0[d_obs == 0])    # selection bias

round(c(true_ATE = mean(y1 - y0), naive_comparison = naive, ATT = att,
        selection_bias = selection, randomized = rct), 3)


        true_ATE naive_comparison              ATT   selection_bias 
          -0.286            0.536           -0.299            0.835 
      randomized 
          -0.287 








TipReading the Result



In the observational world the insured die more often, so insurance looks harmful (+0.54 percentage points). That gap is the effect on the insured (−0.30) plus selection bias (+0.83), because sicker people bought insurance. The coin flip balances risk across the two groups, and the comparison recovers the true effect (−0.29).




The naive comparison says insurance raises mortality, because the insured are sicker to begin with. Randomization removes the selection term and recovers the true protective effect.




Other Ways Correlations Mislead






WarningSix Traps











Trap
What it means
Example




Confounding
A third factor drives both the treatment and the outcome, so the two move together even if the treatment does nothing
Larger, better-managed firms are more likely to adopt AI tools and are more productive anyway


Reverse causality
The outcome, or what predicts it, causes the treatment
Struggling workers are given AI tools because they are struggling, so AI users look less productive


Controlling for a mechanism
Adjusting for something the treatment itself changes removes part of the effect you want to measure
Insurance improves health partly through more doctor visits; holding visits fixed hides that channel


Reversion to the mean
Units picked for an extreme value tend to move back towards average next time, with or without any intervention
Drivers enrolled in a safety program after an unusually bad year file fewer claims the next year anyway


Selection into the sample
The data contain only units that passed a filter related to the outcome
Studying only firms that survived a crisis hides the ones the crisis destroyed


Searching and selective reporting
Trying many analyses and reporting only the significant ones produces chance findings
With 20 outcomes tested, about one will be “significant” at 5% by chance alone







Internal and External Validity






NoteTwo Kinds of Validity




Internal validity: is the estimate right for the people, place, and time studied?
External validity: does it carry over to other populations, places, or scales?

Strong designs often buy internal validity with a narrow setting (one firm, one state, units near a cutoff). Keep both in view.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
The Evaluation Toolkit

Who Decided Who Was Treated?






TipThe Question That Organizes These Notes



Every method finds a counterfactual by exploiting how treatment was assigned. The notes move from designs where the researcher controls assignment, through designs that exploit a known source of variation (a shock, a rule, timing), to designs that rely only on measured characteristics:









Who or what decided treatment?
Where the counterfactual comes from
Method
Part · Ch.




The researcher
A lottery
Randomized experiment
II · 3–5


An outside shock
Units nudged into treatment by something unrelated to outcomes
Instrumental variables
III · 6


A rule
Units just on the other side of the cutoff
Regression discontinuity
IV · 7


The units, observed over time
The same units before treatment, or the change in untreated units
Fixed effects, DiD, synthetic control
V · 8–10


The units, observed once
Similar units, compared on observed characteristics
Regression, matching
VI · 11







Choosing a Design



Walk through the five questions left to right. Each “no” moves to a design with less control over assignment; the final step relies on the strongest untestable assumption, that every confounder is measured.
This is a starting point, not a rule. Strong evaluations often combine designs (Chapter 12).




Moving Between Methods






NoteWhen One Design Runs Into Trouble











Situation
Move to
Why




An experiment where not everyone takes up the treatment
IV (Ch. 5–6)
Random assignment is an instrument for take-up


A cutoff rule that is not followed exactly
Fuzzy RDD = IV at the cutoff (Ch. 6–7)
Crossing the cutoff shifts the probability of treatment


An instrument that is weak or hard to defend, but you have panel data
Fixed effects or DiD (Ch. 8–9)
Use changes within units instead


Treated and comparison groups differ in levels
Fixed effects or DiD (Ch. 8–9)
Fixed differences cancel out


Policy adopted at different times by different units
Heterogeneity-robust DiD (Ch. 9)
Static two-way fixed effects can mislead


Only one or a few treated units, no single good comparison
Synthetic control (Ch. 10)
Build a comparison from a weighted mix


Parallel trends plausible only for similar units
DiD with matching or reweighting (Ch. 9, 11)
Compare like with like, then difference







Methods at a Glance: Designs with Controlled or Quasi-Random Assignment









Method
Key identifying assumption
Main limitation
Ch.




Randomized experiment
Random assignment; no interference
Costly or infeasible; non-compliance, attrition, spillovers
3–5


Instrumental variables
Exclusion restriction; relevance; monotonicity
Untestable exclusion; weak instruments; LATE only
6


Regression discontinuity
Continuity at the cutoff; no manipulation
Effect only at the cutoff
7





Methods at a Glance: Designs Using Time and Observables









Method
Key identifying assumption
Main limitation
Ch.




Panel fixed effects
No time-varying confounders (strict exogeneity)
Time-varying confounders; needs within-unit variation
8


Difference-in-differences
Parallel trends; no anticipation
Trends untestable; staggered-adoption bias in TWFE
9


Synthetic control
Pre-treatment fit carries over
Needs long pre-period; few treated units; placebo inference
10


Regression, matching
No unmeasured confounders; overlap
Blind to unobservables; poor overlap
11





The full comparison table, with the core idea and estimand for each method, is on the course home page.




The Credibility Revolution






NoteDesign Before Estimation



Over the past three decades, empirical economics and management research shifted from “control for everything and hope” to research design: a clear source of variation in treatment that is plausibly as good as random (Angrist and Pischke 2010).
What that means in practice:

State the comparison that identifies the effect, in plain language
Make the identifying assumption explicit
Show evidence for it (balance, pre-trends, placebo tests, first stages)
Report robustness, and state what the design cannot rule out

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
section: Case Study: An AI Assistant in a Support Centre
text:
Case Study: An AI Assistant in a Support Centre

The Setting






NoteA Customer-Support Centre



A software firm runs a customer-support centre. Its agents resolve about two customer issues per hour. The firm wants to know whether a generative AI assistant raises that number.
The data on the next slides are simulated, so we know the true answer: the assistant adds 0.3 resolutions per hour for every agent.
Each slide tells a different story about who got the assistant. The question stays the same. The assignment changes, and so does the method that can answer the question.
In every story, a simple comparison gives the wrong answer. By a simple (or naive) comparison we mean the obvious one: agents with the tool against agents without it, or output after against output before, ignoring how the tool was assigned.




This is an illustrative case with simulated data. The method chapters use published studies; this one keeps the setting fixed so that only the assignment mechanism changes.
The setting echoes the generative AI study of customer-support agents in Chapters 8 and 9, but every number here is made up.




Design 1: Randomized Experiment
The firm considers two ways to roll out the tool. Plan A: managers choose who gets it, and they tend to pick their strongest agents. Plan B: a lottery decides. The plot compares the two plans.


Code
suppressMessages(library(fixest))
f2 <- function(x) sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", x))   # format estimates
blue <- "#1565c0"; orange <- "#c2410c"; grey <- "grey55"
tau <- 0.3                                                # true effect

set.seed(11)
n <- 2000
skill <- rnorm(n)                                         # unobserved by the analyst
y0 <- 2.0 + 0.3 * skill + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)                # resolutions per hour without AI
pick <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(1.5 * skill))                 # managers pick stronger agents
y_pick <- y0 + tau * pick
naive_pick <- mean(y_pick[pick == 1]) - mean(y_pick[pick == 0])

lottery <- sample(rep(0:1, n / 2))                        # the alternative: a lottery
y_rct <- y0 + tau * lottery
rct <- mean(y_rct[lottery == 1]) - mean(y_rct[lottery == 0])

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(skill[pick == 0], breaks = 30, col = adjustcolor(grey, 0.5), border = NA, xlim = c(-3.5, 3.5),
     main = "Plan A: who got the tool, by skill", xlab = "Skill (unobserved)")
hist(skill[pick == 1], breaks = 30, col = adjustcolor(blue, 0.5), border = NA, add = TRUE)
legend("topleft", c("No tool", "Tool"), fill = adjustcolor(c(grey, blue), 0.5), border = NA, bty = "n")
barplot(c("Plan A (managers)" = naive_pick, "Plan B (lottery)" = rct), col = c(grey, blue), border = NA, ylim = c(0, 0.7),
        main = "Estimated effect", ylab = "Resolutions per hour")
abline(h = tau, col = orange, lty = 2, lwd = 2)











Design 1: Randomized Experiment (continued)






TipHow the Method Fits the Story




Plan A, managers choose (simple comparison): comparing agents with the tool against agents without it gives 0.61. Too high, because the chosen agents were stronger to begin with (left panel).
Plan B, a lottery (randomized experiment): chance decides who gets the tool, so both groups have the same mix of skill, measured or not. Their difference is the effect: 0.31.
The lottery is the better design. It needs no assumption beyond the randomization being carried out as planned, and treated agents not affecting untreated ones.
Timing matters: a lottery is only possible before the rollout. If managers have already chosen, see Designs 4 and 7.





Design 2: Instrumental Variables
Use of the tool is voluntary. The firm emails a random half of agents encouraging them to try it. Motivated agents use it more, with or without the email.


Code
set.seed(12)
n_iv <- 8000
email <- rbinom(n_iv, 1, 0.5)                             # randomized encouragement
motiv <- rnorm(n_iv)                                      # unobserved motivation
use <- rbinom(n_iv, 1, plogis(qlogis(0.2) + (qlogis(0.6) - qlogis(0.2)) * email + 1.2 * motiv))
y_iv <- 2.0 + 0.25 * motiv + rnorm(n_iv, 0, 0.3) + tau * use
first <- mean(use[email == 1]) - mean(use[email == 0])    # first stage
itt <- mean(y_iv[email == 1]) - mean(y_iv[email == 0])    # reduced form
as_treated <- mean(y_iv[use == 1]) - mean(y_iv[use == 0])
iv <- itt / first

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
barplot(tapply(use, email, mean), names.arg = c("No email", "Email"), col = c(grey, blue), border = NA,
        ylim = c(0, 0.8), main = "Share using the tool", ylab = "Share")
barplot(tapply(y_iv, email, mean), names.arg = c("No email", "Email"), col = c(grey, blue), border = NA,
        ylim = c(1.8, 2.3), xpd = FALSE, main = "Resolutions per hour", ylab = "Mean")











Design 2: Instrumental Variables (continued)






TipHow the Method Fits the Story




Simple comparison: agents who used the tool against those who did not: 0.51. Too high, because motivated agents both use it more and resolve more.
Instrumental variables: the email is random, so compare agents who got it with those who did not. It raised use by 0.33 and output by 0.10. Output rose only because use rose, so the effect of using the tool is 0.10 ÷ 0.33 = 0.31.
Relies on: the email changing output only through use of the tool.





Design 3: Regression Discontinuity
The firm gives the tool to agents who scored below 70 on a skills test.


Code
set.seed(13)
score <- runif(n, 40, 100)
below <- as.integer(score < 70)                           # the rule
y_rd <- 1.0 + 0.015 * score + tau * below + rnorm(n, 0, 0.15)
naive_rd <- mean(y_rd[below == 1]) - mean(y_rd[below == 0])
near <- abs(score - 70) < 10                              # local linear fit within 10 points
rdd <- unname(coef(lm(y_rd ~ below * I(score - 70), subset = near))["below"])

bins <- cut(score, seq(40, 100, 2.5))
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(tapply(score, bins, mean), tapply(y_rd, bins, mean), pch = 19,
     col = ifelse(tapply(score, bins, mean) < 70, blue, grey),
     xlab = "Test score", ylab = "Resolutions per hour")
for (side in 0:1) {
  s <- if (side == 1) score < 70 & near else score >= 70 & near
  fit <- lm(y_rd[s] ~ score[s]); xs <- range(score[s])
  lines(xs, coef(fit)[1] + coef(fit)[2] * xs, lwd = 3, col = if (side == 1) blue else grey)
}
abline(v = 70, col = orange, lty = 2)











Design 3: Regression Discontinuity (continued)






TipHow the Method Fits the Story




Simple comparison: everyone below 70 against everyone above: −0.14, the wrong sign, because low scorers are weaker agents.
Regression discontinuity: agents scoring 69 and 71 are almost equally skilled; only the tool differs. The jump in output at 70 is the effect: 0.33.
Relies on: nothing else changing at 70, and agents being unable to game their score.





Design 4: Panel Fixed Effects
Managers again give the tool to their strongest agents, at different months. We see every agent’s monthly output for a year.


Code
set.seed(14)
na <- 300
sk <- rnorm(na)
gets <- rbinom(na, 1, plogis(1.5 * sk))                   # stronger agents get the tool
start <- ifelse(gets == 1, sample(4:9, na, replace = TRUE), Inf)
fe <- expand.grid(agent = 1:na, month = 1:12)
fe$tool <- as.integer(fe$month >= start[fe$agent])
fe$y <- 2.0 + 0.3 * sk[fe$agent] + tau * fe$tool + rnorm(nrow(fe), 0, 0.2)
pooled <- unname(coef(lm(y ~ tool, fe))["tool"])
fe_est <- unname(coef(feols(y ~ tool | agent + month, fe))["tool"])

treated <- which(gets == 1)[1:30]
before <- sapply(treated, function(a) mean(fe$y[fe$agent == a & fe$tool == 0]))
after <- sapply(treated, function(a) mean(fe$y[fe$agent == a & fe$tool == 1]))
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0.8, 2.2), ylim = range(before, after), xaxt = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "Resolutions per hour")
axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = c("Before the tool", "After the tool"))
segments(1, before, 2, after, col = adjustcolor(blue, 0.5), lwd = 2)
points(rep(1, 30), before, pch = 19, col = grey); points(rep(2, 30), after, pch = 19, col = blue)











Design 4: Panel Fixed Effects (continued)






TipHow the Method Fits the Story




Simple comparison: months with the tool against months without, pooling all agents: 0.52. Too high, because the agents with the tool are the stronger ones.
Fixed effects: compare each agent with themselves before and after getting the tool (each line in the plot), so permanent skill differences cancel. The average change is 0.29.
Relies on: nothing else changing for an agent at the time they got the tool.





Design 5: Difference-in-Differences
Office A switches the tool on in month 7; office B never does. Output is rising in both offices for other reasons.


Code
set.seed(15)
did <- expand.grid(office = c("A", "B"), month = 1:12, agent = 1:400)
did$tool <- as.integer(did$office == "A" & did$month >= 7)
did$y <- ifelse(did$office == "A", 2.0, 1.8) + 0.03 * did$month + tau * did$tool + rnorm(nrow(did), 0, 0.25)
m <- tapply(did$y, list(did$office, did$month >= 7), mean)
before_after <- m["A", "TRUE"] - m["A", "FALSE"]
did_est <- before_after - (m["B", "TRUE"] - m["B", "FALSE"])

path <- tapply(did$y, list(did$office, did$month), mean)
counterfactual <- path["A", 6] + (path["B", ] - path["B", 6])
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
matplot(1:12, t(path), type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 3, col = c(blue, grey), xlab = "Month", ylab = "Resolutions per hour")
lines(6:12, counterfactual[6:12], lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = blue)
abline(v = 6.5, col = orange, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("Office A", "Office B", "Office A without the tool (implied)"),
       col = c(blue, grey, blue), lty = c(1, 1, 2), lwd = c(3, 3, 2), bty = "n")











Design 5: Difference-in-Differences (continued)






TipHow the Method Fits the Story




Simple comparison: office A after against before: 0.49. Too high, because it includes the rise that would have happened anyway.
Difference-in-differences: office B’s change over the same months (0.16) shows that rise. Subtracting it leaves the effect: 0.33. The dashed line is office A without the tool.
Relies on: office A following office B’s trend had it not adopted (parallel trends).





Design 6: Synthetic Control
Only the Manila office adopts, in month 13. Offices differ in how fast their output grows.


Code
set.seed(16)
J <- 12; T0 <- 12; TT <- 24
load <- c(1.6, runif(J, 0.2, 2))                          # exposure to a growing trend; Manila first
trend <- seq(0, 1, length.out = TT)
Y <- t(sapply(1:(J + 1), function(i) 2.0 + rnorm(1, 0, 0.08) * (i > 1) + load[i] * trend + rnorm(TT, 0, 0.02)))
Y[1, (T0 + 1):TT] <- Y[1, (T0 + 1):TT] + tau               # Manila gets the tool in month 13

sc_weights <- function(y1, Y0) {                          # non-negative weights that sum to one
  loss <- function(a) { w <- exp(a) / sum(exp(a)); sum((y1 - colSums(w * Y0))^2) }
  a <- optim(rep(0, nrow(Y0)), loss, method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 2000))$par
  exp(a) / sum(exp(a))
}
w <- sc_weights(Y[1, 1:T0], Y[-1, 1:T0])
synth <- colSums(w * Y[-1, ])
post <- (T0 + 1):TT
sc_est <- mean(Y[1, post] - synth[post])
did_avg <- (mean(Y[1, post]) - mean(Y[1, 1:T0])) - (mean(colMeans(Y[-1, post])) - mean(colMeans(Y[-1, 1:T0])))

par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(1:TT, Y[1, ], type = "l", lwd = 3, col = blue, ylim = range(Y[1, ], synth, colMeans(Y[-1, ])),
     xlab = "Month", ylab = "Resolutions per hour")
lines(1:TT, synth, lwd = 3, lty = 2, col = blue)
lines(1:TT, colMeans(Y[-1, ]), lwd = 2, lty = 3, col = grey)
abline(v = T0 + 0.5, col = orange, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("Manila", "Synthetic Manila", "Average of other offices"),
       col = c(blue, blue, grey), lty = c(1, 2, 3), lwd = c(3, 3, 2), bty = "n")











Design 6: Synthetic Control (continued)






TipHow the Method Fits the Story




Simple comparison: difference-in-differences against the average of the other offices: 0.59. Too high, because Manila was growing faster than the average office.
Synthetic control: build a “synthetic Manila”: a weighted mix of offices chosen to match Manila’s path in months 1–12. After month 13, the gap between Manila and its synthetic version is the effect: 0.30.
Relies on: the mix that tracked Manila before month 13 continuing to track it.





Design 7: Regression and Matching
Managers give the tool mostly to experienced agents, and experience raises output. We observe each agent’s tenure.


Code
set.seed(17)
tenure <- sample(1:4, n, replace = TRUE)                  # years on the job (observed)
tool_t <- rbinom(n, 1, c(0.15, 0.35, 0.65, 0.85)[tenure]) # more experienced, more likely to get it
y_t <- 1.6 + 0.2 * tenure + tau * tool_t + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)
naive_t <- mean(y_t[tool_t == 1]) - mean(y_t[tool_t == 0])
reg_t <- unname(coef(lm(y_t ~ tool_t + factor(tenure)))["tool_t"])
gaps <- sapply(1:4, function(k) mean(y_t[tool_t == 1 & tenure == k]) - mean(y_t[tool_t == 0 & tenure == k]))
match_t <- sum(gaps * tabulate(tenure[tool_t == 1], 4)) / sum(tool_t)   # exact matching on tenure

mt <- tapply(y_t, list(tool_t, tenure), mean)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
matplot(1:4, t(mt), type = "b", pch = 19, lty = 1, lwd = 3, col = c(grey, blue), xaxt = "n",
        xlab = "Years of tenure", ylab = "Resolutions per hour")
axis(1, at = 1:4)
legend("topleft", c("No tool", "Tool"), col = c(grey, blue), lwd = 3, pch = 19, bty = "n")











Design 7: Regression and Matching (continued)






TipHow the Method Fits the Story




Simple comparison: agents with the tool against agents without it: 0.53. Too high, because experienced agents resolve more anyway.
Regression and matching: compare agents with the same tenure (the gap within each tenure group in the plot), then average: 0.29 by regression, 0.28 by matching.
Relies on: tenure being the only thing managers used. If they also used something unobserved, such as skill in Design 1, this would fail.





Comparing the Estimates


Code
res <- data.frame(
  design = c("1 Randomized experiment", "2 Instrumental variables", "3 Regression discontinuity",
             "4 Fixed effects", "5 Difference-in-differences", "6 Synthetic control", "7 Regression / matching"),
  naive  = c(naive_pick, as_treated, naive_rd, pooled, before_after, did_avg, naive_t),
  design_est = c(rct, iv, rdd, fe_est, did_est, sc_est, reg_t))
par(mar = c(4, 13, 1, 1))
plot(res$naive, 7:1, xlim = c(-0.2, 0.7), pch = 1, cex = 1.6, col = grey, yaxt = "n", ylab = "",
     xlab = "Estimated effect (resolutions per hour)")
points(res$design_est, 7:1, pch = 19, cex = 1.6, col = blue)
axis(2, at = 7:1, labels = res$design, las = 1)
abline(v = tau, col = orange, lty = 2, lwd = 2); abline(v = 0, col = "grey85")
legend("topleft", c("Simple comparison", "Design-based estimate", "Truth"),
       pch = c(1, 19, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, 2), col = c(grey, blue, orange), bty = "n")















WarningWhy the Estimates Agree Here



The tool has the same effect for every agent, so every design recovers 0.3. With real data, effects differ across people, and each design recovers the effect for a different group: everyone (experiment), agents who use the tool because of the email (IV), agents near the cutoff (RDD), or the offices and agents that were treated (DiD, synthetic control). The chapters return to this point.

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
How These Notes Work

The Plan of These Notes

Part I: Foundations: what a causal effect is, and how treatment gets assigned
Part II: Randomized Experiments: the researcher assigns treatment; design, practice, and what goes wrong
Part III: Instrumental Variables: an outside shock shifts treatment; from randomized offers to natural instruments
Part IV: Regression Discontinuity: a rule assigns treatment at a cutoff
Part V: Panel Methods: units choose, but we see them over time; fixed effects, DiD, synthetic control
Part VI: Selection on Observables: units choose, and we observe them once; regression and matching
Part VII: Synthesis: combining designs, accumulating evidence, and reporting



LLMs as Research Tools






WarningMeasuring Variables with LLMs



LLMs are also increasingly used to measure variables, such as classifying text or rating job tasks. A measured variable is only as good as its validation: measurement error in a treatment variable biases estimates (Chapter 8 shows how fixed effects make this worse).




Six Questions for Any Evaluation






TipUse These for Any Evaluation You Read or Design




Question: What is the causal effect of what, on what, for whom?
Estimand: Is the target an ATE, an effect on the treated, or a local effect (compliers, units at a cutoff)?
Identification: What comparison identifies the effect, and what assumption makes it valid?
Threats: What would break that assumption in this setting?
Evidence: How do the authors test or defend the assumption?
External validity: Would the result hold in another place, time, or population?

title: Introduction to Policy Evaluation and Causal Inference
text:
Practicalities

Ethics in Policy Evaluation






WarningEvaluations Involve Real People




Informed consent and institutional review: ethics board approval, and registration in a public trial registry
Equipoise: randomizing is easier to justify when we genuinely do not know whether the policy helps, or when resources are limited and must be rationed anyway
Privacy: linking survey, tax, health, and death records requires secure facilities and disclosure review
Distribution: average effects can hide harm to specific groups; check heterogeneity
Complete reporting: pre-registration, pre-analysis plans, and reporting null results





Software and Code






NoteWorking with the Code in These Notes




All examples use R; the packages used are fixest (fixed effects, IV, DiD, event studies), rdrobust and rddensity (regression discontinuity), did (staggered DiD), Synth (synthetic control), and MatchIt (matching)
Simulations with made-up data and a known true effect show whether each method recovers it; real datasets that ship with these packages (minimum wages, the Basque Country, the LaLonde (1986) job-training data) show the methods at work
Code is folded by default in both the lecture notes and the slides; click “Code” to expand it





Summary


Policy evaluation asks what would have happened without the policy
Individual causal effects are never observed; we estimate averages using a comparison group
Naive comparisons mix the causal effect with selection bias, which can even flip the sign
Each method in these notes finds the counterfactual in a different place: chance, an outside shock, a cutoff, time, a synthetic unit, or observed characteristics
Credible evaluation is about design: a clear comparison, an explicit assumption, and evidence for it




Next Steps


Read: Angrist and Pischke (2010); Holland (1986)
Practice: In the selection-bias simulation, change the strength of selection (1.5 * risk) to 0 and to −1.5. When is the naive comparison right? When does it overstate the benefit of insurance?
Think: Pick one policy you care about. What comparison would identify its effect?
Next Class: The potential outcomes framework in detail (Chapter 2)




References


Angrist, Joshua D, and Jörn-Steffen Pischke. 2010. “The Credibility Revolution in Empirical Economics: How Better Research Design Is Taking the Con Out of Econometrics.” Journal of Economic Perspectives 24 (2): 3–30. https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.24.2.3.


Holland, Paul W. 1986. “Statistics and Causal Inference.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 81 (396): 945–60. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1986.10478354.


LaLonde, Robert J. 1986. “Evaluating the Econometric Evaluations of Training Programs with Experimental Data.” American Economic Review 76 (4): 604–20.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Where This Chapter Fits






Step 1: Can you randomly assign who is treated?



You arrive here when: You control assignment, so you can make it random.
This chapter: Why randomization removes selection bias, how to estimate and test effects, and the design choices that determine power.
Next: Chapter 4: running experiments in real organizations.

See the design flowchart in Chapter 1.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
In Practice: Randomized Experiments






Practitioner Summary



Use it when: you, or a partner organization, control who gets the treatment, and withholding or delaying it for some units is acceptable
What you need: the assignment list, baseline covariates (ideally past outcomes), and an outcome you can measure for nearly everyone
What must hold: assignment really was random and was followed; no spillovers between treated and control units
Checks to run: a power calculation before launch; a balance table with a joint test; attrition by arm
In R: lm_robust(y ~ treat, data) from estimatr (HC2 by default, matching the formula above), or clusters = team if teams were randomized; a permutation loop for randomization inference (this chapter)
Telling a manager: “A lottery decided who got it, so the only systematic difference between the groups is the program. The gap in outcomes is its effect, within this margin of error.”

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Randomization Removes Selection Bias






Independence by Design


If a lottery decides who is treated, treatment status cannot depend on anything about the units, including their potential outcomes:
\big(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)\big) \perp D_i
Then E[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] = E[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0], the selection-bias term from Chapter 2 is zero, and
E[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - E[Y_i \mid D_i = 0] = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)] = \text{ATE}









What Randomization Balances


Randomization balances treatment and control groups in expectation on every characteristic: observed or unobserved, measured before treatment or never measured at all. No other design does this. That is why the rest of the notes ask, for each method, “what would make this comparison as good as random?”

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
section: Unbiased Is Not the Same as Exact
text:
Unbiased Is Not the Same as Exact






Any Single Experiment Can Be Unlucky


Unbiasedness is a property of the procedure: averaged over all possible random assignments, the difference in means equals the ATE. In any one assignment, chance imbalances move the estimate up or down.

With 8 workers (Chapter 2), lottery estimates of a true effect of 0.25 vary with a standard deviation of about 0.4
With thousands of units, chance imbalances shrink and the estimate concentrates around the truth

Quantifying this variation is the job of inference.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
The Difference in Means






The Workhorse Estimator


\hat\tau = \bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0, \qquad \widehat{SE}(\hat\tau) = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_0^2}{n_0}}
where \bar Y_d, s_d^2, and n_d are the mean, variance, and size of group d.

Equivalent to OLS of Y_i on D_i; this standard error equals the heteroskedasticity-robust (HC2) standard error
For the effect in the sample at hand, the formula is conservative: it cannot account for how individual effects vary, which would reduce the true variance. It is exactly right if the sample is a random draw from a larger population
With cluster-level assignment, cluster standard errors at the level of randomization

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Randomization Inference






Testing Without a Model of the Data


Take the sharp null hypothesis that treatment had no effect for anyone: Y_i(1) = Y_i(0) for all i. Under this null we know every unit’s outcome under any assignment, so we can:

Re-randomize treatment many times, following the original design
Recompute the estimate each time
Report the share of re-randomized estimates at least as extreme as the actual one: the p-value

The p-value is exact in finite samples if all possible assignments are used (with a large random sample of them, as below, it is exact up to simulation error). It makes no distributional assumptions and respects the design (blocks, clusters) when re-randomization follows the original design. It is especially useful in small experiments.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Randomization Inference in R


Code
set.seed(2026)
n <- 100
d <- sample(rep(0:1, n / 2))                     # completely randomized design
y <- 50 + 4 * d + rnorm(n, 0, 8)                 # true effect = 4

observed <- mean(y[d == 1]) - mean(y[d == 0])

# Re-randomize under the sharp null of no effect
perm <- replicate(10000, {
  d_star <- sample(d)
  mean(y[d_star == 1]) - mean(y[d_star == 0])
})

c(estimate = round(observed, 2),
  p_randomization = mean(abs(perm) >= abs(observed)),
  p_t_test = round(t.test(y ~ d)$p.value, 4))


       estimate p_randomization        p_t_test 
         4.8400          0.0012          0.0011

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Choosing the Unit of Randomization






Individuals or Clusters?










Randomize…
When
Cost




Individuals
Little risk of spillovers; treatment can be delivered person by person
Spillovers bias the comparison if they occur


Clusters (teams, schools, branches, villages)
Treatment is delivered to groups, or spillovers within groups are likely
Fewer independent units, so less power












The Design Effect


With clusters of size m and intra-cluster correlation \rho (how similar outcomes are within a cluster), the variance of the estimate is inflated by roughly
\text{DEFF} = 1 + (m - 1)\rho
Example: teams of 6 software developers with \rho = 0.2 give \text{DEFF} = 2, so the experiment behaves as if it had half as many developers. Cui et al. (2026, see Chapter 5) randomized some developers individually and others by team.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Blocking (Stratified Randomization)






Randomize Within Groups of Similar Units


Divide units into blocks by characteristics that predict the outcome (age, income, prior performance), then randomize within each block.

Guarantees balance on the blocking variables
Improves precision when blocking variables predict outcomes
Makes subgroup analysis cleaner, since each subgroup is itself a small experiment
Analysis: estimate the effect within each block and take a weighted average by block size; a regression with block fixed effects gives the same answer only when the treated share is the same in every block (otherwise it weights blocks by their treatment variance)

Goldin et al. (2021, case study below) stratified by age, gender, marital status, dependents, income, self-employment, prior penalty status, and state policy environment.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Adjusting for Covariates






Regression Adjustment in Experiments


Y_i = \alpha + \tau D_i + X_i'\beta + \varepsilon_i

Randomization already makes the difference in means unbiased; covariates are about precision (regression adjustment has a small finite-sample bias that vanishes in large samples)
Use pre-treatment covariates only (measured before assignment, or unaffected by it)
Prognostic covariates, especially the baseline value of the outcome, can cut standard errors substantially
Interacting D_i with demeaned covariates gives an estimator that is never less precise asymptotically (Lin 2013)
Pre-specify the covariates to avoid searching for the “best” result

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Power and Sample Size






The Minimum Detectable Effect


With a share P of N units treated, outcome standard deviation \sigma, significance level \alpha, and power 1 - \kappa:
\text{MDE} = \big(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\kappa}\big) \sqrt{\frac{1}{P(1-P)}} \; \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt N}

Power grows with \sqrt N: halving the MDE needs four times the sample
Unequal allocation (P \neq 0.5) costs power; budgets or ethics sometimes require it
Imperfect take-up dilutes the intent-to-treat effect: if only 10% of the treated group take up (and no one in the control group can), the ITT is one-tenth of the effect on those who do, and the required sample grows by a factor of about 100

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Power for a Rare Outcome


Code
# Illustration: annual mortality of 1.0%; we want to detect a fall to 0.94%
# (a 6% relative reduction) with 80% power at the 5% level
pw <- power.prop.test(p1 = 0.0100, p2 = 0.0094, power = 0.80, sig.level = 0.05)
ceiling(pw$n)                                   # required per group


[1] 418864


Code
# Now suppose only 10% of those offered treatment actually take it up:
# the intent-to-treat difference is ten times smaller
pw_itt <- power.prop.test(p1 = 0.0100, p2 = 0.01 - 0.0006 * 0.10, power = 0.80)
ceiling(pw_itt$n)


[1] 43040636




Rare outcomes plus low take-up are why credible experiments on insurance and mortality need millions of participants, or must focus on higher-risk groups. Goldin et al. do both.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Balance Checks






What a Balance Table Can and Cannot Tell You



Purpose: to detect failures of randomization or implementation (wrong lists, manipulated assignment), and to describe the sample
With many covariates, about 1 in 20 will differ at the 5% level by chance; a joint test is more informative than counting stars
A chance imbalance does not make the estimator biased; adjusting for the imbalanced pre-treatment covariate can improve precision
Do not re-run the randomization until the table “looks good” unless that rule was planned in advance

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Multiple Arms and Factorial Designs






Testing More Than One Version



Multiple arms: several versions of treatment against a shared control group (e.g., letters with and without personalized information)
Factorial designs: cross two treatments (A only, B only, both, neither) to estimate each effect and their interaction
Trade-off: each comparison uses a smaller share of the sample, so arms must be chosen with power in mind
Multiple testing: with many arms and outcomes, pre-specify the main comparisons and adjust for multiple hypotheses

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
section: Case Study: Health Insurance and Mortality
text:
Case Study: Health Insurance and Mortality






Goldin, Lurie & McCubbin (2021), Quarterly Journal of Economics (Goldin et al. 2021)


Question: Does health insurance coverage reduce mortality?
Why it is hard: people who buy insurance differ from those who do not (Chapter 1), and mortality is rare, so experiments need enormous samples.
The opportunity: in early 2017 the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) planned to send letters encouraging people who had paid a penalty for being uninsured to look at coverage options. A budget limit meant not everyone could be sent one, so the agencies randomized.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Case Study: The Design






A Very Large, Stratified, Multi-Arm Experiment



Sample: 4.5 million tax returns (8.9 million people) that paid the 2015 penalty for lacking coverage
Assignment: 86% sent a letter, 14% control; randomization stratified by age, gender, marital status, dependents, income, self-employment, prior penalty, and state policy environment
Arms: a baseline letter with a personalized penalty estimate; a non-personalized version; an earlier mailing date; versions with exemption information or a Spanish translation
Outcomes: coverage and mortality from administrative records (tax forms and Social Security death records): no surveys and essentially no attrition
Registered in the AEA RCT Registry and approved by a university ethics board






Point out the unequal allocation (86/14): driven by the program’s goal of broad outreach and its budget, at a cost in power.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Case Study: Results






What the Letters Did



Coverage: previously uninsured recipients were 1.1 percentage points more likely to enroll over two years (+1.9%), about 0.23 extra months of coverage on average
Arms differ: the non-personalized letter was about 26% less effective than the personalized one; the earlier mailing about 40% more effective; exemption information and Spanish translation made no difference
Mortality: among previously uninsured adults aged 45–64, two-year mortality fell by about 0.06 percentage points, roughly one fewer death per 1,587 people sent a letter
No detectable effect for children or younger adults, where deaths are much rarer










From the Letter’s Effect to Insurance’s Effect


The mortality estimate is an intent-to-treat effect of the letter. Dividing by the effect on coverage (an instrumental variables estimate, Chapters 5–6) gives the effect of coverage itself for people induced to enroll by the letter: about −0.18 percentage points per month of coverage, imprecise but large enough to rule out the much smaller estimate from a naive regression of mortality on coverage.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Case Study: Design Lessons






What This Experiment Teaches



Scale beats rare outcomes: a 0.06 pp effect is only detectable with millions of participants
Target where power is: restricting to 45–64-year-olds, whose mortality is higher and whose coverage responded more, sharpened the estimate
Administrative outcomes avoid attrition and self-report bias
Arms answer design questions that matter for the next outreach campaign (personalize, send early)
The control group is not “no outreach”: controls may have seen TV ads or other campaigns, so the estimate is the effect of the letter on top of everything else happening

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Case Study: What to Copy






Practices to Reuse



Piggyback on a decision already being made. A budget limit meant not everyone could get a letter, so randomizing who did cost the agency nothing.
Measure outcomes from records. Tax and death records gave essentially no attrition and no self-report bias.
Add cheap arms that answer operational questions. Personalized vs. generic letters and early vs. late mailing told the agency how to run the next campaign.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Case Study: Discussion Questions

Why did the IRS randomize at the tax return (household) level rather than the individual level?
The split was 86% treated and 14% control. What did this choice cost in power, and why might the agencies still prefer it?
Why does stratifying by income and age matter more for precision here than for bias?
The mortality effect is significant for 45–64-year-olds but not for younger adults. Is that heterogeneity, low power, or both? How would you tell?
Why is the IV estimate of the effect of coverage larger than the effect of the letter? Whose effect does it describe?

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Case Study: Suggested Answers (1–2)

One letter was sent per tax return, addressed to the filers, so the return is the natural unit. People on the same return also make coverage decisions together; randomizing individuals within a return would put treated and control people in the same household and invite spillovers. Standard errors are clustered by household.
For a fixed sample, the variance of a difference in means scales with 1/[P(1-P)]. At P = 0.86 this is about 8.3, against 4 at an even split, so standard errors are about 1.4 times larger. The agencies’ aim was outreach, so they wanted as many people as possible to receive a letter.

Case Study: Suggested Answers (3–4)

Randomization already makes the arms comparable on income and age on average, so stratifying cannot remove bias. It removes chance imbalance on strong predictors of coverage and mortality, which makes estimates more precise.
Probably both. Deaths are rare among younger adults, so power is low, and their coverage response may also differ. Compare confidence intervals, not just significance: a wide interval that includes the older group’s effect points to low power; a precise estimate near zero points to a real difference.

The IV estimate divides the letter’s effect on mortality by its effect on coverage, which is far less than one month per person, so the ratio is larger. It is the effect per month of coverage for compliers: people who enrolled because they received a letter.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Randomization is the benchmark every other method in these notes tries to imitate.
This chapter covers why it works, how to estimate effects and quantify uncertainty, and the design choices that determine whether an experiment can answer its question: the unit of randomization, blocking, covariates, and power.
Case study: a randomized IRS outreach experiment with 4.5 million tax returns, used to estimate the effect of health insurance on mortality.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Why Randomization Works

Randomization Removes Selection Bias






NoteIndependence by Design



If a lottery decides who is treated, treatment status cannot depend on anything about the units, including their potential outcomes:
\big(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)\big) \perp D_i
Then E[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] = E[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0], the selection-bias term from Chapter 2 is zero, and
E[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - E[Y_i \mid D_i = 0] = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)] = \text{ATE}








TipWhat Randomization Balances



Randomization balances treatment and control groups in expectation on every characteristic: observed or unobserved, measured before treatment or never measured at all. No other design does this. That is why the rest of the notes ask, for each method, “what would make this comparison as good as random?”




Unbiased Is Not the Same as Exact






WarningAny Single Experiment Can Be Unlucky



Unbiasedness is a property of the procedure: averaged over all possible random assignments, the difference in means equals the ATE. In any one assignment, chance imbalances move the estimate up or down.

With 8 workers (Chapter 2), lottery estimates of a true effect of 0.25 vary with a standard deviation of about 0.4
With thousands of units, chance imbalances shrink and the estimate concentrates around the truth

Quantifying this variation is the job of inference.

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Estimation and Inference

The Difference in Means






NoteThe Workhorse Estimator



\hat\tau = \bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0, \qquad \widehat{SE}(\hat\tau) = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_0^2}{n_0}}
where \bar Y_d, s_d^2, and n_d are the mean, variance, and size of group d.

Equivalent to OLS of Y_i on D_i; this standard error equals the heteroskedasticity-robust (HC2) standard error
For the effect in the sample at hand, the formula is conservative: it cannot account for how individual effects vary, which would reduce the true variance. It is exactly right if the sample is a random draw from a larger population
With cluster-level assignment, cluster standard errors at the level of randomization





Randomization Inference






TipTesting Without a Model of the Data



Take the sharp null hypothesis that treatment had no effect for anyone: Y_i(1) = Y_i(0) for all i. Under this null we know every unit’s outcome under any assignment, so we can:

Re-randomize treatment many times, following the original design
Recompute the estimate each time
Report the share of re-randomized estimates at least as extreme as the actual one: the p-value

The p-value is exact in finite samples if all possible assignments are used (with a large random sample of them, as below, it is exact up to simulation error). It makes no distributional assumptions and respects the design (blocks, clusters) when re-randomization follows the original design. It is especially useful in small experiments.




Randomization Inference in R


Code
set.seed(2026)
n <- 100
d <- sample(rep(0:1, n / 2))                     # completely randomized design
y <- 50 + 4 * d + rnorm(n, 0, 8)                 # true effect = 4

observed <- mean(y[d == 1]) - mean(y[d == 0])

# Re-randomize under the sharp null of no effect
perm <- replicate(10000, {
  d_star <- sample(d)
  mean(y[d_star == 1]) - mean(y[d_star == 0])
})

c(estimate = round(observed, 2),
  p_randomization = mean(abs(perm) >= abs(observed)),
  p_t_test = round(t.test(y ~ d)$p.value, 4))


       estimate p_randomization        p_t_test 
         4.8400          0.0012          0.0011

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Designing an Experiment

Choosing the Unit of Randomization






NoteIndividuals or Clusters?











Randomize…
When
Cost




Individuals
Little risk of spillovers; treatment can be delivered person by person
Spillovers bias the comparison if they occur


Clusters (teams, schools, branches, villages)
Treatment is delivered to groups, or spillovers within groups are likely
Fewer independent units, so less power











WarningThe Design Effect



With clusters of size m and intra-cluster correlation \rho (how similar outcomes are within a cluster), the variance of the estimate is inflated by roughly
\text{DEFF} = 1 + (m - 1)\rho
Example: teams of 6 software developers with \rho = 0.2 give \text{DEFF} = 2, so the experiment behaves as if it had half as many developers. Cui et al. (2026, see Chapter 5) randomized some developers individually and others by team.




Blocking (Stratified Randomization)






TipRandomize Within Groups of Similar Units



Divide units into blocks by characteristics that predict the outcome (age, income, prior performance), then randomize within each block.

Guarantees balance on the blocking variables
Improves precision when blocking variables predict outcomes
Makes subgroup analysis cleaner, since each subgroup is itself a small experiment
Analysis: estimate the effect within each block and take a weighted average by block size; a regression with block fixed effects gives the same answer only when the treated share is the same in every block (otherwise it weights blocks by their treatment variance)

Goldin et al. (2021, case study below) stratified by age, gender, marital status, dependents, income, self-employment, prior penalty status, and state policy environment.




Adjusting for Covariates






NoteRegression Adjustment in Experiments



Y_i = \alpha + \tau D_i + X_i'\beta + \varepsilon_i

Randomization already makes the difference in means unbiased; covariates are about precision (regression adjustment has a small finite-sample bias that vanishes in large samples)
Use pre-treatment covariates only (measured before assignment, or unaffected by it)
Prognostic covariates, especially the baseline value of the outcome, can cut standard errors substantially
Interacting D_i with demeaned covariates gives an estimator that is never less precise asymptotically (Lin 2013)
Pre-specify the covariates to avoid searching for the “best” result





Power and Sample Size






NoteThe Minimum Detectable Effect



With a share P of N units treated, outcome standard deviation \sigma, significance level \alpha, and power 1 - \kappa:
\text{MDE} = \big(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\kappa}\big) \sqrt{\frac{1}{P(1-P)}} \; \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt N}

Power grows with \sqrt N: halving the MDE needs four times the sample
Unequal allocation (P \neq 0.5) costs power; budgets or ethics sometimes require it
Imperfect take-up dilutes the intent-to-treat effect: if only 10% of the treated group take up (and no one in the control group can), the ITT is one-tenth of the effect on those who do, and the required sample grows by a factor of about 100





Power for a Rare Outcome


Code
# Illustration: annual mortality of 1.0%; we want to detect a fall to 0.94%
# (a 6% relative reduction) with 80% power at the 5% level
pw <- power.prop.test(p1 = 0.0100, p2 = 0.0094, power = 0.80, sig.level = 0.05)
ceiling(pw$n)                                   # required per group


[1] 418864


Code
# Now suppose only 10% of those offered treatment actually take it up:
# the intent-to-treat difference is ten times smaller
pw_itt <- power.prop.test(p1 = 0.0100, p2 = 0.01 - 0.0006 * 0.10, power = 0.80)
ceiling(pw_itt$n)


[1] 43040636




Rare outcomes plus low take-up are why credible experiments on insurance and mortality need millions of participants, or must focus on higher-risk groups. Goldin et al. do both.




Balance Checks






WarningWhat a Balance Table Can and Cannot Tell You




Purpose: to detect failures of randomization or implementation (wrong lists, manipulated assignment), and to describe the sample
With many covariates, about 1 in 20 will differ at the 5% level by chance; a joint test is more informative than counting stars
A chance imbalance does not make the estimator biased; adjusting for the imbalanced pre-treatment covariate can improve precision
Do not re-run the randomization until the table “looks good” unless that rule was planned in advance





Multiple Arms and Factorial Designs






TipTesting More Than One Version




Multiple arms: several versions of treatment against a shared control group (e.g., letters with and without personalized information)
Factorial designs: cross two treatments (A only, B only, both, neither) to estimate each effect and their interaction
Trade-off: each comparison uses a smaller share of the sample, so arms must be chosen with power in mind
Multiple testing: with many arms and outcomes, pre-specify the main comparisons and adjust for multiple hypotheses

title: Randomized Experiments: Design and Inference
text:
Case Study

Case Study: Health Insurance and Mortality






NoteGoldin, Lurie & McCubbin (2021), Quarterly Journal of Economics (Goldin et al. 2021)



Question: Does health insurance coverage reduce mortality?
Why it is hard: people who buy insurance differ from those who do not (Chapter 1), and mortality is rare, so experiments need enormous samples.
The opportunity: in early 2017 the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) planned to send letters encouraging people who had paid a penalty for being uninsured to look at coverage options. A budget limit meant not everyone could be sent one, so the agencies randomized.




Case Study: The Design






TipA Very Large, Stratified, Multi-Arm Experiment




Sample: 4.5 million tax returns (8.9 million people) that paid the 2015 penalty for lacking coverage
Assignment: 86% sent a letter, 14% control; randomization stratified by age, gender, marital status, dependents, income, self-employment, prior penalty, and state policy environment
Arms: a baseline letter with a personalized penalty estimate; a non-personalized version; an earlier mailing date; versions with exemption information or a Spanish translation
Outcomes: coverage and mortality from administrative records (tax forms and Social Security death records): no surveys and essentially no attrition
Registered in the AEA RCT Registry and approved by a university ethics board





Point out the unequal allocation (86/14): driven by the program’s goal of broad outreach and its budget, at a cost in power.




Case Study: Results






TipWhat the Letters Did




Coverage: previously uninsured recipients were 1.1 percentage points more likely to enroll over two years (+1.9%), about 0.23 extra months of coverage on average
Arms differ: the non-personalized letter was about 26% less effective than the personalized one; the earlier mailing about 40% more effective; exemption information and Spanish translation made no difference
Mortality: among previously uninsured adults aged 45–64, two-year mortality fell by about 0.06 percentage points, roughly one fewer death per 1,587 people sent a letter
No detectable effect for children or younger adults, where deaths are much rarer









NoteFrom the Letter’s Effect to Insurance’s Effect



The mortality estimate is an intent-to-treat effect of the letter. Dividing by the effect on coverage (an instrumental variables estimate, Chapters 5–6) gives the effect of coverage itself for people induced to enroll by the letter: about −0.18 percentage points per month of coverage, imprecise but large enough to rule out the much smaller estimate from a naive regression of mortality on coverage.




Case Study: Design Lessons






WarningWhat This Experiment Teaches




Scale beats rare outcomes: a 0.06 pp effect is only detectable with millions of participants
Target where power is: restricting to 45–64-year-olds, whose mortality is higher and whose coverage responded more, sharpened the estimate
Administrative outcomes avoid attrition and self-report bias
Arms answer design questions that matter for the next outreach campaign (personalize, send early)
The control group is not “no outreach”: controls may have seen TV ads or other campaigns, so the estimate is the effect of the letter on top of everything else happening





Case Study: What to Copy






TipPractices to Reuse




Piggyback on a decision already being made. A budget limit meant not everyone could get a letter, so randomizing who did cost the agency nothing.
Measure outcomes from records. Tax and death records gave essentially no attrition and no self-report bias.
Add cheap arms that answer operational questions. Personalized vs. generic letters and early vs. late mailing told the agency how to run the next campaign.





Case Study: Discussion Questions


Why did the IRS randomize at the tax return (household) level rather than the individual level?
The split was 86% treated and 14% control. What did this choice cost in power, and why might the agencies still prefer it?
Why does stratifying by income and age matter more for precision here than for bias?
The mortality effect is significant for 45–64-year-olds but not for younger adults. Is that heterogeneity, low power, or both? How would you tell?
Why is the IV estimate of the effect of coverage larger than the effect of the letter? Whose effect does it describe?








NoteSuggested Answers (click to expand)






One letter was sent per tax return, addressed to the filers, so the return is the natural unit. People on the same return also make coverage decisions together; randomizing individuals within a return would put treated and control people in the same household and invite spillovers. Standard errors are clustered by household.
For a fixed sample, the variance of a difference in means scales with 1/[P(1-P)]. At P = 0.86 this is about 8.3, against 4 at an even split, so standard errors are about 1.4 times larger. The agencies’ aim was outreach, so they wanted as many people as possible to receive a letter.
Randomization already makes the arms comparable on income and age on average, so stratifying cannot remove bias. It removes chance imbalance on strong predictors of coverage and mortality, which makes estimates more precise.
Probably both. Deaths are rare among younger adults, so power is low, and their coverage response may also differ. Compare confidence intervals, not just significance: a wide interval that includes the older group’s effect points to low power; a precise estimate near zero points to a real difference.
The IV estimate divides the letter’s effect on mortality by its effect on coverage, which is far less than one month per person, so the ratio is larger. It is the effect per month of coverage for compliers: people who enrolled because they received a letter.

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Where This Chapter Fits






Step 1, when it goes wrong



You arrive here when: You randomized, but people did not comply, outcomes went missing, or treatment spilled over.
This chapter: Intent-to-treat effects, scaling by take-up, attrition bounds, and designs for spillovers.
Next: Chapter 6: a randomized offer is an instrument. The same logic works for shocks you did not create.

See the design flowchart in Chapter 1.

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
section: In Practice: When the Experiment Goes Wrong
text:
In Practice: When the Experiment Goes Wrong






Practitioner Summary



Use it when: people did not take what they were offered, outcomes are missing, or the treatment leaked to the control group
What you need: take-up in both arms, attrition by arm, and the team or cluster structure of the units
What must hold: exclusion (the offer affects outcomes only through use); no defiers if controls can get the treatment; for Lee bounds, treatment changes whether outcomes are observed in one direction only
Checks to run: take-up and attrition by arm; baseline traits of those who leave; control-group take-up over time
In R: intent-to-treat feols(y ~ z, data), effect of use feols(y ~ 1 | d ~ z, data)
Telling a manager: “Offering the tool raised output by X. Among the people who used it because we offered it, the gain was Y.”

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
section: Assigned Is Not the Same as Treated
text:
Assigned Is Not the Same as Treated






Two Treatment Variables



Z_i: assignment, which the researcher randomizes (offered the AI tool, sent a letter, invited to a program)
D_i: receipt, which the unit chooses (actually used the tool, actually enrolled)










Experiment
Assignment Z
Receipt D
Take-up




IRS outreach (Chapter 3)
Letter sent
Enrolled in coverage
+1.1 percentage points (difference between arms)


AI coding assistant (this chapter)
Access offered
Developer used the tool
About 60–70% of those offered eventually tried it



When D \neq Z for some units, we have non-compliance.

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
section: Three Tempting Comparisons, Two of Them Wrong
text:
Three Tempting Comparisons, Two of Them Wrong






Comparing by Receipt Breaks Randomization










Comparison
What it compares
Valid?




Intent-to-treat (ITT)
Everyone assigned vs. everyone not assigned, regardless of take-up
Yes: this is the randomized comparison


As-treated
Those who used the treatment vs. those who did not
No: who uses it is a choice


Naive per-protocol
Units that followed their assignment in each arm (takers if offered, non-takers if not)
No: drops a self-selected subset



Developers who choose to use an AI tool may be more motivated, more junior, or working on different tasks. Once we compare by choice, selection bias is back. The as-treated and naive per-protocol comparisons are really observational analyses inside an experiment: they could only be rescued by adjusting for everything that drives take-up (Hernán and Robins 2020).

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Compliance Types






Four Kinds of Units


Each unit has two potential receipts: D_i(1) if assigned, D_i(0) if not.









Type
D_i(0)
D_i(1)
Example




Compliers
0
1
Use the tool if and only if offered


Never-takers
0
0
Never use it, even if offered


Always-takers
1
1
Find a way to use it even in the control group


Defiers
1
0
Use it only if not offered



We never observe a unit’s type directly, because we only see one of the two receipts.

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
When Experiments Go Wrong
section: Simulation: As-Treated vs. ITT vs. CACE
text:
Simulation: As-Treated vs. ITT vs. CACE


Code
library(fixest)
set.seed(2026)
n <- 4000
motivation <- rnorm(n)                                  # unobserved
z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)                                  # random offer
# Only offered developers can adopt; motivated ones adopt more often
d <- z * rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.5 + 1.2 * motivation))
y <- 5 + 2 * motivation + 1.5 * d + rnorm(n)            # true effect of use = 1.5

itt_y <- mean(y[z == 1]) - mean(y[z == 0])
itt_d <- mean(d[z == 1]) - mean(d[z == 0])

round(c(take_up       = itt_d,
        as_treated    = mean(y[d == 1]) - mean(y[d == 0]),
        ITT           = itt_y,
        CACE_wald     = itt_y / itt_d,
        CACE_2SLS     = unname(coef(feols(y ~ 1 | d ~ z, data = data.frame(y, d, z)))["fit_d"])), 2)


   take_up as_treated        ITT  CACE_wald  CACE_2SLS 
      0.39       2.87       0.58       1.47       1.47 




As-treated is badly biased upwards: motivated developers both adopt more and produce more.
The ITT is unbiased for the effect of the offer, but diluted by non-adopters.
Dividing by take-up recovers the effect of use for compliers. Two-stage least squares gives the same number; Chapter 6 develops it in general.

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Two-Sided Non-Compliance






When Some Controls Get Treated Anyway


If control units can obtain the treatment, always-takers exist. The same ratio still identifies the effect for compliers, now called the local average treatment effect (LATE), under one more assumption:
Monotonicity (no defiers): being offered the treatment never makes anyone less likely to take it.
\text{LATE} = \frac{E[Y \mid Z=1] - E[Y \mid Z=0]}{E[D \mid Z=1] - E[D \mid Z=0]}

The denominator is now the difference in take-up between arms
As control units gain access, the difference shrinks, the instrument weakens, and estimates become noisy
This is an instrumental variables estimator, with random assignment as the instrument (Chapter 6)

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
section: Which Effect Does a Decision-Maker Need?
text:
Which Effect Does a Decision-Maker Need?






ITT or LATE?



ITT: what happens if you offer the treatment without forcing it. Relevant for a manager deciding whether to buy licences for everyone (seat-based pricing), or a government deciding whether to send letters
LATE / CACE: what happens to those who use it because it was offered. Relevant if you pay only for usage, or want to know whether the treatment itself works
LATE is the effect for compliers only. Never-takers and always-takers may respond differently, so LATE need not equal the ATE

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Missing Outcomes






When Attrition Breaks Randomization


Attrition: outcomes are missing for some units (survey non-response, people moving, firms closing, employees leaving).

If attrition is unrelated to treatment and potential outcomes, the remaining sample is still balanced, just smaller
If treatment affects who stays (e.g., the treated group is easier to contact), the remaining treated and control units are no longer comparable
Always check: attrition rates by arm, and baseline characteristics of those who leave vs. stay

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Responses to Attrition






Prevention First, Then Bounds


Prevention: use administrative outcomes where possible (tax, health, payroll, code repositories); track participants; incentivize responses.
Bounds: when attrition differs by arm, bound the effect instead of assuming it away. Lee bounds trim the arm with less attrition so both arms have the same share of observed outcomes, once from the top and once from the bottom of the outcome distribution (Lee 2009). Assuming treatment affects whether an outcome is observed in only one direction, the effect for units that would be observed in either arm lies between the two.
Reporting: report attrition, and report experiments that failed. Selective reporting of only the experiments that “worked” is attrition at the level of the literature.

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
When Treatment Leaks Across Units






Interference in Practice



Learning: a developer using an AI tool shares prompts or code with untreated teammates
Task reallocation: treated workers finish faster and take over harder tasks from untreated colleagues
Contamination: control units hear about the treatment and seek it out
Markets: a subsidy for some buyers raises prices for everyone

Positive spillovers to the control group make the treated–control difference smaller than the true effect; negative spillovers (for example, treated workers taking easy tasks from untreated ones) make it larger. In markets they can change its meaning entirely.

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Designing for Spillovers






Options



Randomize clusters (teams, offices, villages) so spillovers stay within treatment or control (at a cost in power; Chapter 3)
Separate treated and control units in space or time
Measure spillovers deliberately: randomize the share of each cluster that is treated, and compare untreated units in highly treated clusters with untreated units in untreated clusters
Check for contamination: does the control group’s take-up rise over time?

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Other Threats Worth Naming






Beyond the Big Three



Hawthorne effects: being studied changes behaviour
Demand effects: participants guess the hypothesis and act on it (a concern in lab studies)
Peeking and early stopping: checking results repeatedly and stopping when significant inflates false positives (common in A/B tests)
Scale-up: effects in a pilot may not hold when everyone is treated, because markets and organizations adjust

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
section: Case Study: Low Take-Up, Contamination, and Attrition
text:
Case Study: Low Take-Up, Contamination, and Attrition






Cui, Demirer, Jaffe, Musolff, Peng & Salz (2026), Management Science (Cui et al. 2026)


Three randomized experiments offering GitHub Copilot to 4,867 developers at Microsoft, Accenture, and a Fortune 100 firm (design details in Chapter 4). The paper is a good guide to analyzing and reporting an imperfect experiment.









The Complications



Low take-up: in the first two weeks at Microsoft only 8.5% of the treated group signed up; two reminder emails raised it to 42.5%
Never-takers: across experiments, 30–40% of developers never tried the tool, despite low adoption costs
Always-takers: a few Microsoft control developers (0.5%) needed access for their work
Contamination and early end: the Microsoft experiment ended earlier than planned as control developers sought access
Attrition: a second Accenture experiment was abandoned after a layoff affected 42% of participants, leaving no reliable data on who used the tool
Noisy outcomes: most developer-weeks have zero completed pull requests, so each experiment has low power

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
section: Case Study: How the Authors Responded
text:
Case Study: How the Authors Responded






Analyzing an Imperfect Experiment



Instrumental variables: random assignment instruments for adoption, giving a LATE for developers who adopted because they were offered access
Weighted IV: once control groups gain access, the adoption gap shrinks and the instrument weakens. The authors weight each period by the adoption difference between arms, so periods with more experimental variation count more
Fixed effects: developer and week fixed effects absorb stable productivity differences and calendar shocks, improving precision
Pooling: a precision-weighted average across the three experiments: +26.1% completed pull requests (SE 10.3%)
Reporting the failure: the abandoned Accenture experiment is reported in an appendix; including it, with conservatively imputed adoption, changes the pooled estimate to +21.3%
ITT vs. LATE: the ITT is much smaller than the LATE because many developers never adopted. Which matters depends on whether the firm pays per licence or per use

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Case Study: What to Copy






Practices to Reuse



Report the ITT and the LATE side by side, and say which one the decision needs (paying per licence vs. per use).
Down-weight periods with little experimental variation. Once controls gain access, weighting by the adoption gap keeps weak periods from adding noise.
Report the experiment that failed, and show how including it changes the answer (+26.1% to +21.3%).

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Case Study: Discussion Questions

Why would comparing developers who used Copilot with those who did not give a misleading answer?
Reminder emails raised take-up from 8.5% to 42.5%. How does that change the ITT, and the precision of the LATE?
What does the exclusion restriction require here? Could the invitation email itself change productivity?
Who are the compliers in this experiment? Would you expect their effect to be larger or smaller than for never-takers?
Why is reporting the abandoned experiment important, even though it is noisy?

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Case Study: Suggested Answers (1–2)

Developers choose whether to use the tool. Those who do may be more motivated, more junior, or working on tasks where it helps, so the comparison mixes the tool’s effect with these differences.
With one-sided non-compliance, the ITT equals the take-up gap times the effect for compliers, so higher take-up makes the ITT larger. The LATE becomes more precise, because its standard error is roughly the ITT’s standard error divided by the take-up gap.

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Case Study: Suggested Answers (3–5)

The invitation must change output only through using Copilot. An email that signals management attention or prompts developers to work harder would violate exclusion and inflate the estimated effect of use.
Compliers adopt when offered, often after reminders. Never-takers may expect little benefit, for example because their tasks suit the tool less, so their effect could well be smaller; the data cannot confirm this.
Leaving out experiments that went badly biases the evidence, just as attrition biases a single study. Reporting it shows how much the conclusion depends on the experiments that did work (+26.1% vs. +21.3%).

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Summary

Non-compliance: analyze by assignment (ITT); scale by take-up to get the effect for compliers (CACE/LATE); never compare by receipt
One-sided non-compliance needs exclusion; two-sided also needs monotonicity, and the estimator becomes IV
Attrition: prevent it, check it by arm, and bound it when it differs
Spillovers: randomize at the right level, and measure contamination
Imperfect experiments can still be informative, if analyzed carefully and reported in full

References
