Lee, David S. 2009. “Training, Wages, and Sample Selection: Estimating Sharp Bounds on Treatment Effects.” Review of Economic Studies 76 (3): 1071–102. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-937X.2009.00536.x.

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Real experiments rarely go exactly to plan. People offered a treatment do not take it; people in the control group find a way to get it; outcomes go missing; treated units affect untreated ones.
This chapter covers the three most common problems and what to do about each. The running case study is the set of AI coding-assistant experiments at Microsoft, Accenture, and a Fortune 100 firm, which ran into all three.
Non-compliance leads naturally to instrumental variables, the topic of Chapter 6.

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Non-Compliance

Assigned Is Not the Same as Treated






NoteTwo Treatment Variables




Z_i: assignment, which the researcher randomizes (offered the AI tool, sent a letter, invited to a program)
D_i: receipt, which the unit chooses (actually used the tool, actually enrolled)










Experiment
Assignment Z
Receipt D
Take-up




IRS outreach (Chapter 3)
Letter sent
Enrolled in coverage
+1.1 percentage points (difference between arms)


AI coding assistant (this chapter)
Access offered
Developer used the tool
About 60–70% of those offered eventually tried it



When D \neq Z for some units, we have non-compliance.




Three Tempting Comparisons, Two of Them Wrong






WarningComparing by Receipt Breaks Randomization











Comparison
What it compares
Valid?




Intent-to-treat (ITT)
Everyone assigned vs. everyone not assigned, regardless of take-up
Yes: this is the randomized comparison


As-treated
Those who used the treatment vs. those who did not
No: who uses it is a choice


Naive per-protocol
Units that followed their assignment in each arm (takers if offered, non-takers if not)
No: drops a self-selected subset



Developers who choose to use an AI tool may be more motivated, more junior, or working on different tasks. Once we compare by choice, selection bias is back. The as-treated and naive per-protocol comparisons are really observational analyses inside an experiment: they could only be rescued by adjusting for everything that drives take-up (Hernán and Robins 2020).




Compliance Types






NoteFour Kinds of Units



Each unit has two potential receipts: D_i(1) if assigned, D_i(0) if not.









Type
D_i(0)
D_i(1)
Example




Compliers
0
1
Use the tool if and only if offered


Never-takers
0
0
Never use it, even if offered


Always-takers
1
1
Find a way to use it even in the control group


Defiers
1
0
Use it only if not offered



We never observe a unit’s type directly, because we only see one of the two receipts.




One-Sided Non-Compliance






TipWhen the Control Group Cannot Get the Treatment



If control units have no access (D_i(0) = 0 for all), there are no always-takers or defiers. Then:
\underbrace{\text{ITT}_Y}_{\text{effect of assignment on } Y} = \underbrace{\text{ITT}_D}_{\text{share of compliers}} \times \underbrace{\text{CACE}}_{\text{effect for compliers}}
\text{CACE} = \frac{\text{ITT}_Y}{\text{ITT}_D} = \frac{E[Y \mid Z=1] - E[Y \mid Z=0]}{E[D \mid Z=1] - E[D \mid Z=0]}
Key assumption, exclusion: assignment affects outcomes only through receipt. An email offering an AI tool must not raise productivity by itself (for example, by signalling that management is watching).




Simulation: As-Treated vs. ITT vs. CACE


Code
library(fixest)
set.seed(2026)
n <- 4000
motivation <- rnorm(n)                                  # unobserved
z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)                                  # random offer
# Only offered developers can adopt; motivated ones adopt more often
d <- z * rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.5 + 1.2 * motivation))
y <- 5 + 2 * motivation + 1.5 * d + rnorm(n)            # true effect of use = 1.5

itt_y <- mean(y[z == 1]) - mean(y[z == 0])
itt_d <- mean(d[z == 1]) - mean(d[z == 0])

round(c(take_up       = itt_d,
        as_treated    = mean(y[d == 1]) - mean(y[d == 0]),
        ITT           = itt_y,
        CACE_wald     = itt_y / itt_d,
        CACE_2SLS     = unname(coef(feols(y ~ 1 | d ~ z, data = data.frame(y, d, z)))["fit_d"])), 2)


   take_up as_treated        ITT  CACE_wald  CACE_2SLS 
      0.39       2.87       0.58       1.47       1.47 




As-treated is badly biased upwards: motivated developers both adopt more and produce more.
The ITT is unbiased for the effect of the offer, but diluted by non-adopters.
Dividing by take-up recovers the effect of use for compliers. Two-stage least squares gives the same number; Chapter 6 develops it in general.




Two-Sided Non-Compliance






WarningWhen Some Controls Get Treated Anyway



If control units can obtain the treatment, always-takers exist. The same ratio still identifies the effect for compliers, now called the local average treatment effect (LATE), under one more assumption:
Monotonicity (no defiers): being offered the treatment never makes anyone less likely to take it.
\text{LATE} = \frac{E[Y \mid Z=1] - E[Y \mid Z=0]}{E[D \mid Z=1] - E[D \mid Z=0]}

The denominator is now the difference in take-up between arms
As control units gain access, the difference shrinks, the instrument weakens, and estimates become noisy
This is an instrumental variables estimator, with random assignment as the instrument (Chapter 6)





Which Effect Does a Decision-Maker Need?






TipITT or LATE?




ITT: what happens if you offer the treatment without forcing it. Relevant for a manager deciding whether to buy licences for everyone (seat-based pricing), or a government deciding whether to send letters
LATE / CACE: what happens to those who use it because it was offered. Relevant if you pay only for usage, or want to know whether the treatment itself works
LATE is the effect for compliers only. Never-takers and always-takers may respond differently, so LATE need not equal the ATE

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Attrition

Missing Outcomes






WarningWhen Attrition Breaks Randomization



Attrition: outcomes are missing for some units (survey non-response, people moving, firms closing, employees leaving).

If attrition is unrelated to treatment and potential outcomes, the remaining sample is still balanced, just smaller
If treatment affects who stays (e.g., the treated group is easier to contact), the remaining treated and control units are no longer comparable
Always check: attrition rates by arm, and baseline characteristics of those who leave vs. stay





Responses to Attrition






TipPrevention First, Then Bounds



Prevention: use administrative outcomes where possible (tax, health, payroll, code repositories); track participants; incentivize responses.
Bounds: when attrition differs by arm, bound the effect instead of assuming it away. Lee bounds trim the arm with less attrition so both arms have the same share of observed outcomes, once from the top and once from the bottom of the outcome distribution (Lee 2009). Assuming treatment affects whether an outcome is observed in only one direction, the effect for units that would be observed in either arm lies between the two.
Reporting: report attrition, and report experiments that failed. Selective reporting of only the experiments that “worked” is attrition at the level of the literature.

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
text:
Spillovers

When Treatment Leaks Across Units






WarningInterference in Practice




Learning: a developer using an AI tool shares prompts or code with untreated teammates
Task reallocation: treated workers finish faster and take over harder tasks from untreated colleagues
Contamination: control units hear about the treatment and seek it out
Markets: a subsidy for some buyers raises prices for everyone

Positive spillovers to the control group make the treated–control difference smaller than the true effect; negative spillovers (for example, treated workers taking easy tasks from untreated ones) make it larger. In markets they can change its meaning entirely.




Designing for Spillovers






TipOptions




Randomize clusters (teams, offices, villages) so spillovers stay within treatment or control (at a cost in power; Chapter 3)
Separate treated and control units in space or time
Measure spillovers deliberately: randomize the share of each cluster that is treated, and compare untreated units in highly treated clusters with untreated units in untreated clusters
Check for contamination: does the control group’s take-up rise over time?





Other Threats Worth Naming






NoteBeyond the Big Three




Hawthorne effects: being studied changes behaviour
Demand effects: participants guess the hypothesis and act on it (a concern in lab studies)
Peeking and early stopping: checking results repeatedly and stopping when significant inflates false positives (common in A/B tests)
Scale-up: effects in a pilot may not hold when everyone is treated, because markets and organizations adjust

title: When Experiments Go Wrong
section: Case Study: AI Experiments in Three Firms
text:
Case Study: AI Experiments in Three Firms

Case Study: Low Take-Up, Contamination, and Attrition






NoteCui, Demirer, Jaffe, Musolff, Peng & Salz (2026), Management Science (Cui et al. 2026)



Three randomized experiments offering GitHub Copilot to 4,867 developers at Microsoft, Accenture, and a Fortune 100 firm (design details in Chapter 4). The paper is a good guide to analyzing and reporting an imperfect experiment.








WarningThe Complications




Low take-up: in the first two weeks at Microsoft only 8.5% of the treated group signed up; two reminder emails raised it to 42.5%
Never-takers: across experiments, 30–40% of developers never tried the tool, despite low adoption costs
Always-takers: a few Microsoft control developers (0.5%) needed access for their work
Contamination and early end: the Microsoft experiment ended earlier than planned as control developers sought access
Attrition: a second Accenture experiment was abandoned after a layoff affected 42% of participants, leaving no reliable data on who used the tool
Noisy outcomes: most developer-weeks have zero completed pull requests, so each experiment has low power





Case Study: How the Authors Responded






TipAnalyzing an Imperfect Experiment




Instrumental variables: random assignment instruments for adoption, giving a LATE for developers who adopted because they were offered access
Weighted IV: once control groups gain access, the adoption gap shrinks and the instrument weakens. The authors weight each period by the adoption difference between arms, so periods with more experimental variation count more
Fixed effects: developer and week fixed effects absorb stable productivity differences and calendar shocks, improving precision
Pooling: a precision-weighted average across the three experiments: +26.1% completed pull requests (SE 10.3%)
Reporting the failure: the abandoned Accenture experiment is reported in an appendix; including it, with conservatively imputed adoption, changes the pooled estimate to +21.3%
ITT vs. LATE: the ITT is much smaller than the LATE because many developers never adopted. Which matters depends on whether the firm pays per licence or per use





Case Study: What to Copy






TipPractices to Reuse




Report the ITT and the LATE side by side, and say which one the decision needs (paying per licence vs. per use).
Down-weight periods with little experimental variation. Once controls gain access, weighting by the adoption gap keeps weak periods from adding noise.
Report the experiment that failed, and show how including it changes the answer (+26.1% to +21.3%).





Case Study: Discussion Questions


Why would comparing developers who used Copilot with those who did not give a misleading answer?
Reminder emails raised take-up from 8.5% to 42.5%. How does that change the ITT, and the precision of the LATE?
What does the exclusion restriction require here? Could the invitation email itself change productivity?
Who are the compliers in this experiment? Would you expect their effect to be larger or smaller than for never-takers?
Why is reporting the abandoned experiment important, even though it is noisy?








NoteSuggested Answers (click to expand)






Developers choose whether to use the tool. Those who do may be more motivated, more junior, or working on tasks where it helps, so the comparison mixes the tool’s effect with these differences.
With one-sided non-compliance, the ITT equals the take-up gap times the effect for compliers, so higher take-up makes the ITT larger. The LATE becomes more precise, because its standard error is roughly the ITT’s standard error divided by the take-up gap.
The invitation must change output only through using Copilot. An email that signals management attention or prompts developers to work harder would violate exclusion and inflate the estimated effect of use.
Compliers adopt when offered, often after reminders. Never-takers may expect little benefit, for example because their tasks suit the tool less, so their effect could well be smaller; the data cannot confirm this.
Leaving out experiments that went badly biases the evidence, just as attrition biases a single study. Reporting it shows how much the conclusion depends on the experiments that did work (+26.1% vs. +21.3%).

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Where This Chapter Fits






Step 3: Is treatment decided by a cutoff on a score?



You arrive here when: A rule assigns treatment to units above (or below) a threshold on a score, such as income, a test score, or a credit score.
This chapter: Sharp and fuzzy designs, local linear estimation, bandwidths, and checks for manipulation.
Next: Chapter 8: when there is no cutoff, but you observe units over time.

See the design flowchart in Chapter 1.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
In Practice: Regression Discontinuity






Practitioner Summary



Use it when: a rule gives treatment to units above (or below) a cutoff on a score
What you need: the score, the cutoff, the outcome, and many observations close to the cutoff
What must hold: nothing else changes at the cutoff, and units cannot precisely sort to the favourable side
Checks to run: a plot of binned means; a density test; smooth covariates; several bandwidths, a donut, and placebo cutoffs; the first stage if the design is fuzzy
In R: rdrobust(y, x, c = 0) (add fuzzy = d), rdplot(), rddensity()
Telling a manager: “Households just either side of the threshold are alike except for the subsidy, so the jump at the threshold is the subsidy’s effect for households near it.”

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Rules with Thresholds Are Everywhere






Treatment Assigned by a Score










Running variable (score)
Cutoff
Treatment




Household income
A share of the poverty line
Larger insurance subsidy


Credit score (FICO)
A lender’s internal cutoff
Higher credit limit


Age
65
Eligibility for public health insurance


Exam score
Admission mark
Selective school place


Firm size
Number of employees
Regulation or reporting rules



The score usually also affects the outcome directly (richer households buy more insurance anyway), so comparing everyone above with everyone below is confounded.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
The RDD Idea






Compare Units Just on Either Side


A household at 199% of the poverty line and one at 201% differ in income by very little, but face different subsidies. If nothing else jumps at the cutoff, a jump in the outcome at the cutoff can only come from the jump in treatment.

The comparison is local: it tells us the effect for units near the cutoff
In exchange, it requires only that outcomes would have changed smoothly through the cutoff without the treatment

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Setup and Estimand






Sharp RDD



Running variable X_i (the score); cutoff c
Treatment is fully determined by the score: D_i = \mathbb{1}[X_i \geq c] (or X_i < c, as for an income test)
Estimand: the effect at the cutoff (written here with treatment above the cutoff; reverse the sign when treatment is below it)

\tau_{RD} = \lim_{x \downarrow c} E[Y_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} E[Y_i \mid X_i = x] = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid X_i = c]









The Key Assumption: Continuity


E[Y_i(0) \mid X_i = x] and E[Y_i(1) \mid X_i = x] are continuous at x = c: without the treatment, average outcomes would not jump at the cutoff.
This fails if units can precisely manipulate their score to land on the preferred side, or if another policy changes at the same cutoff.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Estimation: Local Linear Regression






Fit a Line on Each Side, Near the Cutoff


Within a bandwidth h of the cutoff, regress Y on X - c separately on each side (or with an interaction), usually weighting observations closer to the cutoff more heavily (a triangular kernel). The estimate is the gap between the two fitted lines at X = c.

Bandwidth trade-off: a narrow window reduces bias (units are more similar) but increases noise
Data-driven bandwidths choose h to balance the two (Imbens and Kalyanaraman 2012); robust bias-corrected confidence intervals account for the approximation error (Calonico et al. 2014)
Avoid high-order global polynomials fitted to all the data: they can produce misleading jumps (Gelman and Imbens 2019)
Software: rdrobust (estimation), rddensity (manipulation tests), rdplot (graphs)

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Simulation: A Sharp RDD


Code
suppressMessages({library(rdrobust); library(rddensity)})
set.seed(2026)
n <- 5000

# Income relative to a subsidy cutoff (in % of the poverty line); subsidy below the cutoff
x <- runif(n, -100, 100)
d <- as.integer(x < 0)
# Take-up rises with income anyway, and the subsidy adds 8 points
y <- 40 + 0.15 * x - 0.0008 * x^2 + 8 * d + rnorm(n, 0, 6)

naive <- mean(y[d == 1]) - mean(y[d == 0])
rd <- rdrobust(y, x, c = 0)           # estimates right side minus left side
round(c(naive_comparison = naive,
        RD_effect = -rd$coef[1],      # subsidy is on the left, so flip the sign
        robust_CI_low = -rd$ci[3, 2], robust_CI_high = -rd$ci[3, 1],
        bandwidth = rd$bws[1, 1]), 2)


naive_comparison        RD_effect    robust_CI_low   robust_CI_high 
           -7.02             8.10             6.57             9.71 
       bandwidth 
           28.42 




The naive comparison of eligible and ineligible households even has the wrong sign: richer households buy more insurance regardless of the subsidy.
RDD compares households near the cutoff and recovers the true 8-point effect.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Seeing the Discontinuity


Code
bins <- cut(x, breaks = seq(-100, 100, by = 5))
bx <- tapply(x, bins, mean); by <- tapply(y, bins, mean)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(bx, by, pch = 19, col = "grey35", xlab = "Income relative to cutoff (% of poverty line)",
     ylab = "Take-up (%)", main = "Binned means and local linear fits")
left <- x < 0 & x > -rd$bws[1, 1]; right <- x >= 0 & x < rd$bws[1, 1]
abline(v = 0, col = "#c2410c", lty = 2)
fl <- lm(y ~ x, subset = left); fr <- lm(y ~ x, subset = right)
lines(c(-rd$bws[1, 1], 0), predict(fl, data.frame(x = c(-rd$bws[1, 1], 0))), lwd = 3, col = "#1565c0")
lines(c(0, rd$bws[1, 1]), predict(fr, data.frame(x = c(0, rd$bws[1, 1]))), lwd = 3, col = "#1565c0")

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
section: When the Rule Is Not Followed Exactly
text:
When the Rule Is Not Followed Exactly






Fuzzy RDD


Crossing the cutoff changes the probability or amount of treatment, but does not determine it: some units below get treated, some above do not, or the treatment is continuous (a credit limit).
\tau_{FRD} = \frac{\lim_{x \downarrow c} E[Y \mid X = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} E[Y \mid X = x]}{\lim_{x \downarrow c} E[D \mid X = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} E[D \mid X = x]} = \frac{\text{jump in outcome}}{\text{jump in treatment}}

This is an instrumental variables estimator (Chapter 6), with “being above the cutoff” as the instrument, used only near the cutoff
It estimates a LATE for compliers at the cutoff: units whose treatment changes because they cross it
Needs the IV assumptions locally: the cutoff affects outcomes only through treatment, and monotonicity

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Simulation: A Fuzzy RDD


Code
# Credit score relative to a lender's cutoff; the credit limit jumps by about $1,500 above it
fico   <- runif(n, -50, 50)
above  <- as.integer(fico >= 0)
limit  <- 3000 + 20 * fico + 1500 * above + rnorm(n, 0, 400)
borrow <- 1000 + 10 * fico + 0.30 * limit + rnorm(n, 0, 500)   # 30 cents borrowed per extra $1 of limit

fz <- rdrobust(borrow, fico, c = 0, fuzzy = limit)
round(c(estimate = fz$coef[1], robust_CI_low = fz$ci[3, 1], robust_CI_high = fz$ci[3, 2]), 3)


      estimate  robust_CI_low robust_CI_high 
         0.338          0.272          0.422

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Threats and Diagnostics






What Can Break an RDD









Threat
Diagnostic




Manipulation: units sort precisely to the favourable side
Density test: is there a spike in the number of units just on one side? (McCrary 2008; Cattaneo et al. 2020)


Other differences at the cutoff
Covariate continuity: predetermined characteristics should not jump


Another policy uses the same cutoff
Institutional knowledge; drop that cutoff as a check


Spurious jumps
Placebo cutoffs where nothing changes should show no effect


Sensitivity to choices
Report results for several bandwidths, and a donut that drops units right at the cutoff

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Manipulation Test in R


Code
dens <- rddensity(x, c = 0)
c(density_test_p_value = round(dens$test$p_jk, 3))


density_test_p_value 
               0.249 




A large p-value means no evidence that units bunch on one side. In the simulation, incomes were drawn without manipulation, so the test should not reject.
In real data, think about who controls the score: households can sometimes adjust reported income; it is much harder for consumers to fine-tune a credit score to land just above a particular lender’s cutoff.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
section: Case Study 1: How Much Will People Pay for Insurance?
text:
Case Study 1: How Much Will People Pay for Insurance?






Finkelstein, Hendren & Shepard (2019), American Economic Review (Finkelstein et al. 2019)


Question: How much are low-income adults willing to pay for health insurance, and what does that imply for subsidy design?
Setting: Massachusetts’ subsidized insurance exchange (CommCare), 2009–2013, for adults below 300% of the federal poverty line (FPL) without access to other coverage.
The rule: subsidies fall in steps at 150%, 200%, and 250% of FPL. At each threshold the monthly premium an enrollee pays jumps by about $40, while the plans on offer stay largely the same.
Data: administrative enrollment and claims records, plus survey data to count the eligible population at each income level.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 1: The Design






Three Discontinuities in Price



Running variable: income as a percentage of FPL; treatment: the premium an enrollee faces
Outcomes: take-up of insurance, and the medical costs of those who enroll
Estimation: linear fits in income on each side of each threshold (a bandwidth of 50% of FPL), with robustness to a 25% bandwidth and quadratic fits
Demand and cost curves: each threshold gives a price change and a change in who enrolls, tracing out willingness to pay and the costs of marginal enrollees

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 1: Results






Main Findings



Take-up falls by about 25% (20–24 percentage points) for each $40 increase in the monthly premium: demand is very price-sensitive
People who drop out when prices rise are cheaper to insure: evidence of adverse selection
Across the range observed, enrollees’ willingness to pay is less than half of the costs they impose on insurers
Implication: even generous subsidies leave many uninsured. With premiums at 25% of insurers’ average costs, at most half would enrol; at 10%, at least 20% would remain uninsured

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 1: Threats and Checks






Could People Manipulate Their Income?



Density checks: no bunching of the eligible population at the thresholds in survey data; slight bunching in enrollment data in 2012–13 has an administrative explanation, and none appears in the base year
Why manipulation is hard here: applicants reported income, but the formula translating it into subsidy brackets was largely hidden from them, and proof of income was required
Another change at 200% FPL: at that threshold some groups also lose Medicaid eligibility and copayments rise slightly. Results are robust to dropping that threshold

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 1: What to Copy






Practices to Reuse



Use every cutoff the rule offers, and drop the one where another policy also changes (200% FPL) as a check.
Look for bunching in data units cannot influence (survey counts) as well as data they can (enrollment).
Turn local effects into the curve the decision needs: three price jumps trace out willingness to pay against cost.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 1: Discussion Questions

Why does comparing take-up for everyone above and below 200% FPL not identify the effect of price?
What would you expect to see in the data if people misreported income to stay below a threshold?
Why is dropping the 200% FPL threshold a useful robustness check?
The estimates apply to people near 150%, 200%, and 250% FPL. How far would you extrapolate them?
What does “willingness to pay is less than half of expected costs” imply for an insurance mandate?

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 1: Suggested Answers (1–3)

Income affects take-up directly: richer households differ in needs, preferences, and access to other coverage. A comparison of everyone above and below mixes the price change with these differences; the RD uses only households close to the threshold.
Bunching: more enrollees just below each threshold than just above, and a jump in the density of reported income at the cutoff.
At 200% FPL some groups also lose Medicaid eligibility and copayments rise, so more than the premium changes there. Results that hold without that threshold rely only on cutoffs where the premium is the main change.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 1: Suggested Answers (4–5)

Only cautiously. The estimates describe people near 150–250% FPL in Massachusetts’ exchange. The roughly linear patterns between thresholds support modest interpolation within that range, not extrapolation to much poorer or richer people or other markets.
Many low-income adults would not buy insurance at its cost even if it were offered at a fair price. Reaching high coverage would need large subsidies or a mandate. One reason the paper discusses is uncompensated care: the uninsured receive some care without paying for it, which lowers the value of insurance to them.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
section: Case Study 2: Do Consumers Borrow More When Banks Lend More?
text:
Case Study 2: Do Consumers Borrow More When Banks Lend More?






Agarwal, Chomsisengphet, Mahoney & Stroebel (2018), Quarterly Journal of Economics (Agarwal et al. 2018)


Question: When banks’ cost of funds falls (for example, through monetary policy), does extra credit reach consumers who want to borrow?
Key quantity: the marginal propensity to borrow (MPB): how much extra a consumer borrows for each extra dollar of credit limit.
The rule: banks set credit limits partly by FICO score cutoffs (for example 660, 700, 720, 740, 760). At a cutoff, the credit limit jumps, while consumers just below and just above are otherwise similar.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 2: The Design






A Fuzzy RDD, Many Times Over



743 credit-limit discontinuities across lenders and cutoffs, covering 8.5 million new credit cards within 50 FICO points of a cutoff
First stage: the credit limit jumps at each cutoff, and the jump persists for years
Fuzzy RD: the jump in borrowing divided by the jump in credit limit, a local Wald estimator
Bandwidth: chosen by a data-driven rule for each discontinuity; estimates pooled across discontinuities and by FICO group
Checks: interest rates, borrower characteristics, and the number of new accounts all move smoothly through the cutoffs

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 2: Results






Main Findings



The MPB falls with credit score: about 59 cents borrowed per extra dollar of credit limit for consumers with FICO scores below 660, and essentially zero above 740
For the riskiest borrowers, higher limits reduce banks’ profits, so banks are least willing to lend more to the consumers who most want to borrow
Policy implication: cheaper funding for banks raises household borrowing only if extra credit reaches low-score consumers, which banks have little incentive to do










Why Credit Scores Are a Good Running Variable


Banks’ credit-limit rules are not known to consumers, and the FICO formula is proprietary, so even a consumer who knew a cutoff would find it very hard to move their score precisely across it (the authors’ argument). Consistent with this, the authors show that the number of new accounts, borrower characteristics, and interest rates all move smoothly through the cutoffs.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 2: What to Copy






Practices to Reuse



Pool many discontinuities (743) for precision and to compare groups of borrowers.
Show the first stage persists before interpreting effects on borrowing.
Report the parameter policymakers use: the marginal propensity to borrow, by credit score.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 2: Discussion Questions

Why is this a fuzzy rather than a sharp design? What is the “treatment”?
Write the fuzzy RD estimate as an IV estimate. What are the instrument, the first stage, and the reduced form?
Who are the compliers at a FICO cutoff, and is their MPB the one a central bank cares about?
What could make outcomes jump at a FICO cutoff other than the credit limit? How do the authors check?
Why does having 743 discontinuities, rather than one, strengthen the conclusions?

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 2: Suggested Answers (1–2)

Crossing the cutoff raises the average credit limit, but limits also depend on other factors and vary within each side. The treatment is the credit limit, a continuous amount, so the jump in borrowing is scaled by the jump in the limit.
Instrument: an indicator for being above the cutoff. First stage: the jump in the credit limit at the cutoff. Reduced form: the jump in borrowing. The MPB is the reduced form divided by the first stage, estimated near the cutoff.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 2: Suggested Answers (3–4)

New cardholders near a lender’s cutoff whose limit is set by that rule. Central banks care about households whose credit changes when banks’ funding costs change; these borrowers are a relevant group, but local to particular scores and lenders.
Other loan terms (interest rates, fees), or banks approving more accounts above the cutoff, which would change who is in the sample. The authors show interest rates, borrower characteristics, and the number of accounts are smooth through the cutoffs.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 2: Suggested Answers (5)

Many cutoffs give precision and let the authors estimate effects across the score distribution. A single cutoff could coincide with some other rule; consistent results across many lenders and cutoffs make that explanation unlikely.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Many policies allocate treatment by a rule: a subsidy for incomes below a threshold, a higher credit limit above a credit score, a scholarship above an exam mark.
Units just below and just above the threshold are almost identical, except for treatment. Comparing them gives a credible, if local, causal effect.
Two case studies: subsidized health insurance in Massachusetts (premiums jump at income thresholds), and credit card limits that jump at credit-score cutoffs (a fuzzy design, which links back to IV).

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Motivation

Rules with Thresholds Are Everywhere






NoteTreatment Assigned by a Score











Running variable (score)
Cutoff
Treatment




Household income
A share of the poverty line
Larger insurance subsidy


Credit score (FICO)
A lender’s internal cutoff
Higher credit limit


Age
65
Eligibility for public health insurance


Exam score
Admission mark
Selective school place


Firm size
Number of employees
Regulation or reporting rules



The score usually also affects the outcome directly (richer households buy more insurance anyway), so comparing everyone above with everyone below is confounded.




The RDD Idea






TipCompare Units Just on Either Side



A household at 199% of the poverty line and one at 201% differ in income by very little, but face different subsidies. If nothing else jumps at the cutoff, a jump in the outcome at the cutoff can only come from the jump in treatment.

The comparison is local: it tells us the effect for units near the cutoff
In exchange, it requires only that outcomes would have changed smoothly through the cutoff without the treatment

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
The Sharp Design

Setup and Estimand






NoteSharp RDD




Running variable X_i (the score); cutoff c
Treatment is fully determined by the score: D_i = \mathbb{1}[X_i \geq c] (or X_i < c, as for an income test)
Estimand: the effect at the cutoff (written here with treatment above the cutoff; reverse the sign when treatment is below it)

\tau_{RD} = \lim_{x \downarrow c} E[Y_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} E[Y_i \mid X_i = x] = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid X_i = c]








ImportantThe Key Assumption: Continuity



E[Y_i(0) \mid X_i = x] and E[Y_i(1) \mid X_i = x] are continuous at x = c: without the treatment, average outcomes would not jump at the cutoff.
This fails if units can precisely manipulate their score to land on the preferred side, or if another policy changes at the same cutoff.




Estimation: Local Linear Regression






TipFit a Line on Each Side, Near the Cutoff



Within a bandwidth h of the cutoff, regress Y on X - c separately on each side (or with an interaction), usually weighting observations closer to the cutoff more heavily (a triangular kernel). The estimate is the gap between the two fitted lines at X = c.

Bandwidth trade-off: a narrow window reduces bias (units are more similar) but increases noise
Data-driven bandwidths choose h to balance the two (Imbens and Kalyanaraman 2012); robust bias-corrected confidence intervals account for the approximation error (Calonico et al. 2014)
Avoid high-order global polynomials fitted to all the data: they can produce misleading jumps (Gelman and Imbens 2019)
Software: rdrobust (estimation), rddensity (manipulation tests), rdplot (graphs)





Simulation: A Sharp RDD


Code
suppressMessages({library(rdrobust); library(rddensity)})
set.seed(2026)
n <- 5000

# Income relative to a subsidy cutoff (in % of the poverty line); subsidy below the cutoff
x <- runif(n, -100, 100)
d <- as.integer(x < 0)
# Take-up rises with income anyway, and the subsidy adds 8 points
y <- 40 + 0.15 * x - 0.0008 * x^2 + 8 * d + rnorm(n, 0, 6)

naive <- mean(y[d == 1]) - mean(y[d == 0])
rd <- rdrobust(y, x, c = 0)           # estimates right side minus left side
round(c(naive_comparison = naive,
        RD_effect = -rd$coef[1],      # subsidy is on the left, so flip the sign
        robust_CI_low = -rd$ci[3, 2], robust_CI_high = -rd$ci[3, 1],
        bandwidth = rd$bws[1, 1]), 2)


naive_comparison        RD_effect    robust_CI_low   robust_CI_high 
           -7.02             8.10             6.57             9.71 
       bandwidth 
           28.42 




The naive comparison of eligible and ineligible households even has the wrong sign: richer households buy more insurance regardless of the subsidy.
RDD compares households near the cutoff and recovers the true 8-point effect.




Seeing the Discontinuity


Code
bins <- cut(x, breaks = seq(-100, 100, by = 5))
bx <- tapply(x, bins, mean); by <- tapply(y, bins, mean)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(bx, by, pch = 19, col = "grey35", xlab = "Income relative to cutoff (% of poverty line)",
     ylab = "Take-up (%)", main = "Binned means and local linear fits")
left <- x < 0 & x > -rd$bws[1, 1]; right <- x >= 0 & x < rd$bws[1, 1]
abline(v = 0, col = "#c2410c", lty = 2)
fl <- lm(y ~ x, subset = left); fr <- lm(y ~ x, subset = right)
lines(c(-rd$bws[1, 1], 0), predict(fl, data.frame(x = c(-rd$bws[1, 1], 0))), lwd = 3, col = "#1565c0")
lines(c(0, rd$bws[1, 1]), predict(fr, data.frame(x = c(0, rd$bws[1, 1]))), lwd = 3, col = "#1565c0")

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
The Fuzzy Design

When the Rule Is Not Followed Exactly






NoteFuzzy RDD



Crossing the cutoff changes the probability or amount of treatment, but does not determine it: some units below get treated, some above do not, or the treatment is continuous (a credit limit).
\tau_{FRD} = \frac{\lim_{x \downarrow c} E[Y \mid X = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} E[Y \mid X = x]}{\lim_{x \downarrow c} E[D \mid X = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} E[D \mid X = x]} = \frac{\text{jump in outcome}}{\text{jump in treatment}}

This is an instrumental variables estimator (Chapter 6), with “being above the cutoff” as the instrument, used only near the cutoff
It estimates a LATE for compliers at the cutoff: units whose treatment changes because they cross it
Needs the IV assumptions locally: the cutoff affects outcomes only through treatment, and monotonicity





Simulation: A Fuzzy RDD


Code
# Credit score relative to a lender's cutoff; the credit limit jumps by about $1,500 above it
fico   <- runif(n, -50, 50)
above  <- as.integer(fico >= 0)
limit  <- 3000 + 20 * fico + 1500 * above + rnorm(n, 0, 400)
borrow <- 1000 + 10 * fico + 0.30 * limit + rnorm(n, 0, 500)   # 30 cents borrowed per extra $1 of limit

fz <- rdrobust(borrow, fico, c = 0, fuzzy = limit)
round(c(estimate = fz$coef[1], robust_CI_low = fz$ci[3, 1], robust_CI_high = fz$ci[3, 2]), 3)


      estimate  robust_CI_low robust_CI_high 
         0.338          0.272          0.422

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Checking the Design

Threats and Diagnostics






WarningWhat Can Break an RDD










Threat
Diagnostic




Manipulation: units sort precisely to the favourable side
Density test: is there a spike in the number of units just on one side? (McCrary 2008; Cattaneo et al. 2020)


Other differences at the cutoff
Covariate continuity: predetermined characteristics should not jump


Another policy uses the same cutoff
Institutional knowledge; drop that cutoff as a check


Spurious jumps
Placebo cutoffs where nothing changes should show no effect


Sensitivity to choices
Report results for several bandwidths, and a donut that drops units right at the cutoff







Manipulation Test in R


Code
dens <- rddensity(x, c = 0)
c(density_test_p_value = round(dens$test$p_jk, 3))


density_test_p_value 
               0.249 




A large p-value means no evidence that units bunch on one side. In the simulation, incomes were drawn without manipulation, so the test should not reject.
In real data, think about who controls the score: households can sometimes adjust reported income; it is much harder for consumers to fine-tune a credit score to land just above a particular lender’s cutoff.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Case Study 1: Subsidized Health Insurance

Case Study 1: How Much Will People Pay for Insurance?






NoteFinkelstein, Hendren & Shepard (2019), American Economic Review (Finkelstein et al. 2019)



Question: How much are low-income adults willing to pay for health insurance, and what does that imply for subsidy design?
Setting: Massachusetts’ subsidized insurance exchange (CommCare), 2009–2013, for adults below 300% of the federal poverty line (FPL) without access to other coverage.
The rule: subsidies fall in steps at 150%, 200%, and 250% of FPL. At each threshold the monthly premium an enrollee pays jumps by about $40, while the plans on offer stay largely the same.
Data: administrative enrollment and claims records, plus survey data to count the eligible population at each income level.




Case Study 1: The Design






TipThree Discontinuities in Price




Running variable: income as a percentage of FPL; treatment: the premium an enrollee faces
Outcomes: take-up of insurance, and the medical costs of those who enroll
Estimation: linear fits in income on each side of each threshold (a bandwidth of 50% of FPL), with robustness to a 25% bandwidth and quadratic fits
Demand and cost curves: each threshold gives a price change and a change in who enrolls, tracing out willingness to pay and the costs of marginal enrollees





Case Study 1: Results






TipMain Findings




Take-up falls by about 25% (20–24 percentage points) for each $40 increase in the monthly premium: demand is very price-sensitive
People who drop out when prices rise are cheaper to insure: evidence of adverse selection
Across the range observed, enrollees’ willingness to pay is less than half of the costs they impose on insurers
Implication: even generous subsidies leave many uninsured. With premiums at 25% of insurers’ average costs, at most half would enrol; at 10%, at least 20% would remain uninsured





Case Study 1: Threats and Checks






WarningCould People Manipulate Their Income?




Density checks: no bunching of the eligible population at the thresholds in survey data; slight bunching in enrollment data in 2012–13 has an administrative explanation, and none appears in the base year
Why manipulation is hard here: applicants reported income, but the formula translating it into subsidy brackets was largely hidden from them, and proof of income was required
Another change at 200% FPL: at that threshold some groups also lose Medicaid eligibility and copayments rise slightly. Results are robust to dropping that threshold





Case Study 1: What to Copy






TipPractices to Reuse




Use every cutoff the rule offers, and drop the one where another policy also changes (200% FPL) as a check.
Look for bunching in data units cannot influence (survey counts) as well as data they can (enrollment).
Turn local effects into the curve the decision needs: three price jumps trace out willingness to pay against cost.





Case Study 1: Discussion Questions


Why does comparing take-up for everyone above and below 200% FPL not identify the effect of price?
What would you expect to see in the data if people misreported income to stay below a threshold?
Why is dropping the 200% FPL threshold a useful robustness check?
The estimates apply to people near 150%, 200%, and 250% FPL. How far would you extrapolate them?
What does “willingness to pay is less than half of expected costs” imply for an insurance mandate?








NoteSuggested Answers (click to expand)






Income affects take-up directly: richer households differ in needs, preferences, and access to other coverage. A comparison of everyone above and below mixes the price change with these differences; the RD uses only households close to the threshold.
Bunching: more enrollees just below each threshold than just above, and a jump in the density of reported income at the cutoff.
At 200% FPL some groups also lose Medicaid eligibility and copayments rise, so more than the premium changes there. Results that hold without that threshold rely only on cutoffs where the premium is the main change.
Only cautiously. The estimates describe people near 150–250% FPL in Massachusetts’ exchange. The roughly linear patterns between thresholds support modest interpolation within that range, not extrapolation to much poorer or richer people or other markets.
Many low-income adults would not buy insurance at its cost even if it were offered at a fair price. Reaching high coverage would need large subsidies or a mandate. One reason the paper discusses is uncompensated care: the uninsured receive some care without paying for it, which lowers the value of insurance to them.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Where This Chapter Fits






Step 4: Do you observe the same units before and after treatment?



You arrive here when: A policy switches on for some units and not others, and you observe both groups before and after.
This chapter: Parallel trends, event studies, and what goes wrong with staggered adoption.
Next: Chapter 10: when only one or a few units are treated and no single comparison group is credible.

See the design flowchart in Chapter 1.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
In Practice: Difference-in-Differences






Practitioner Summary



Use it when: a policy switches on for some units at a known date, and you observe treated and untreated units before and after
What you need: outcomes for both groups over several periods before and after the policy
What must hold: parallel trends without the policy; no anticipation; no spillovers onto the control group
Checks to run: a plot of raw trends; an event study and the power of its pre-trend test; a heterogeneity-robust estimator if timing is staggered; placebo groups and dates; clustering at the policy level
In R: feols(y ~ sunab(cohort, period) | unit + period, data), did::att_gt()
Telling a manager: “Before the policy the two groups moved together; afterwards the treated group pulled away by X. That gap is our estimate.”

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Did Medicaid Expansion Save Lives?






The Policy Question


From 2014, the Affordable Care Act (ACA) let US states expand Medicaid to low-income adults. Some states expanded; others did not.
Question: Did the expansion reduce mortality among low-income adults?









Two Tempting but Wrong Comparisons


Before vs. after, in expansion states only: mortality changes over time for many reasons: people age, medicine improves, the economy moves. A before–after difference mixes the policy with all of these.
Expansion vs. non-expansion states, after 2014 only: the states that chose to expand differ systematically (income, politics, health systems). A cross-sectional difference mixes the policy with these differences.

title: Difference-in-Differences
Difference-in-Differences
text:
Setup and Target Parameter






Notation



Units i in a treated group (D_i = 1) or control group (D_i = 0)
Two periods: before (t = 0) and after (t = 1); treatment switches on between them for the treated group only
Potential outcomes Y_{it}(1) and Y_{it}(0); observed Y_{it} = Y_{it}(0) + D_i \cdot \mathbb{1}[t = 1] \cdot (Y_{it}(1) - Y_{it}(0))

Target: the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT)
\tau_{ATT} = E[Y_{i1}(1) - Y_{i1}(0) \mid D_i = 1]
The problem: E[Y_{i1}(0) \mid D_i = 1], the treated group’s outcome without the policy after it started, is never observed.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
The Key Assumption: Parallel Trends






Parallel Trends


In the absence of treatment, the treated and control groups would have experienced the same average change in outcomes:
E[Y_{i1}(0) - Y_{i0}(0) \mid D_i = 1] = E[Y_{i1}(0) - Y_{i0}(0) \mid D_i = 0]
Plus two supporting assumptions:

No anticipation: treatment does not affect outcomes before it starts, so Y_{i0} = Y_{i0}(0) for the treated group
No interference (SUTVA): the control group is not affected by the treated group’s treatment










Identification in One Line


Under these assumptions, E[Y_{i1}(0) \mid D_i = 1] = E[Y_{i0} \mid D_i = 1] + \big(E[Y_{i1} \mid D_i = 0] - E[Y_{i0} \mid D_i = 0]\big), so
\tau_{ATT} = \big(E[Y_{i1} \mid D_i=1] - E[Y_{i0} \mid D_i=1]\big) - \big(E[Y_{i1} \mid D_i=0] - E[Y_{i0} \mid D_i=0]\big)

title: Difference-in-Differences
section: What Parallel Trends Does and Does Not Allow
text:
What Parallel Trends Does and Does Not Allow






Allowed



Treated and control groups can have different levels of the outcome
Selection into treatment can depend on fixed characteristics, observed or not (the same idea as unit fixed effects in Chapter 8)
Common shocks that hit both groups equally










Not Allowed



Selection on trends: units adopt the policy because their outcomes were already changing (e.g., the “Ashenfelter dip”: workers join training programs after an earnings drop, then recover anyway)
Group-specific shocks at the same time as the policy (another reform, a local recession)
Spillovers onto the control group










Parallel Trends Depends on the Scale


Parallel trends in levels and in logs are different assumptions: if it holds for one, it generally fails for the other. It holds for every transformation of the outcome only under strong conditions, roughly that the whole distribution of untreated outcomes evolves in parallel, as it would under random assignment (Roth and Sant’Anna 2023). Choose the scale on substantive grounds before looking at results.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Regression Form






The 2×2 as a Regression


Y_{it} = \alpha + \beta D_i + \gamma \,\text{Post}_t + \tau \,(D_i \times \text{Post}_t) + \varepsilon_{it}

\beta: fixed difference between groups
\gamma: common change over time
\tau: the DiD estimate, numerically identical to the difference of the four means










With Panel Data: Two-Way Fixed Effects


Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \tau \,\text{Treat}_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
where \text{Treat}_{it} = D_i \times \text{Post}_t. Unit fixed effects \alpha_i replace \beta D_i; time fixed effects \lambda_t replace \gamma \,\text{Post}_t. This is the two-way fixed effects (TWFE) model from Chapter 8, with a binary treatment that turns on at a known date.
Covariates can be added, but only those not affected by treatment (otherwise they are bad controls).

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
From One Coefficient to Many






Event-Study Specification


Let E_i be the period unit i is first treated (never-treated units have no event time). Estimate
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \sum_{k \neq -1} \beta_k \,\mathbb{1}[t - E_i = k] + \varepsilon_{it}

\beta_k for k \geq 0 (lags): how the effect evolves k periods after treatment
\beta_k for k < -1 (leads): differences before treatment, which should be close to zero under parallel trends and no anticipation
k = -1 is the reference period, normalized to zero
Distant leads and lags are usually binned into end-point indicators






Every case study in this chapter shows an event-study plot. Make sure students can read one: flat pre-period, then the dynamic path of the effect.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Pre-Trend Tests: Handle with Care






Flat Leads Are Evidence, Not Proof



Pre-trends test parallel trends before treatment; the assumption is about the counterfactual after treatment, which is untestable
Pre-trend tests often have low power: a violation large enough to matter may not be statistically detectable
Pretest bias: if we only report designs that pass a pre-trend test, the surviving estimates can be more biased, not less (Roth 2022)










Better Practice



Report the power of the pre-trend test: how big a trend could you detect?
Use sensitivity analysis: how large could post-treatment violations of parallel trends be, relative to observed pre-trends, before the conclusion changes? (Rambachan and Roth 2023)
Show robustness to unit-specific or group-specific linear trends

Case study 1 (Miller et al. 2021) does all three.

title: Difference-in-Differences
section: When Units Are Treated at Different Times
text:
When Units Are Treated at Different Times






Staggered (Rolling) Adoption


Most real policies roll out unevenly:

Medicaid expansion: 21 states in 2014, 3 in 2015, 2 in 2016, 1 in 2017
A firm gives an AI tool to different workers in different months
Laws adopted by different states in different years

The TWFE regression Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \tau \,\text{Treat}_{it} + \varepsilon_{it} is still the default. But with staggered timing and effects that vary over time or across cohorts, \hat\tau_{TWFE} can be badly misleading.

title: Difference-in-Differences
section: Why TWFE Breaks: The Goodman-Bacon Decomposition
text:
Why TWFE Breaks: The Goodman-Bacon Decomposition






TWFE Is a Weighted Average of Many 2×2 Comparisons (Goodman-Bacon 2021)


With staggered timing, \hat\tau_{TWFE} averages every possible 2×2 DiD:

Treated vs. never-treated units: fine
Early-treated vs. not-yet-treated units: fine
Late-treated vs. already-treated units, used as the “control”: the forbidden comparison

In comparison 3, the control group’s outcomes include its own treatment effect. If effects grow over time, the already-treated controls are trending up for reasons unrelated to the late cohort, and the comparison subtracts part of the true effect.
Result: the decomposition weights on the 2×2 comparisons are all positive, but because already-treated units serve as controls, some group-by-period treatment effects enter \hat\tau_{TWFE} with negative weights. \hat\tau_{TWFE} can then be far from any meaningful average effect, and in extreme cases have the wrong sign (Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2020).

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Heterogeneity-Robust Estimators






The Fix: Only Make Clean Comparisons










Estimator
Idea
R package




Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021)
Estimate each cohort × period ATT against never- or not-yet-treated units, then aggregate
did


Sun and Abraham (2021)
Interaction-weighted event study: interact event time with cohort
fixest::sunab()


Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020)
Compare switchers with units whose treatment did not change
DIDmultiplegt


Borusyak et al. (2024)
Impute Y(0) from untreated observations, then average
didimputation


Arkhangelsky et al. (2021)
Synthetic DiD: reweight units and periods to match pre-trends
synthdid



Practical advice: with staggered timing, report a robust estimator alongside TWFE. If they agree, the TWFE weighting problem did little harm here. If they differ, the robust estimate is the better summary, but it still rests on parallel trends for its comparison group and on no anticipation. All three case studies in this chapter follow this advice.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Standard Errors in DiD






Cluster at the Level of the Policy



Outcomes are serially correlated within units, and the treatment indicator is extremely persistent (0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1). Ignoring this badly understates standard errors (Bertrand et al. 2004)
Cluster at the level at which treatment is assigned (e.g., state for a state law)
With few clusters, or few treated clusters, cluster-robust standard errors are unreliable: use the wild cluster bootstrap or randomization inference (Chapter 8)










Case study
Treatment varies by
Clustered by

title: Difference-in-Differences
section: A 2×2 DiD by Hand and by Regression
text:
A 2×2 DiD by Hand and by Regression


Code
library(fixest)
setFixest_notes(FALSE)
set.seed(2026)

n <- 200
d22 <- expand.grid(id = 1:n, post = 0:1)
d22$treated <- as.integer(d22$id <= n / 2)

# Treated units start at a higher level (allowed under parallel trends)
unit_level <- rnorm(n) + 0.8 * (1:n <= n / 2)
d22$y <- unit_level[d22$id] + 0.5 * d22$post +          # common trend
         1.0 * d22$treated * d22$post +                  # true effect = 1
         rnorm(nrow(d22), 0, 0.5)

# Four means and their difference
means <- with(d22, tapply(y, list(treated = treated, post = post), mean))
round(means, 2)


       post
treated    0    1
      0 0.08 0.70
      1 0.75 2.27


Code
(means["1", "1"] - means["1", "0"]) - (means["0", "1"] - means["0", "0"])


[1] 0.9062927


Code
# Same number from the regression
coeftable(feols(y ~ treated * post, data = d22, cluster = ~id))["treated:post", 1:2]


  Estimate Std. Error 
 0.9062927  0.1025802

title: Difference-in-Differences
section: Staggered Adoption: TWFE vs. a Robust Estimator
text:
Staggered Adoption: TWFE vs. a Robust Estimator


Code
# Three adoption cohorts plus never-treated units; effects grow over time
n_units <- 300
cohorts <- sample(c(6, 11, 16, Inf), n_units, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.3, .3, .2, .2))
stag <- expand.grid(id = 1:n_units, t = 1:20)
stag$first_treat <- cohorts[stag$id]
stag$event_time  <- stag$t - stag$first_treat
stag$treated_now <- as.integer(stag$event_time >= 0)
stag$tau <- ifelse(stag$treated_now == 1, 0.3 * (stag$event_time + 1), 0)
stag$y   <- rnorm(n_units)[stag$id] + 0.1 * stag$t + stag$tau + rnorm(nrow(stag), 0, 0.5)

# Static TWFE (uses forbidden comparisons)
m_twfe <- feols(y ~ treated_now | id + t, data = stag, cluster = ~id)

# Sun & Abraham (2021): never-treated cohort coded as a large number
stag$cohort <- ifelse(is.infinite(stag$first_treat), 10000, stag$first_treat)
m_sa <- feols(y ~ sunab(cohort, t) | id + t, data = stag, cluster = ~id)

data.frame(
  estimator = c("True ATT", "TWFE", "Sun & Abraham"),
  estimate  = round(c(mean(stag$tau[stag$treated_now == 1]),
                      coef(m_twfe)["treated_now"],
                      summary(m_sa, agg = "ATT")$coeftable["ATT", "Estimate"]), 2)
)


      estimator estimate
1      True ATT     1.97
2          TWFE     0.75
3 Sun & Abraham     2.01




TWFE recovers well under half of the true average effect here, because effects grow over time and already-treated units serve as controls for later cohorts.
Ask students to set the effect to a constant (e.g., tau = 1 for all treated observations) and re-run: TWFE and Sun & Abraham then agree.

title: Difference-in-Differences
section: Where the Static Bias Comes From
text:
Where the Static Bias Comes From


Code
# TWFE event study: never-treated units get a reference event time
stag$rel <- ifelse(is.infinite(stag$first_treat), -1000, stag$event_time)
m_es_twfe <- feols(y ~ i(rel, ref = c(-1, -1000)) | id + t, data = stag, cluster = ~id)

iplot(list(m_es_twfe, m_sa), xlim = c(-8, 10), ylim = c(-1, 5),
      main = "Event studies: TWFE vs. Sun & Abraham",
      xlab = "Periods since treatment")
lines(0:10, 0.3 * (0:10 + 1), lty = 2, col = "grey40")
legend("topleft", c("TWFE", "Sun & Abraham", "True effect"),
       col = c("black", "#CC0000", "grey40"), lty = c(1, 1, 2), pch = c(20, 20, NA), bty = "n")









Reading the Plot


Both event studies track the true dynamic effect here, because each period since treatment gets its own coefficient, every cohort follows the same dynamic path, and never-treated units give clean comparisons. The problem is the single static coefficient, which averages these growing effects using already-treated units as controls. A TWFE event study is not safe in general: when the dynamic path differs across cohorts, or when periods are binned or dropped, each coefficient can mix in effects from other periods, and spurious pre-trends can appear (Sun and Abraham 2021).

title: Difference-in-Differences
section: Real Data: Minimum Wages and Teen Employment
text:
Real Data: Minimum Wages and Teen Employment


Code
suppressMessages(library(did))
data(mpdta)   # 500 US counties, 2003-2007; some states raised their minimum wage in 2004, 2006, or 2007
mpdta$treated_now <- as.integer(mpdta$first.treat > 0 & mpdta$year >= mpdta$first.treat)

# Static TWFE vs. Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021), which only compares with not-yet- or never-treated counties
twfe <- feols(lemp ~ treated_now | countyreal + year, data = mpdta, cluster = ~countyreal)
set.seed(2026)
cs <- att_gt(yname = "lemp", tname = "year", idname = "countyreal", gname = "first.treat", data = mpdta)

round(c(TWFE = unname(coef(twfe)), Callaway_SantAnna = aggte(cs, type = "simple")$overall.att), 3)


             TWFE Callaway_SantAnna 
           -0.037            -0.040 




mpdta ships with the did package: log teen employment by county, a subset of the data in Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021). Treated counties are in states that raised the minimum wage; controls are counties at the federal minimum throughout.
The two estimates are close here (about −4% teen employment), so TWFE does little harm. That is a finding, not a guarantee: always check.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Real Data: The Event Study


Code
es <- aggte(cs, type = "dynamic")
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(es$egt, es$att.egt, pch = 19, ylim = range(es$att.egt - 2 * es$se.egt, es$att.egt + 2 * es$se.egt),
     xlab = "Years since the minimum wage increase", ylab = "Effect on log teen employment")
arrows(es$egt, es$att.egt - 1.96 * es$se.egt, es$egt, es$att.egt + 1.96 * es$se.egt, angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.04)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2); abline(v = -0.5, col = "#c2410c")









Reading the Result


The effect grows with time since the increase. Before the increase, the estimates are close to zero but not perfectly flat, which is when the power of the pre-trend test and a sensitivity analysis (Rambachan and Roth 2023) matter.

title: Difference-in-Differences
section: Three Case Studies at a Glance
text:
Three Case Studies at a Glance










Miller, Johnson & Wherry (2021)
Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond (2025)
Demirci, Hannane & Zhu (2025)




Journal
Quarterly Journal of Economics
Quarterly Journal of Economics
Management Science


Question
Does Medicaid expansion reduce mortality?
Does a generative AI assistant raise worker productivity?
Which freelance jobs does generative AI replace?


Treated
Low-income adults in expansion states
Customer-support agents given the AI tool
Automation-prone job categories (writing, coding)


Control
Same group in non-expansion states
Agents not yet or never given the tool
Manual-intensive job categories


Timing
Staggered by state (2014–2017)
Staggered by agent (2020–2021)
One date: ChatGPT release (Nov 2022)


Robust estimator
Sun & Abraham (2021); Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition
Sun & Abraham; CS; dCDH; BJS
Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021); synthetic DiD





Keep asking the same three questions for each paper: (1) Who is the control group, and why is it a credible counterfactual? (2) What could break parallel trends? (3) How did the authors check?

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 1: Medicaid and Mortality






Miller, Johnson & Wherry (2021), QJE (Miller et al. 2021)


Question: Did the ACA Medicaid expansions reduce mortality among low-income adults?
Data: a linkage of three federal sources:

American Community Survey (2008–2013) to identify people likely to gain eligibility: income at or below 138% of the poverty line or less than high school education; citizens; not already on disability benefits
Medicaid enrollment records to measure take-up
Census Numident death records to measure mortality through 2017

Sample: ~566,000 adults aged 55–64 in 2014 (a high-mortality group), excluding states that expanded before 2014.
Why it matters: earlier studies used aggregate death records and could not tell who was eligible, so they were underpowered to detect effects of plausible size.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 1: Specification






Event Study with Staggered State Adoption


Y_{isjt} = \text{Expansion}_s \times \sum_{\substack{y=-6 \\ y \neq -1}}^{3} \beta_y \,\mathbb{1}[t - t^*_s = y] + \beta_t + \beta_s + \beta_j + \gamma\,\mathbb{1}[j = t] + \varepsilon_{isjt}

Y: died during year t (linear probability model); individual i, state s, survey wave j
\beta_s state FE, \beta_t year FE, \beta_j survey-wave FE
t^*_s: the state’s expansion year (21 states in 2014; 6 later)
\beta_y for y < -1: pre-trend checks; y \geq 0: effects in each year after expansion
Standard errors clustered by state; ACS survey weights

A subtle point: the sample is a fixed cohort that ages, so mortality rises over time everywhere. The pre-period mean is the wrong baseline; the authors compute a counterfactual post-period mortality rate instead.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 1: Checking the Design






Checks the Authors Ran


First stage: Medicaid eligibility rises 49–51 pp and enrollment rises 12.8 pp in expansion states; flat beforehand.
Pre-trends: mortality trends are parallel before 2014. The authors then ask whether the test had power (Roth 2022): they could detect a linear pre-trend of 0.032 pp per year with 80% power; even such a trend would bias the estimate for event year 3 (the fourth year of expansion) by at most 0.089 pp, under half the estimated effect (0.208 pp).
Staggered timing: Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition shows only 11% of the TWFE weight comes from comparisons between differently timed states; dropping late expanders and using Sun & Abraham (2021) give similar results.
Placebo groups: no effect for people 65+ (already on Medicare), and only small effects for higher-income people, who were less likely to gain coverage.
Placebo period: no relative change in the pre-ACA period.
Other confounders: results are stable when adding state-specific linear trends, county economic trends, or alternative comparison groups.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 1: Results






Main Findings



Mortality falls by 0.132 percentage points per year, a 9.4% reduction relative to the sample mean
The effect grows over time: 0.089 pp in year 1, 0.208 pp by year 4
Driven by disease-related and health care–amenable deaths, not external causes such as accidents
Scaling: if non-expansion states had expanded, roughly 15,600 deaths could have been averted










From Intent-to-Treat to the Effect of Coverage


The DiD estimate is an intent-to-treat effect of living in an expansion state. Dividing by the first stage gives the effect of Medicaid itself, the same logic as IV in Chapters 5–6:
\frac{\text{reduced form}}{\text{first stage}} = \frac{0.132 \text{ pp}}{0.375 \text{ years of Medicaid}} \approx 0.35 \text{ pp lower mortality per year of coverage}
This scaled effect is a LATE for compliers: people who enrolled because of the expansion.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 1: What to Copy






Practices to Reuse



Define the exposed group precisely. Linked records identify people likely to gain eligibility, instead of diluting the effect over everyone.
Report the power of the pre-trend test: the trend they could have missed would bias the estimate by at most 0.089 pp.
Use a group that should not respond (people aged 65+, already on Medicare) as a placebo, and scale the ITT by the first stage.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 1: Discussion Questions

States chose whether to expand. Why doesn’t this choice by itself invalidate the design? What kind of state-level choice would?
Why is the elderly (65+) sample a useful placebo? What would a significant effect in that group have suggested?
The pre-trend test “passes”. Why do the authors still compute the size of trend they could have missed?
Only 11% of the TWFE weight comes from timing comparisons. Why does that make staggered-adoption bias a small concern here, but potentially a large one in other settings?
Why is the scaled effect (0.35 pp per year of coverage) a LATE, and for whom?

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 1: Suggested Answers (1–2)

DiD allows expanding states to differ in levels, for example in income or politics. The design fails only if the expansion decision was related to trends in mortality, or coincided with other changes affecting low-income adults’ health.
People aged 65 and over already have Medicare, so the expansion should not affect them. An effect there would point to state-level health shocks or policies that coincided with expansion, not Medicaid.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 1: Suggested Answers (3–4)

A test with low power can pass even when the trend is large enough to matter. Computing the trend they could have missed (and the bias it would cause) shows whether passing the test is informative.
Most of the weight comes from comparisons with states that never expanded, because few states expanded late. Where most units adopt at different dates and few are never treated, comparisons with already-treated units get more weight, and growing effects can bias TWFE badly.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 1: Suggested Answers (5)

It divides the effect of living in an expansion state by the increase in Medicaid coverage. Under exclusion and monotonicity it is the effect per year of coverage for people who enrolled because of the expansion.

title: Difference-in-Differences
section: Case Study 2: Generative AI at Work
text:
Case Study 2: Generative AI at Work






Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond (2025), QJE (Brynjolfsson et al. 2025)


Question: Does a generative AI assistant raise the productivity of customer-support workers, and who benefits most?
Setting: a Fortune 500 software firm’s customer support. An AI tool built on GPT-3 reads live chats and suggests responses; agents can accept, edit, or ignore suggestions.
Data: 3 million chats by 5,172 agents (89% outside the US, mainly the Philippines), aggregated to agent × month.
Main outcome: resolutions per hour (issues successfully resolved per hour).
Why DiD: the tool was not given to everyone at once. Access was rolled out agent by agent between fall 2020 and early 2021.

title: Difference-in-Differences
section: Case Study 2: Where the Variation Comes From
text:
Case Study 2: Where the Variation Comes From






Rollout Was Not Random. Is It Good Enough?


Constraints that created staggered timing:

Agents had to complete a 3-hour training session, run by only two trainers with limited weekly capacity
The firm had a fixed contractual budget for AI seats
Managers spread a team’s members across different sessions to avoid service disruption

The worry: managers chose who to onboard. Ever-treated agents were already better before AI access (2.0 vs. 1.7 resolutions per hour).
Why the design can still work: agent fixed effects absorb level differences. The threat is selection on trends: managers picking agents who were about to improve anyway.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 2: Specification and Checks






TWFE with Agent and Time Fixed Effects


y_{it} = \delta_t + \alpha_i + \beta \,AI_{it} + \gamma X_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}

\alpha_i agent FE; \delta_t year-month FE; X_{it} tenure FE (months on the job, since agents improve with experience)
AI_{it} = 1 once agent i has access; standard errors clustered by agent

Robustness:

Event study with the Sun & Abraham (2021) estimator: flat before access, immediate jump after
Similar results with Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021), de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille (2020), and Borusyak, Jaravel & Spiess (2024) estimators
IV: instrument each agent’s adoption date with the date the first person in their team got access (rules out within-team selection by managers)
A small earlier RCT pilot (~50 workers) gives similar effects

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 2: Results






Main Findings





Specification (resolutions per hour)
Estimate

Time + location FE
+0.47 (+24%)
Year-month, location


+ Agent FE

Adding agent FE shrinks the estimate: part of the raw gap was selection of stronger agents, which is what unit FE are for (Chapter 8).

Who gains: least-skilled and newest agents improve ~30%; the most skilled gain little, with a small decline in quality
Learning: agents with two months of tenure and AI perform like agents with six or more months without it; productivity stays higher even during AI outages
Work experience: customers are more polite and less likely to ask for a manager; attrition of new agents falls

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 2: What to Copy






Practices to Reuse



Document how timing arose (trainer capacity, seat budgets) to argue it is unrelated to workers’ trends.
Report several heterogeneity-robust estimators next to TWFE.
Add a different design for the same question: a team-level instrument and a small randomized pilot.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 2: Discussion Questions

Ever-treated agents were more productive before AI. Why is this a problem for a cross-sectional comparison but not, by itself, for DiD with agent FE?
Why include tenure fixed effects in addition to agent and month FE? What bias would remain without them?
Why does instrumenting with the team’s first adoption date address manager selection? What does it assume?
The paper studies one firm in the medium run. What does it not tell us about generative AI’s effect on employment or wages?
The most-skilled agents follow AI suggestions more over time, even though quality falls slightly. Connect this to the idea of “cognitive surrender” (Chapter 4).

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 2: Suggested Answers (1–2)

A cross-section compares strong agents with weaker ones, which credits AI with pre-existing differences. With agent fixed effects each agent is compared with themselves, so level differences cancel; only differences in trends would bias the result.
New agents improve quickly with experience, and agents gain access at different points in their careers. Without tenure effects, normal learning on the job would be counted as an AI effect.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 2: Suggested Answers (3–5)

The team’s first access date depends on scheduling and team-level rollout, not on a manager picking particular agents within the team. It assumes team timing is unrelated to team trends and affects agents only through their own access, which spillovers within teams would violate.
It says nothing about hiring, wages, or the number of support jobs, how other firms respond, or effects in other occupations and over longer periods.
Accepting more AI suggestions while quality slips is consistent with adopting outputs with less scrutiny. But field data cannot separate over-reliance from a sensible choice to save time; the lab design in Chapter 4 can.

title: Difference-in-Differences
section: Case Study 3: Who Is AI Replacing?
text:
Case Study 3: Who Is AI Replacing?






Demirci, Hannane & Zhu (2025), Management Science (Demirci et al. 2025)


Question: How did ChatGPT (and image-generating AI) change demand for freelance work, and for which kinds of jobs?
Data: all job posts on a leading global freelancing platform, 2021–mid-2023: 1.2 million fixed-price posts from 542,000 employers in 61 countries.
Treated and control groups: job posts are clustered by skill tags into categories, then grouped by exposure to language models:

Treated (automation-prone): writing; software, app and web development; engineering
Control (manual-intensive): data and office management, video services, audio services
A separate analysis treats graphic design and 3D modeling as exposed to image-generating AI (Midjourney, DALL-E 2, Stable Diffusion)

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 3: Specification






DiD with a Single, Common Shock


y_{ctl} = \beta \,(\text{Post}_t \times T_c) + \gamma_{cl} + \gamma_t + \varepsilon_{ctl}

y: log number of job posts in category c, week t, country l
\text{Post}_t: after ChatGPT’s release (30 November 2022); T_c: automation-prone category
\gamma_{cl} category × country FE; \gamma_t week FE (seasonality, platform trends)
Event-study version by month to check pre-trends
Standard errors clustered by job category

Note: everyone is “treated” on the same date, so there is no staggered-adoption problem. The authors still report Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) and synthetic DiD estimates, plus a negative binomial model because log counts with zeros are problematic (Chen and Roth 2024).

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 3: Results and Checks






Main Findings



Job posts in automation-prone categories fall 21% relative to manual-intensive ones within eight months (coefficient −0.234 on log posts)
By category: writing −30%, software/app/web development −21%, engineering −10%
Image-generating AI: graphic design and 3D modeling posts fall 17%
The effect grows over time and after more capable model releases
Remaining automation-prone jobs pay more (+5.7% maximum budget), are more complex (+2.2% skill tags), and attract more bids (+8.6%)










Strengthening the Causal Story



Dose-response: categories with larger increases in Google searches for “ChatGPT + [category]” saw larger declines
Placebo release dates give no effect
Robust to alternative control groups and to aggregating to category × week

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 3: What to Copy






Practices to Reuse



When a shock hits everyone at once, compare exposed with unexposed categories, and argue that the controls are not exposed.
Add dose-response evidence (search intensity by category) and placebo release dates.
Pick a model that suits counts with zeros and be open about having few clusters.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 3: Discussion Questions

The “treatment” is a worldwide technology release on one date. Why is a comparison across job categories still needed? What would a simple before–after comparison of writing jobs pick up?
Could ChatGPT also affect the control categories (e.g., freelancers switching from writing to video editing, or clients using ChatGPT to write video scripts)? Which direction would that bias \hat\beta?
Standard errors are clustered by job category, with only a handful of categories. What inference concern does that raise, and what would you do about it?
Why might log(job posts) be a problematic outcome, and why does a negative binomial model help?
Compare with Case Study 2: one paper finds AI raises worker productivity, the other finds AI reduces demand for freelancers. Can both be true?

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 3: Suggested Answers (1–3)

Freelance demand changes for other reasons at the same time: seasonality, platform growth, interest rates, and tech-sector layoffs in 2022–23. A before–after comparison of writing jobs would attribute all of these to ChatGPT.
If ChatGPT also reduces demand for control jobs, the control group falls too and the estimated decline is understated. If employers move budgets towards control categories, the control rises and the decline is overstated.
With few clusters, cluster-robust standard errors are too small and tests reject too often. Use the wild cluster bootstrap or randomization inference across categories, and report results at several aggregation levels.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Study 3: Suggested Answers (4–5)

The log of zero is undefined, and log(y + 1) gives results that depend on the units of y. A count model such as the negative binomial includes zeros and estimates a proportional effect directly.
Yes. They study different margins and people: inside a firm, AI helps workers who use it, especially new ones; across a market, firms can do some outsourced tasks themselves, which cuts demand for freelancers. Higher productivity can also mean fewer hours are needed.
