title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
DiD Checklist






Before Estimating



Plot the raw data: treated and control group means over time
Justify the control group: why is its change a credible counterfactual?
Ask who chose treatment and why: selection on levels is fine; selection on trends is not
Choose the outcome scale (levels vs. logs) before looking at results
Decide the clustering level from how treatment was assigned










After Estimating



Show an event study and discuss the power of pre-trend tests
With staggered timing, report a heterogeneity-robust estimator alongside TWFE
Run placebo tests: unaffected groups, fake treatment dates
Check for spillovers onto the control group
Interpret the estimand: ATT for whom, over what horizon; scale by the first stage if treatment take-up is incomplete

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Common Pitfalls






Mistakes to Avoid



Treating flat pre-trends as proof of parallel trends
Running static TWFE with staggered adoption and dynamic effects
Using already-treated units as controls without realizing it
Clustering too finely (by individual when the policy varies by state)
Controlling for post-treatment variables that the policy itself changes
Ignoring anticipation: units changing behaviour before the official start date
Ignoring spillovers: the control group is partly treated
Taking logs of outcomes with many zeros without thinking about what the estimate means

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Summary
Key Ideas:

DiD compares changes, not levels: the control group’s change stands in for the treated group’s counterfactual change
Identification rests on parallel trends, plus no anticipation and no spillovers
DiD is the two-way fixed effects model from Chapter 8 with a policy that switches on at a known date

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Difference-in-differences (DiD) is the most widely used design for evaluating policies that switch on for some units and not others.
It builds directly on Chapter 8: DiD is a two-way fixed effects model with a binary treatment that turns on at a known date.
We cover the 2×2 design, event studies, what goes wrong with staggered adoption, and inference. Then three case studies: Medicaid expansion and mortality, and two papers on generative AI at work.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Motivation

Did Medicaid Expansion Save Lives?






NoteThe Policy Question



From 2014, the Affordable Care Act (ACA) let US states expand Medicaid to low-income adults. Some states expanded; others did not.
Question: Did the expansion reduce mortality among low-income adults?








WarningTwo Tempting but Wrong Comparisons



Before vs. after, in expansion states only: mortality changes over time for many reasons: people age, medicine improves, the economy moves. A before–after difference mixes the policy with all of these.
Expansion vs. non-expansion states, after 2014 only: the states that chose to expand differ systematically (income, politics, health systems). A cross-sectional difference mixes the policy with these differences.




The DiD Idea






TipUse Each Comparison to Fix the Other’s Problem




The control group’s change over time tells us how the treated group would have changed without the policy
Subtracting it removes common time shocks; differencing within groups removes fixed group differences











Before
After
Change




Treated (expansion states)
\bar Y_{T,0}
\bar Y_{T,1}
\bar Y_{T,1} - \bar Y_{T,0}


Control (non-expansion states)
\bar Y_{C,0}
\bar Y_{C,1}
\bar Y_{C,1} - \bar Y_{C,0}


Difference


\hat\tau_{DiD} = (\bar Y_{T,1} - \bar Y_{T,0}) - (\bar Y_{C,1} - \bar Y_{C,0})







Classic example: Card and Krueger (1994), minimum wage in New Jersey vs. Pennsylvania fast-food restaurants.
Ask students: what would make the control group’s change a bad guess for the treated group’s counterfactual change?

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
The 2×2 Design

Setup and Target Parameter






NoteNotation




Units i in a treated group (D_i = 1) or control group (D_i = 0)
Two periods: before (t = 0) and after (t = 1); treatment switches on between them for the treated group only
Potential outcomes Y_{it}(1) and Y_{it}(0); observed Y_{it} = Y_{it}(0) + D_i \cdot \mathbb{1}[t = 1] \cdot (Y_{it}(1) - Y_{it}(0))

Target: the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT)
\tau_{ATT} = E[Y_{i1}(1) - Y_{i1}(0) \mid D_i = 1]
The problem: E[Y_{i1}(0) \mid D_i = 1], the treated group’s outcome without the policy after it started, is never observed.




The Key Assumption: Parallel Trends






ImportantParallel Trends



In the absence of treatment, the treated and control groups would have experienced the same average change in outcomes:
E[Y_{i1}(0) - Y_{i0}(0) \mid D_i = 1] = E[Y_{i1}(0) - Y_{i0}(0) \mid D_i = 0]
Plus two supporting assumptions:

No anticipation: treatment does not affect outcomes before it starts, so Y_{i0} = Y_{i0}(0) for the treated group
No interference (SUTVA): the control group is not affected by the treated group’s treatment









TipIdentification in One Line



Under these assumptions, E[Y_{i1}(0) \mid D_i = 1] = E[Y_{i0} \mid D_i = 1] + \big(E[Y_{i1} \mid D_i = 0] - E[Y_{i0} \mid D_i = 0]\big), so
\tau_{ATT} = \big(E[Y_{i1} \mid D_i=1] - E[Y_{i0} \mid D_i=1]\big) - \big(E[Y_{i1} \mid D_i=0] - E[Y_{i0} \mid D_i=0]\big)




What Parallel Trends Does and Does Not Allow






NoteAllowed




Treated and control groups can have different levels of the outcome
Selection into treatment can depend on fixed characteristics, observed or not (the same idea as unit fixed effects in Chapter 8)
Common shocks that hit both groups equally









WarningNot Allowed




Selection on trends: units adopt the policy because their outcomes were already changing (e.g., the “Ashenfelter dip”: workers join training programs after an earnings drop, then recover anyway)
Group-specific shocks at the same time as the policy (another reform, a local recession)
Spillovers onto the control group









ImportantParallel Trends Depends on the Scale



Parallel trends in levels and in logs are different assumptions: if it holds for one, it generally fails for the other. It holds for every transformation of the outcome only under strong conditions, roughly that the whole distribution of untreated outcomes evolves in parallel, as it would under random assignment (Roth and Sant’Anna 2023). Choose the scale on substantive grounds before looking at results.




Regression Form






NoteThe 2×2 as a Regression



Y_{it} = \alpha + \beta D_i + \gamma \,\text{Post}_t + \tau \,(D_i \times \text{Post}_t) + \varepsilon_{it}

\beta: fixed difference between groups
\gamma: common change over time
\tau: the DiD estimate, numerically identical to the difference of the four means









TipWith Panel Data: Two-Way Fixed Effects



Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \tau \,\text{Treat}_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
where \text{Treat}_{it} = D_i \times \text{Post}_t. Unit fixed effects \alpha_i replace \beta D_i; time fixed effects \lambda_t replace \gamma \,\text{Post}_t. This is the two-way fixed effects (TWFE) model from Chapter 8, with a binary treatment that turns on at a known date.
Covariates can be added, but only those not affected by treatment (otherwise they are bad controls).

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Event Studies

From One Coefficient to Many






NoteEvent-Study Specification



Let E_i be the period unit i is first treated (never-treated units have no event time). Estimate
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \sum_{k \neq -1} \beta_k \,\mathbb{1}[t - E_i = k] + \varepsilon_{it}

\beta_k for k \geq 0 (lags): how the effect evolves k periods after treatment
\beta_k for k < -1 (leads): differences before treatment, which should be close to zero under parallel trends and no anticipation
k = -1 is the reference period, normalized to zero
Distant leads and lags are usually binned into end-point indicators





Every case study in this chapter shows an event-study plot. Make sure students can read one: flat pre-period, then the dynamic path of the effect.




Pre-Trend Tests: Handle with Care






WarningFlat Leads Are Evidence, Not Proof




Pre-trends test parallel trends before treatment; the assumption is about the counterfactual after treatment, which is untestable
Pre-trend tests often have low power: a violation large enough to matter may not be statistically detectable
Pretest bias: if we only report designs that pass a pre-trend test, the surviving estimates can be more biased, not less (Roth 2022)









TipBetter Practice




Report the power of the pre-trend test: how big a trend could you detect?
Use sensitivity analysis: how large could post-treatment violations of parallel trends be, relative to observed pre-trends, before the conclusion changes? (Rambachan and Roth 2023)
Show robustness to unit-specific or group-specific linear trends

Case study 1 (Miller et al. 2021) does all three.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Staggered Adoption

When Units Are Treated at Different Times






NoteStaggered (Rolling) Adoption



Most real policies roll out unevenly:

Medicaid expansion: 21 states in 2014, 3 in 2015, 2 in 2016, 1 in 2017
A firm gives an AI tool to different workers in different months
Laws adopted by different states in different years

The TWFE regression Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \tau \,\text{Treat}_{it} + \varepsilon_{it} is still the default. But with staggered timing and effects that vary over time or across cohorts, \hat\tau_{TWFE} can be badly misleading.




Why TWFE Breaks: The Goodman-Bacon Decomposition






WarningTWFE Is a Weighted Average of Many 2×2 Comparisons (Goodman-Bacon 2021)



With staggered timing, \hat\tau_{TWFE} averages every possible 2×2 DiD:

Treated vs. never-treated units: fine
Early-treated vs. not-yet-treated units: fine
Late-treated vs. already-treated units, used as the “control”: the forbidden comparison

In comparison 3, the control group’s outcomes include its own treatment effect. If effects grow over time, the already-treated controls are trending up for reasons unrelated to the late cohort, and the comparison subtracts part of the true effect.
Result: the decomposition weights on the 2×2 comparisons are all positive, but because already-treated units serve as controls, some group-by-period treatment effects enter \hat\tau_{TWFE} with negative weights. \hat\tau_{TWFE} can then be far from any meaningful average effect, and in extreme cases have the wrong sign (Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2020).




Heterogeneity-Robust Estimators






TipThe Fix: Only Make Clean Comparisons











Estimator
Idea
R package




Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021)
Estimate each cohort × period ATT against never- or not-yet-treated units, then aggregate
did


Sun and Abraham (2021)
Interaction-weighted event study: interact event time with cohort
fixest::sunab()


Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020)
Compare switchers with units whose treatment did not change
DIDmultiplegt


Borusyak et al. (2024)
Impute Y(0) from untreated observations, then average
didimputation


Arkhangelsky et al. (2021)
Synthetic DiD: reweight units and periods to match pre-trends
synthdid



Practical advice: with staggered timing, report a robust estimator alongside TWFE. If they agree, the TWFE weighting problem did little harm here. If they differ, the robust estimate is the better summary, but it still rests on parallel trends for its comparison group and on no anticipation. All three case studies in this chapter follow this advice.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Inference

Standard Errors in DiD






ImportantCluster at the Level of the Policy




Outcomes are serially correlated within units, and the treatment indicator is extremely persistent (0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1). Ignoring this badly understates standard errors (Bertrand et al. 2004)
Cluster at the level at which treatment is assigned (e.g., state for a state law)
With few clusters, or few treated clusters, cluster-robust standard errors are unreliable: use the wild cluster bootstrap or randomization inference (Chapter 8)










Case study
Treatment varies by
Clustered by

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Simulation

A 2×2 DiD by Hand and by Regression


Code
library(fixest)
setFixest_notes(FALSE)
set.seed(2026)

n <- 200
d22 <- expand.grid(id = 1:n, post = 0:1)
d22$treated <- as.integer(d22$id <= n / 2)

# Treated units start at a higher level (allowed under parallel trends)
unit_level <- rnorm(n) + 0.8 * (1:n <= n / 2)
d22$y <- unit_level[d22$id] + 0.5 * d22$post +          # common trend
         1.0 * d22$treated * d22$post +                  # true effect = 1
         rnorm(nrow(d22), 0, 0.5)

# Four means and their difference
means <- with(d22, tapply(y, list(treated = treated, post = post), mean))
round(means, 2)


       post
treated    0    1
      0 0.08 0.70
      1 0.75 2.27


Code
(means["1", "1"] - means["1", "0"]) - (means["0", "1"] - means["0", "0"])


[1] 0.9062927


Code
# Same number from the regression
coeftable(feols(y ~ treated * post, data = d22, cluster = ~id))["treated:post", 1:2]


  Estimate Std. Error 
 0.9062927  0.1025802 




Staggered Adoption: TWFE vs. a Robust Estimator


Code
# Three adoption cohorts plus never-treated units; effects grow over time
n_units <- 300
cohorts <- sample(c(6, 11, 16, Inf), n_units, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.3, .3, .2, .2))
stag <- expand.grid(id = 1:n_units, t = 1:20)
stag$first_treat <- cohorts[stag$id]
stag$event_time  <- stag$t - stag$first_treat
stag$treated_now <- as.integer(stag$event_time >= 0)
stag$tau <- ifelse(stag$treated_now == 1, 0.3 * (stag$event_time + 1), 0)
stag$y   <- rnorm(n_units)[stag$id] + 0.1 * stag$t + stag$tau + rnorm(nrow(stag), 0, 0.5)

# Static TWFE (uses forbidden comparisons)
m_twfe <- feols(y ~ treated_now | id + t, data = stag, cluster = ~id)

# Sun & Abraham (2021): never-treated cohort coded as a large number
stag$cohort <- ifelse(is.infinite(stag$first_treat), 10000, stag$first_treat)
m_sa <- feols(y ~ sunab(cohort, t) | id + t, data = stag, cluster = ~id)

data.frame(
  estimator = c("True ATT", "TWFE", "Sun & Abraham"),
  estimate  = round(c(mean(stag$tau[stag$treated_now == 1]),
                      coef(m_twfe)["treated_now"],
                      summary(m_sa, agg = "ATT")$coeftable["ATT", "Estimate"]), 2)
)


      estimator estimate
1      True ATT     1.97
2          TWFE     0.75
3 Sun & Abraham     2.01




TWFE recovers well under half of the true average effect here, because effects grow over time and already-treated units serve as controls for later cohorts.
Ask students to set the effect to a constant (e.g., tau = 1 for all treated observations) and re-run: TWFE and Sun & Abraham then agree.




Where the Static Bias Comes From


Code
# TWFE event study: never-treated units get a reference event time
stag$rel <- ifelse(is.infinite(stag$first_treat), -1000, stag$event_time)
m_es_twfe <- feols(y ~ i(rel, ref = c(-1, -1000)) | id + t, data = stag, cluster = ~id)

iplot(list(m_es_twfe, m_sa), xlim = c(-8, 10), ylim = c(-1, 5),
      main = "Event studies: TWFE vs. Sun & Abraham",
      xlab = "Periods since treatment")
lines(0:10, 0.3 * (0:10 + 1), lty = 2, col = "grey40")
legend("topleft", c("TWFE", "Sun & Abraham", "True effect"),
       col = c("black", "#CC0000", "grey40"), lty = c(1, 1, 2), pch = c(20, 20, NA), bty = "n")















NoteReading the Plot



Both event studies track the true dynamic effect here, because each period since treatment gets its own coefficient, every cohort follows the same dynamic path, and never-treated units give clean comparisons. The problem is the single static coefficient, which averages these growing effects using already-treated units as controls. A TWFE event study is not safe in general: when the dynamic path differs across cohorts, or when periods are binned or dropped, each coefficient can mix in effects from other periods, and spurious pre-trends can appear (Sun and Abraham 2021).

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Real Data

Real Data: Minimum Wages and Teen Employment


Code
suppressMessages(library(did))
data(mpdta)   # 500 US counties, 2003-2007; some states raised their minimum wage in 2004, 2006, or 2007
mpdta$treated_now <- as.integer(mpdta$first.treat > 0 & mpdta$year >= mpdta$first.treat)

# Static TWFE vs. Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021), which only compares with not-yet- or never-treated counties
twfe <- feols(lemp ~ treated_now | countyreal + year, data = mpdta, cluster = ~countyreal)
set.seed(2026)
cs <- att_gt(yname = "lemp", tname = "year", idname = "countyreal", gname = "first.treat", data = mpdta)

round(c(TWFE = unname(coef(twfe)), Callaway_SantAnna = aggte(cs, type = "simple")$overall.att), 3)


             TWFE Callaway_SantAnna 
           -0.037            -0.040 




mpdta ships with the did package: log teen employment by county, a subset of the data in Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021). Treated counties are in states that raised the minimum wage; controls are counties at the federal minimum throughout.
The two estimates are close here (about −4% teen employment), so TWFE does little harm. That is a finding, not a guarantee: always check.




Real Data: The Event Study


Code
es <- aggte(cs, type = "dynamic")
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(es$egt, es$att.egt, pch = 19, ylim = range(es$att.egt - 2 * es$se.egt, es$att.egt + 2 * es$se.egt),
     xlab = "Years since the minimum wage increase", ylab = "Effect on log teen employment")
arrows(es$egt, es$att.egt - 1.96 * es$se.egt, es$egt, es$att.egt + 1.96 * es$se.egt, angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.04)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2); abline(v = -0.5, col = "#c2410c")















NoteReading the Result



The effect grows with time since the increase. Before the increase, the estimates are close to zero but not perfectly flat, which is when the power of the pre-trend test and a sensitivity analysis (Rambachan and Roth 2023) matter.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Case Studies

Three Case Studies at a Glance










Miller, Johnson & Wherry (2021)
Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond (2025)
Demirci, Hannane & Zhu (2025)




Journal
Quarterly Journal of Economics
Quarterly Journal of Economics
Management Science


Question
Does Medicaid expansion reduce mortality?
Does a generative AI assistant raise worker productivity?
Which freelance jobs does generative AI replace?


Treated
Low-income adults in expansion states
Customer-support agents given the AI tool
Automation-prone job categories (writing, coding)


Control
Same group in non-expansion states
Agents not yet or never given the tool
Manual-intensive job categories


Timing
Staggered by state (2014–2017)
Staggered by agent (2020–2021)
One date: ChatGPT release (Nov 2022)


Robust estimator
Sun & Abraham (2021); Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition
Sun & Abraham; CS; dCDH; BJS
Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021); synthetic DiD





Keep asking the same three questions for each paper: (1) Who is the control group, and why is it a credible counterfactual? (2) What could break parallel trends? (3) How did the authors check?




Case Study 1: Medicaid and Mortality






NoteMiller, Johnson & Wherry (2021), QJE (Miller et al. 2021)



Question: Did the ACA Medicaid expansions reduce mortality among low-income adults?
Data: a linkage of three federal sources:

American Community Survey (2008–2013) to identify people likely to gain eligibility: income at or below 138% of the poverty line or less than high school education; citizens; not already on disability benefits
Medicaid enrollment records to measure take-up
Census Numident death records to measure mortality through 2017

Sample: ~566,000 adults aged 55–64 in 2014 (a high-mortality group), excluding states that expanded before 2014.
Why it matters: earlier studies used aggregate death records and could not tell who was eligible, so they were underpowered to detect effects of plausible size.




Case Study 1: Specification






TipEvent Study with Staggered State Adoption



Y_{isjt} = \text{Expansion}_s \times \sum_{\substack{y=-6 \\ y \neq -1}}^{3} \beta_y \,\mathbb{1}[t - t^*_s = y] + \beta_t + \beta_s + \beta_j + \gamma\,\mathbb{1}[j = t] + \varepsilon_{isjt}

Y: died during year t (linear probability model); individual i, state s, survey wave j
\beta_s state FE, \beta_t year FE, \beta_j survey-wave FE
t^*_s: the state’s expansion year (21 states in 2014; 6 later)
\beta_y for y < -1: pre-trend checks; y \geq 0: effects in each year after expansion
Standard errors clustered by state; ACS survey weights

A subtle point: the sample is a fixed cohort that ages, so mortality rises over time everywhere. The pre-period mean is the wrong baseline; the authors compute a counterfactual post-period mortality rate instead.




Case Study 1: Checking the Design






WarningChecks the Authors Ran



First stage: Medicaid eligibility rises 49–51 pp and enrollment rises 12.8 pp in expansion states; flat beforehand.
Pre-trends: mortality trends are parallel before 2014. The authors then ask whether the test had power (Roth 2022): they could detect a linear pre-trend of 0.032 pp per year with 80% power; even such a trend would bias the estimate for event year 3 (the fourth year of expansion) by at most 0.089 pp, under half the estimated effect (0.208 pp).
Staggered timing: Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition shows only 11% of the TWFE weight comes from comparisons between differently timed states; dropping late expanders and using Sun & Abraham (2021) give similar results.
Placebo groups: no effect for people 65+ (already on Medicare), and only small effects for higher-income people, who were less likely to gain coverage.
Placebo period: no relative change in the pre-ACA period.
Other confounders: results are stable when adding state-specific linear trends, county economic trends, or alternative comparison groups.




Case Study 1: Results






TipMain Findings




Mortality falls by 0.132 percentage points per year, a 9.4% reduction relative to the sample mean
The effect grows over time: 0.089 pp in year 1, 0.208 pp by year 4
Driven by disease-related and health care–amenable deaths, not external causes such as accidents
Scaling: if non-expansion states had expanded, roughly 15,600 deaths could have been averted









NoteFrom Intent-to-Treat to the Effect of Coverage



The DiD estimate is an intent-to-treat effect of living in an expansion state. Dividing by the first stage gives the effect of Medicaid itself, the same logic as IV in Chapters 5–6:
\frac{\text{reduced form}}{\text{first stage}} = \frac{0.132 \text{ pp}}{0.375 \text{ years of Medicaid}} \approx 0.35 \text{ pp lower mortality per year of coverage}
This scaled effect is a LATE for compliers: people who enrolled because of the expansion.




Case Study 1: What to Copy






TipPractices to Reuse




Define the exposed group precisely. Linked records identify people likely to gain eligibility, instead of diluting the effect over everyone.
Report the power of the pre-trend test: the trend they could have missed would bias the estimate by at most 0.089 pp.
Use a group that should not respond (people aged 65+, already on Medicare) as a placebo, and scale the ITT by the first stage.





Case Study 1: Discussion Questions


States chose whether to expand. Why doesn’t this choice by itself invalidate the design? What kind of state-level choice would?
Why is the elderly (65+) sample a useful placebo? What would a significant effect in that group have suggested?
The pre-trend test “passes”. Why do the authors still compute the size of trend they could have missed?
Only 11% of the TWFE weight comes from timing comparisons. Why does that make staggered-adoption bias a small concern here, but potentially a large one in other settings?
Why is the scaled effect (0.35 pp per year of coverage) a LATE, and for whom?








NoteSuggested Answers (click to expand)






DiD allows expanding states to differ in levels, for example in income or politics. The design fails only if the expansion decision was related to trends in mortality, or coincided with other changes affecting low-income adults’ health.
People aged 65 and over already have Medicare, so the expansion should not affect them. An effect there would point to state-level health shocks or policies that coincided with expansion, not Medicaid.
A test with low power can pass even when the trend is large enough to matter. Computing the trend they could have missed (and the bias it would cause) shows whether passing the test is informative.
Most of the weight comes from comparisons with states that never expanded, because few states expanded late. Where most units adopt at different dates and few are never treated, comparisons with already-treated units get more weight, and growing effects can bias TWFE badly.
It divides the effect of living in an expansion state by the increase in Medicaid coverage. Under exclusion and monotonicity it is the effect per year of coverage for people who enrolled because of the expansion.






Case Study 2: Generative AI at Work






NoteBrynjolfsson, Li & Raymond (2025), QJE (Brynjolfsson et al. 2025)



Question: Does a generative AI assistant raise the productivity of customer-support workers, and who benefits most?
Setting: a Fortune 500 software firm’s customer support. An AI tool built on GPT-3 reads live chats and suggests responses; agents can accept, edit, or ignore suggestions.
Data: 3 million chats by 5,172 agents (89% outside the US, mainly the Philippines), aggregated to agent × month.
Main outcome: resolutions per hour (issues successfully resolved per hour).
Why DiD: the tool was not given to everyone at once. Access was rolled out agent by agent between fall 2020 and early 2021.




Case Study 2: Where the Variation Comes From






WarningRollout Was Not Random. Is It Good Enough?



Constraints that created staggered timing:

Agents had to complete a 3-hour training session, run by only two trainers with limited weekly capacity
The firm had a fixed contractual budget for AI seats
Managers spread a team’s members across different sessions to avoid service disruption

The worry: managers chose who to onboard. Ever-treated agents were already better before AI access (2.0 vs. 1.7 resolutions per hour).
Why the design can still work: agent fixed effects absorb level differences. The threat is selection on trends: managers picking agents who were about to improve anyway.




Case Study 2: Specification and Checks






TipTWFE with Agent and Time Fixed Effects



y_{it} = \delta_t + \alpha_i + \beta \,AI_{it} + \gamma X_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}

\alpha_i agent FE; \delta_t year-month FE; X_{it} tenure FE (months on the job, since agents improve with experience)
AI_{it} = 1 once agent i has access; standard errors clustered by agent

Robustness:

Event study with the Sun & Abraham (2021) estimator: flat before access, immediate jump after
Similar results with Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021), de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille (2020), and Borusyak, Jaravel & Spiess (2024) estimators
IV: instrument each agent’s adoption date with the date the first person in their team got access (rules out within-team selection by managers)
A small earlier RCT pilot (~50 workers) gives similar effects





Case Study 2: Results






TipMain Findings






Specification (resolutions per hour)
Estimate
Fixed effects




Time + location FE
+0.47 (+24%)
Year-month, location


+ Agent FE
+0.37
+ agent


+ Tenure FE (preferred)
+0.30 (+15%)
+ months of tenure



Adding agent FE shrinks the estimate: part of the raw gap was selection of stronger agents, which is what unit FE are for (Chapter 8).

Who gains: least-skilled and newest agents improve ~30%; the most skilled gain little, with a small decline in quality
Learning: agents with two months of tenure and AI perform like agents with six or more months without it; productivity stays higher even during AI outages
Work experience: customers are more polite and less likely to ask for a manager; attrition of new agents falls





Case Study 2: What to Copy






TipPractices to Reuse




Document how timing arose (trainer capacity, seat budgets) to argue it is unrelated to workers’ trends.
Report several heterogeneity-robust estimators next to TWFE.
Add a different design for the same question: a team-level instrument and a small randomized pilot.





Case Study 2: Discussion Questions


Ever-treated agents were more productive before AI. Why is this a problem for a cross-sectional comparison but not, by itself, for DiD with agent FE?
Why include tenure fixed effects in addition to agent and month FE? What bias would remain without them?
Why does instrumenting with the team’s first adoption date address manager selection? What does it assume?
The paper studies one firm in the medium run. What does it not tell us about generative AI’s effect on employment or wages?
The most-skilled agents follow AI suggestions more over time, even though quality falls slightly. Connect this to the idea of “cognitive surrender” (Chapter 4).








NoteSuggested Answers (click to expand)






A cross-section compares strong agents with weaker ones, which credits AI with pre-existing differences. With agent fixed effects each agent is compared with themselves, so level differences cancel; only differences in trends would bias the result.
New agents improve quickly with experience, and agents gain access at different points in their careers. Without tenure effects, normal learning on the job would be counted as an AI effect.
The team’s first access date depends on scheduling and team-level rollout, not on a manager picking particular agents within the team. It assumes team timing is unrelated to team trends and affects agents only through their own access, which spillovers within teams would violate.
It says nothing about hiring, wages, or the number of support jobs, how other firms respond, or effects in other occupations and over longer periods.
Accepting more AI suggestions while quality slips is consistent with adopting outputs with less scrutiny. But field data cannot separate over-reliance from a sensible choice to save time; the lab design in Chapter 4 can.






Case Study 3: Who Is AI Replacing?






NoteDemirci, Hannane & Zhu (2025), Management Science (Demirci et al. 2025)



Question: How did ChatGPT (and image-generating AI) change demand for freelance work, and for which kinds of jobs?
Data: all job posts on a leading global freelancing platform, 2021–mid-2023: 1.2 million fixed-price posts from 542,000 employers in 61 countries.
Treated and control groups: job posts are clustered by skill tags into categories, then grouped by exposure to language models:

Treated (automation-prone): writing; software, app and web development; engineering
Control (manual-intensive): data and office management, video services, audio services
A separate analysis treats graphic design and 3D modeling as exposed to image-generating AI (Midjourney, DALL-E 2, Stable Diffusion)





Case Study 3: Specification






TipDiD with a Single, Common Shock



y_{ctl} = \beta \,(\text{Post}_t \times T_c) + \gamma_{cl} + \gamma_t + \varepsilon_{ctl}

y: log number of job posts in category c, week t, country l
\text{Post}_t: after ChatGPT’s release (30 November 2022); T_c: automation-prone category
\gamma_{cl} category × country FE; \gamma_t week FE (seasonality, platform trends)
Event-study version by month to check pre-trends
Standard errors clustered by job category

Note: everyone is “treated” on the same date, so there is no staggered-adoption problem. The authors still report Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) and synthetic DiD estimates, plus a negative binomial model because log counts with zeros are problematic (Chen and Roth 2024).




Case Study 3: Results and Checks






TipMain Findings




Job posts in automation-prone categories fall 21% relative to manual-intensive ones within eight months (coefficient −0.234 on log posts)
By category: writing −30%, software/app/web development −21%, engineering −10%
Image-generating AI: graphic design and 3D modeling posts fall 17%
The effect grows over time and after more capable model releases
Remaining automation-prone jobs pay more (+5.7% maximum budget), are more complex (+2.2% skill tags), and attract more bids (+8.6%)









NoteStrengthening the Causal Story




Dose-response: categories with larger increases in Google searches for “ChatGPT + [category]” saw larger declines
Placebo release dates give no effect
Robust to alternative control groups and to aggregating to category × week





Case Study 3: What to Copy






TipPractices to Reuse




When a shock hits everyone at once, compare exposed with unexposed categories, and argue that the controls are not exposed.
Add dose-response evidence (search intensity by category) and placebo release dates.
Pick a model that suits counts with zeros and be open about having few clusters.





Case Study 3: Discussion Questions


The “treatment” is a worldwide technology release on one date. Why is a comparison across job categories still needed? What would a simple before–after comparison of writing jobs pick up?
Could ChatGPT also affect the control categories (e.g., freelancers switching from writing to video editing, or clients using ChatGPT to write video scripts)? Which direction would that bias \hat\beta?
Standard errors are clustered by job category, with only a handful of categories. What inference concern does that raise, and what would you do about it?
Why might log(job posts) be a problematic outcome, and why does a negative binomial model help?
Compare with Case Study 2: one paper finds AI raises worker productivity, the other finds AI reduces demand for freelancers. Can both be true?








NoteSuggested Answers (click to expand)






Freelance demand changes for other reasons at the same time: seasonality, platform growth, interest rates, and tech-sector layoffs in 2022–23. A before–after comparison of writing jobs would attribute all of these to ChatGPT.
If ChatGPT also reduces demand for control jobs, the control group falls too and the estimated decline is understated. If employers move budgets towards control categories, the control rises and the decline is overstated.
With few clusters, cluster-robust standard errors are too small and tests reject too often. Use the wild cluster bootstrap or randomization inference across categories, and report results at several aggregation levels.
The log of zero is undefined, and log(y + 1) gives results that depend on the units of y. A count model such as the negative binomial includes zeros and estimates a proportional effect directly.
Yes. They study different margins and people: inside a firm, AI helps workers who use it, especially new ones; across a market, firms can do some outsourced tasks themselves, which cuts demand for freelancers. Higher productivity can also mean fewer hours are needed.






Comparing the Three Designs






NoteComparing the Three Designs













Miller et al. (2021)
Brynjolfsson et al. (2025)
Demirci et al. (2025)




Who chose treatment?
States (politics)
Managers and trainers
Nobody (technology release)


Main threat
State-level shocks around 2014
Selection of improving agents
Spillovers to control jobs


Key defence
Placebo groups, power analysis
Agent + tenure FE, team-level IV, RCT pilot
Dose-response via search data, placebo dates


Staggered timing?
Yes, mild
Yes, strong
No


Inference concern
46 state clusters
None (many agents)
Few category clusters

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Best Practices

DiD Checklist






TipBefore Estimating




Plot the raw data: treated and control group means over time
Justify the control group: why is its change a credible counterfactual?
Ask who chose treatment and why: selection on levels is fine; selection on trends is not
Choose the outcome scale (levels vs. logs) before looking at results
Decide the clustering level from how treatment was assigned









TipAfter Estimating




Show an event study and discuss the power of pre-trend tests
With staggered timing, report a heterogeneity-robust estimator alongside TWFE
Run placebo tests: unaffected groups, fake treatment dates
Check for spillovers onto the control group
Interpret the estimand: ATT for whom, over what horizon; scale by the first stage if treatment take-up is incomplete





Common Pitfalls






WarningMistakes to Avoid




Treating flat pre-trends as proof of parallel trends
Running static TWFE with staggered adoption and dynamic effects
Using already-treated units as controls without realizing it
Clustering too finely (by individual when the policy varies by state)
Controlling for post-treatment variables that the policy itself changes
Ignoring anticipation: units changing behaviour before the official start date
Ignoring spillovers: the control group is partly treated
Taking logs of outcomes with many zeros without thinking about what the estimate means





Summary

Key Ideas:

DiD compares changes, not levels: the control group’s change stands in for the treated group’s counterfactual change
Identification rests on parallel trends, plus no anticipation and no spillovers
DiD is the two-way fixed effects model from Chapter 8 with a policy that switches on at a known date




Summary: Modern Practice and Case Studies

Modern Practice:

Event studies show dynamics and pre-trends, but pre-trend tests have limited power
With staggered adoption, TWFE can mix in forbidden comparisons; use robust estimators
Cluster at the policy level; beware of few clusters

From the Case Studies:

Linked administrative data plus careful placebo tests make the Medicaid–mortality result credible
Generative AI raises productivity most for less experienced workers inside a firm…
…while reducing demand for automation-prone freelance work across a platform




Next Steps


Read: Miller et al. (2021) Sections IV–VI; Brynjolfsson et al. (2025) Sections IV–V
Practice: In the staggered simulation, make the effect constant and re-run. When does TWFE work?
Assignment: Write a one-page referee report on Demirci et al. (2025) focusing on the control group and inference
Next Class: Synthetic control, for when there is only one treated unit and no single good control group




References


Arkhangelsky, Dmitry, Susan Athey, David A Hirshberg, Guido W Imbens, and Stefan Wager. 2021. “Synthetic Difference-in-Differences.” American Economic Review 111 (12): 4088–118. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20190159.


Bertrand, Marianne, Esther Duflo, and Sendhil Mullainathan. 2004. “How Much Should We Trust Differences-in-Differences Estimates?” The Quarterly Journal of Economics 119 (1): 249–75.


Borusyak, Kirill, Xavier Jaravel, and Jann Spiess. 2024. “Revisiting Event-Study Designs: Robust and Efficient Estimation.” Review of Economic Studies 91 (6): 3253–85. https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdae007.


Brynjolfsson, Erik, Danielle Li, and Lindsey Raymond. 2025. “Generative AI at Work.” The Quarterly Journal of Economics 140 (2): 889–942. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjae044.


Callaway, Brantly, and Pedro H C Sant’Anna. 2021. “Difference-in-Differences with Multiple Time Periods.” Journal of Econometrics 225 (2): 200–230. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2020.12.001.


Chaisemartin, Clément de, and Xavier D’Haultfœuille. 2020. “Two-Way Fixed Effects Estimators with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects.” American Economic Review 110 (9): 2964–96. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20181169.


Chen, Jiafeng, and Jonathan Roth. 2024. “Logs with Zeros? Some Problems and Solutions.” The Quarterly Journal of Economics 139 (2): 891–936. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjad054.


Demirci, Ozge, Jonas Hannane, and Xinrong Zhu. 2025. “Who Is AI Replacing? The Impact of Generative AI on Online Freelancing Platforms.” Management Science 71 (10): 8097–108. https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05420.


Goodman-Bacon, Andrew. 2021. “Difference-in-Differences with Variation in Treatment Timing.” Journal of Econometrics 225 (2): 254–77.


Miller, Sarah, Norman Johnson, and Laura R Wherry. 2021. “Medicaid and Mortality: New Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data.” The Quarterly Journal of Economics 136 (3): 1783–829. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjab004.


Rambachan, Ashesh, and Jonathan Roth. 2023. “A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends.” Review of Economic Studies 90 (5): 2555–91. https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdad018.


Roth, Jonathan. 2022. “Pretest with Caution: Event-Study Estimates After Testing for Parallel Trends.” American Economic Review: Insights 4 (3): 305–22. https://doi.org/10.1257/aeri.20210236.


Roth, Jonathan, and Pedro H C Sant’Anna. 2023. “When Is Parallel Trends Sensitive to Functional Form?” Econometrica 91 (2): 737–47. https://doi.org/10.3982/ECTA19402.


Sun, Liyang, and Sarah Abraham. 2021. “Estimating Dynamic Treatment Effects in Event Studies with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects.” Journal of Econometrics 225 (2): 175–99. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2020.09.006.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Where This Chapter Fits






Step 5: Do you observe every factor that drives both treatment and the outcome?



You arrive here when: Units chose their treatment, you observe them only once, and you can argue that all confounders are measured.
This chapter: Selection on observables, regression adjustment, matching, propensity scores, balance checks, and sensitivity analysis.
Next: Chapter 12: backing up any single design with others that have different weaknesses.

See the design flowchart in Chapter 1.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
In Practice: Regression and Matching






Practitioner Summary



Use it when: no design-based source of variation exists, and you can argue you observe what drove treatment
What you need: rich pre-treatment covariates, especially past outcomes, and untreated units similar to the treated ones
What must hold: no unmeasured confounders, and overlap
Checks to run: an overlap plot; standardized differences before and after (below 0.1); several estimators; a sensitivity analysis
In R: MatchIt::matchit() and match.data(), sensemakr for sensitivity
Telling a manager: “Among customers with the same purchase history, joiners visited 5% more. A hidden factor would need to be this strong to explain that away.”

title: Regression and Matching
text:
The Assumption






Conditional Independence and Overlap


Conditional independence (no unmeasured confounders): among units with the same observed characteristics X, treatment is as good as random
\big(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)\big) \perp D_i \mid X_i
Overlap (common support): for every value of X, there are both treated and untreated units: 0 < P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i) < 1. For the ATT it is enough that every treated unit has comparable untreated units: P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i) < 1, and Y_i(0) \perp D_i \mid X_i
Under both, the effect is identified by comparing like with like and averaging:
\text{ATT} = E\big[\, E[Y \mid D=1, X] - E[Y \mid D=0, X] \;\big|\; D = 1 \big]









The Strongest Untestable Assumption in These Notes


Every other design in these notes uses a source of variation in treatment (a lottery, a shock, a cutoff, timing). Here, the claim is simply that we have measured everything that matters. Data cannot confirm that claim, so the case must be made with knowledge of how treatment was chosen.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
When Is It Plausible?






Arguments That Help



Treatment was assigned by a known process based on recorded information (an underwriting rule, a targeting algorithm, a caseworker’s checklist)
Rich pre-treatment data, especially past values of the outcome, which capture much of what drives future outcomes
Institutional knowledge of why some units were treated and others not
Results are insensitive to adding or removing controls, and survive formal sensitivity analysis










Signs of Trouble



Units chose treatment based on private information (motivation, health, expected gains) that is not in the data
Treated and untreated units look very different on observables, suggesting they differ on unobservables too
Estimates move a lot as controls are added

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Regression Adjustment






Controlling for X in a Regression


Y_i = \alpha + \tau D_i + X_i'\beta + \varepsilon_i

Simple and easy to check; the default first step
Assumes the outcome depends on X in the specified form (usually linear)
Where treated and untreated units do not overlap, regression extrapolates from the functional form without warning
With heterogeneous effects and a dummy for every value of X, OLS weights each covariate group by the variance of treatment within it, P(D=1 \mid X)\,[1 - P(D=1 \mid X)], which need not give the ATT or ATE. With other specifications the weights are harder to describe, and can be negative
Only control for pre-treatment variables (Chapter 2: no mediators, no colliders)

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Matching






Pair Each Treated Unit with Similar Untreated Units









Approach
Idea




Exact matching
Match on identical values of X (feasible with few, discrete covariates)


Coarsened exact matching
Bin continuous variables, then match exactly on the bins


Nearest-neighbour matching
Match each treated unit to the closest untreated unit(s) by a distance on X


Caliper
Discard matches that are farther apart than a set tolerance


With or without replacement
Reusing controls gives closer matches but higher variance



Matching makes overlap visible: treated units without good matches are dropped, and the estimand becomes the effect for the units that remain.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
The Propensity Score






Collapsing Many Covariates into One Number


The propensity score is the probability of treatment given covariates: e(X_i) = P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i).
Key result: if treatment is as good as random given X, it is also as good as random given e(X) (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983). So we can match or weight on a single score instead of many covariates.
Ways to use it:

Matching treated and untreated units with similar scores
Inverse probability weighting (IPW): weight untreated units by e(X) / (1 - e(X)) to estimate the ATT
Doubly robust estimators combine a propensity model with an outcome regression; consistent if either model is right

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Diagnostics: Overlap and Balance






Check, Then Estimate



Overlap: plot the propensity score distributions for treated and untreated units; trim units outside the common range
Balance: after matching or weighting, compare covariates using standardized mean differences (difference in means divided by the pooled standard deviation). A common rule of thumb is below 0.1
Variance ratios near 1 for continuous covariates
Do not judge balance with p-values: they shrink with sample size and say nothing about bias
Balance on observables is necessary, not sufficient: it tells us nothing about unobservables

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Matching and Weighting in R


Code
suppressMessages(library(MatchIt))
set.seed(2026)
n <- 4000

# Customers decide whether to join a retailer's loyalty app.
# Frequent and loyal customers are more likely to join, and visit more anyway.
past_visits <- rpois(n, 6)
loyalty     <- runif(n)
join   <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-3 + 0.3 * past_visits + 2 * loyalty))
visits <- 2 + 0.8 * past_visits + 3 * loyalty + 1.0 * join + rnorm(n)   # true effect = 1
dat <- data.frame(visits, join, past_visits, loyalty)

# Nearest-neighbour propensity score matching with a caliper
m  <- matchit(join ~ past_visits + loyalty, data = dat, method = "nearest",
              distance = "glm", caliper = 0.1)
md <- match.data(m)

# Inverse probability weighting for the ATT
ps <- glm(join ~ past_visits + loyalty, family = binomial, data = dat)$fitted
w  <- ifelse(dat$join == 1, 1, ps / (1 - ps))

round(c(true_effect = 1,
        naive       = mean(visits[join == 1]) - mean(visits[join == 0]),
        regression  = unname(coef(lm(visits ~ join + past_visits + loyalty, dat))["join"]),
        PS_matching = unname(coef(lm(visits ~ join, md, weights = weights))["join"]),
        IPW         = weighted.mean(visits[join == 1], w[join == 1]) -
                      weighted.mean(visits[join == 0], w[join == 0])), 2)


true_effect       naive  regression PS_matching         IPW 
       1.00        2.64        1.02        1.09        1.08

Checking Balance


Code
smd <- cbind(before = summary(m)$sum.all[, "Std. Mean Diff."],
             after  = summary(m)$sum.matched[, "Std. Mean Diff."])
round(smd, 2)


            before after
distance      0.83  0.05
past_visits   0.63  0.05
loyalty       0.47  0.01




Before matching, joiners differ from non-joiners by about half a standard deviation or more on past visits and loyalty. After matching, the differences are below 0.1.

text:
When the Assumption Fails


Code
# Now an unobserved trait (enthusiasm) drives both joining and visiting
enthusiasm <- rnorm(n)
join2   <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-3 + 0.3 * past_visits + 2 * loyalty + 1.2 * enthusiasm))
visits2 <- 2 + 0.8 * past_visits + 3 * loyalty + 1.0 * join2 + 1.5 * enthusiasm + rnorm(n)
dat2 <- data.frame(visits = visits2, join = join2, past_visits, loyalty)

m2 <- matchit(join ~ past_visits + loyalty, data = dat2, method = "nearest",
              distance = "glm", caliper = 0.1)
c(true_effect = 1,
  PS_matching = round(unname(coef(lm(visits ~ join, match.data(m2), weights = weights))["join"]), 2))


true_effect PS_matching

section: Real Data: Can Matching Recover the Experiment?
text:
Real Data: Can Matching Recover the Experiment?


Code
data("lalonde", package = "MatchIt")   # 185 NSW trainees and 429 comparison men from a national survey (PSID)
f <- treat ~ age + educ + race + married + nodegree + re74 + re75

m_ll <- matchit(f, data = lalonde, method = "nearest", distance = "glm", caliper = 0.1, replace = TRUE)
md_ll <- match.data(m_ll)

round(c(experimental_benchmark = 1794,   # Dehejia & Wahba (1999), same 185 trainees
        naive      = with(lalonde, mean(re78[treat == 1]) - mean(re78[treat == 0])),
        regression = unname(coef(lm(update(f, re78 ~ treat + .), lalonde))["treat"]),
        PS_matching = unname(coef(lm(re78 ~ treat, md_ll, weights = weights))["treat"])))


experimental_benchmark                  naive             regression 
                  1794                   -635                   1548 
           PS_matching 
                  2039 








Reading the Result


The raw comparison says training lowered 1978 earnings by about $600, because the survey men earned far more to begin with. Controlling for earnings in 1974 and 1975 moves the estimate close to the experimental $1,794; matching does as well. The experiment is what tells us so: with observational data alone, we could not have known which estimate to trust (Dehejia and Wahba 1999).





lalonde ships with MatchIt. Note the effective sample: 183 of 185 trainees are matched, but only a few dozen distinct comparison men are used, because matching is with replacement.

title: Regression and Matching
section: How Strong Would a Hidden Confounder Have to Be?
text:
How Strong Would a Hidden Confounder Have to Be?






Measuring Sensitivity to Hidden Confounding



Rosenbaum bounds (Rosenbaum 2002): how much could an unobserved factor change the odds of treatment, between otherwise matched units, before the conclusion changes?
Omitted variable bias benchmarks: how strongly would an unobserved confounder need to be related to treatment and outcome, compared with an observed covariate, to explain away the estimate? (Cinelli and Hazlett 2020)
Coefficient stability: how much do estimates move as controls are added, relative to how much explanatory power they add? (Oster 2019)

A result that survives only a very weak hidden confounder should not be presented as causal.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Combining Matching with Other Designs






Matching Is Often Most Useful as a Helper



Matching + difference-in-differences: match treated units to similar untreated units before treatment, then compare changes. Fixed differences on unobservables cancel out (Chapter 9); matching makes parallel trends more plausible
Matching within an RDD bandwidth or an IV sample to improve balance and precision
Synthetic control (Chapter 10) is itself a form of matching on the pre-treatment path of the outcome

Case Study 2 uses this combination.

title: Regression and Matching
section: Case Study 1: Can Non-Experimental Methods Recover an Experiment?
text:
Case Study 1: Can Non-Experimental Methods Recover an Experiment?






LaLonde (1986), American Economic Review (LaLonde 1986)


Setting: the National Supported Work (NSW) demonstration, a US job-training program in the 1970s for disadvantaged workers (women receiving welfare benefits, and disadvantaged men), run as a randomized experiment.
The test: keep the treated group, but replace the randomized control group with comparison groups drawn from national surveys (the Panel Study of Income Dynamics and the Current Population Survey). Then apply standard non-experimental methods and compare their estimates with the experimental benchmark.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Case Study 1: What LaLonde Found






Non-Experimental Estimates Often Missed



The survey comparison groups were very different from program participants. In 1979, women in the experiment’s control group earned about $3,800; women in the broadest survey comparison group earned about $8,000
Many standard estimators (regressions with controls, before–after comparisons, two-step selection models) produced estimates far from the experimental result
Specification tests did not reliably flag which estimates were wrong

The lesson: without a design, controlling for observables can leave large biases, and the data may not tell you so.

title: Regression and Matching
section: Case Study 1: The Debate That Followed
text:
Case Study 1: The Debate That Followed






Can Propensity Scores Do Better?



Dehejia and Wahba (1999) showed that propensity score methods, with careful attention to overlap (dropping comparison units unlike any participant) and to pre-program earnings, came much closer to the experimental benchmark
Smith and Todd (2005) found that this success was sensitive to the sample and specification, and that difference-in-differences matching performed more reliably
Synthesis: matching helps when you have the right covariates (especially lagged outcomes) and enforce overlap; it cannot rescue a comparison group drawn from a different population

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Case Study 1: What to Copy






Practices to Reuse



Benchmark against an experiment when you can. It is the only direct test of whether an observational method works in your setting.
Draw comparison units from the same population, and drop those with no comparable treated unit.
Condition on past outcomes (earnings before the program); demographics alone are not enough.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Case Study 1: Discussion Questions

Why does replacing the experimental control group with a national survey sample create such large differences in earnings?
Why are pre-program earnings so important as covariates in job-training evaluations?
What does “specification tests did not flag the problem” imply for applied work?
Why might matching on changes in earnings (DiD matching) be more robust than matching on levels?

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Case Study 1: Suggested Answers (1–3)

The national surveys sample the wider population: older, more often employed, and with much higher earnings than the disadvantaged people the program enrolled. Those differences dwarf the program’s effect.
Past earnings are the strongest predictor of future earnings, and people often enter training after an earnings drop. Without earnings history, comparisons confuse this dip and recovery with the program’s effect.
Passing standard specification tests does not show an estimate is right. Applied work needs a design argument, benchmarks where possible, and sensitivity analysis.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Case Study 1: Suggested Answers (4)

Differencing removes fixed differences in earning ability that matching on observed characteristics misses, so only differences in earnings growth remain.

title: Regression and Matching
section: Case Study 2: Does Joining a Brand’s Social Media Page Change Customers?
text:
Case Study 2: Does Joining a Brand’s Social Media Page Change Customers?






Rishika, Kumar, Janakiraman & Bezawada (2013), Information Systems Research (Rishika et al. 2013)


Question: Do customers who join a retailer’s social media page (becoming a Facebook “fan”) visit more often and become more profitable?
Setting: a wine retailer in the northeastern United States that launched a Facebook page.
Data: transaction records for each customer from January 2008 to March 2011, linked to social media participation. Participants were identified through a customer survey (sent to 5,000 customers) and matched to the firm’s records of page members: 394 participants with enough data.
The selection problem: customers choose to join. Loyal, frequent buyers are more likely to join, and would visit often anyway.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Case Study 2: The Design






Propensity Score Matching, Then Difference-in-Differences



Propensity score: a logit model of joining, using 82 weeks of transaction and demographic data from before the page launched
Optimal pair matching: each participant paired with a similar non-participant; 287 matched pairs
Diagnostics: overlap of propensity scores (histograms and a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test); covariate balance before and after matching; Rosenbaum sensitivity analysis for hidden bias
Difference-in-differences on the matched sample, with customer fixed effects: compare the change in monthly visits after joining for participants with the change for their matched non-participants






This is the “matching as a helper” idea: matching makes the comparison group similar on observables; the DiD and customer fixed effects then remove any remaining fixed differences.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Case Study 2: Results and Checks






Main Findings



Joining the page raises visit frequency by about 5.2% relative to matched non-participants
Profits per customer rise by a similar proportion (an estimated elasticity of about 5.6%)
Effects are larger when the page is more active, and for customers who are more loyal, buy premium products, and are less deal-sensitive










Robustness



Estimates are positive and significant when the post-period is restricted to 3, 6, 9, 12, or 15 months, and converge towards the full-period estimate
Alternative matching methods give similar results
Placebo launch dates within the 18 months before the real launch give estimates indistinguishable from zero

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Case Study 2: Threats






What Matching Plus DiD Cannot Rule Out



Time-varying unobservables: a customer whose enthusiasm for wine is rising may both join the page and start visiting more; DiD removes fixed differences, not changing ones
Who is in the sample: participants were identified through a survey (about a quarter of the 5,000 customers surveyed responded), so the matched sample may not represent all page members
Single retailer and category: effects for a wine retailer may differ elsewhere

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Case Study 2: What to Copy






Practices to Reuse



Draw controls from the same firm’s customers and match on long pre-period behaviour (82 weeks).
Follow matching with difference-in-differences to remove remaining fixed differences.
Add placebo launch dates and a Rosenbaum sensitivity analysis.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Case Study 2: Discussion Questions

Why match on 82 weeks of pre-launch behaviour rather than only on demographics?
What does the DiD step add after matching? What would remain if the authors had only compared matched customers after launch?
Describe a confounder that would survive both matching and DiD.
How would you design an experiment to answer the same question? What would it cost the retailer?

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Case Study 2: Suggested Answers (1–3)

Past buying shows loyalty, interest in wine, and how often a customer visits, which drive both joining the page and future visits. Demographics capture these only weakly.
DiD removes any remaining differences that are constant over time. A comparison of matched customers after launch only would still include differences that matching did not balance, such as unobserved loyalty.
A change that starts around the time of joining, such as a new interest in wine, higher income, or moving closer to a store, could raise both joining and visits.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Case Study 2: Suggested Answers (4)

Randomly invite customers to join the page, for example by email with a small incentive, and use the invitation as an instrument for joining. Costs include the incentives, reaching fewer customers through the page during the test, and a large sample because take-up would be low.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Two Lessons About Observables






What the Two Studies Show











LaLonde (1986)
Rishika et al. (2013)




Role
Benchmark against an experiment
Applied study without an experiment


Comparison group
National survey samples
Matched customers of the same retailer


Key covariates
Demographics, some earnings history
82 weeks of transaction history


Design
Regression, difference-in-differences, and selection models
Propensity score matching + DiD


Lesson
Observables-only estimates can be far off
Same population, rich history, and DiD make matching more credible

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Selection-on-Observables Checklist






Before and After Estimating



Explain how treatment was chosen and why the observed covariates capture it
Use only pre-treatment covariates, including past outcomes where possible
Check overlap and trim units without comparable counterparts; say how the estimand changes
Report balance with standardized differences, before and after
Compare estimators (regression, matching, weighting, doubly robust); large disagreements signal problems
Run a sensitivity analysis for unobserved confounding
Where possible, combine with a design that uses another source of variation (DiD, an instrument, a cutoff)

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Common Pitfalls






Mistakes to Avoid



Treating good balance on observables as evidence of no hidden bias
Controlling for post-treatment variables (mediators) or colliders
Ignoring lack of overlap and letting regression extrapolate
Searching over covariates and matching settings until the estimate is significant
Judging balance with p-values
Presenting an observables-only estimate as causal without sensitivity analysis

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Summary

Regression, matching, and propensity scores share one assumption: no unmeasured confounders, plus overlap
They differ in how they use covariates: functional form (regression), similar units (matching), a single score (propensity), or weights
Check overlap and balance; quantify how strong hidden confounding would have to be
The LaLonde (1986) benchmark is the standing warning: observables-only estimates can be badly wrong
Matching is most credible as a helper to designs with another source of variation

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Next Steps

Read: LaLonde (1986) Sections I–III; Rishika et al. (2013) Sections 3–6 and 8
Practice: In the simulation, drop loyalty from the matching model. How much bias appears, and does the balance table warn you?
Next Class: Putting it together: combining designs, accumulating evidence, and reporting (Chapter 12)

title: Regression and Matching
text:
This is the last step of the design flowchart: units chose their treatment, we observe them only once (or have no credible variation over time), and we must argue that we observe every factor that drives both treatment and outcome.
Regression, matching, and propensity scores all rest on that same assumption. They differ in how they use the observed characteristics, not in what they assume.
Two case studies: LaLonde’s comparison of non-experimental estimates with an experiment (the classic warning), and a study of customers who join a retailer’s social media page (matching combined with difference-in-differences).

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Selection on Observables

The Assumption






ImportantConditional Independence and Overlap



Conditional independence (no unmeasured confounders): among units with the same observed characteristics X, treatment is as good as random
\big(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)\big) \perp D_i \mid X_i
Overlap (common support): for every value of X, there are both treated and untreated units: 0 < P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i) < 1. For the ATT it is enough that every treated unit has comparable untreated units: P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i) < 1, and Y_i(0) \perp D_i \mid X_i
Under both, the effect is identified by comparing like with like and averaging:
\text{ATT} = E\big[\, E[Y \mid D=1, X] - E[Y \mid D=0, X] \;\big|\; D = 1 \big]








WarningThe Strongest Untestable Assumption in These Notes



Every other design in these notes uses a source of variation in treatment (a lottery, a shock, a cutoff, timing). Here, the claim is simply that we have measured everything that matters. Data cannot confirm that claim, so the case must be made with knowledge of how treatment was chosen.




When Is It Plausible?






TipArguments That Help




Treatment was assigned by a known process based on recorded information (an underwriting rule, a targeting algorithm, a caseworker’s checklist)
Rich pre-treatment data, especially past values of the outcome, which capture much of what drives future outcomes
Institutional knowledge of why some units were treated and others not
Results are insensitive to adding or removing controls, and survive formal sensitivity analysis









WarningSigns of Trouble




Units chose treatment based on private information (motivation, health, expected gains) that is not in the data
Treated and untreated units look very different on observables, suggesting they differ on unobservables too
Estimates move a lot as controls are added

title: Regression and Matching
section: Three Ways to Compare Like with Like
text:
Three Ways to Compare Like with Like

Regression Adjustment






NoteControlling for X in a Regression



Y_i = \alpha + \tau D_i + X_i'\beta + \varepsilon_i

Simple and easy to check; the default first step
Assumes the outcome depends on X in the specified form (usually linear)
Where treated and untreated units do not overlap, regression extrapolates from the functional form without warning
With heterogeneous effects and a dummy for every value of X, OLS weights each covariate group by the variance of treatment within it, P(D=1 \mid X)\,[1 - P(D=1 \mid X)], which need not give the ATT or ATE. With other specifications the weights are harder to describe, and can be negative
Only control for pre-treatment variables (Chapter 2: no mediators, no colliders)





Matching






TipPair Each Treated Unit with Similar Untreated Units










Approach
Idea




Exact matching
Match on identical values of X (feasible with few, discrete covariates)


Coarsened exact matching
Bin continuous variables, then match exactly on the bins


Nearest-neighbour matching
Match each treated unit to the closest untreated unit(s) by a distance on X


Caliper
Discard matches that are farther apart than a set tolerance


With or without replacement
Reusing controls gives closer matches but higher variance



Matching makes overlap visible: treated units without good matches are dropped, and the estimand becomes the effect for the units that remain.




The Propensity Score






NoteCollapsing Many Covariates into One Number



The propensity score is the probability of treatment given covariates: e(X_i) = P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i).
Key result: if treatment is as good as random given X, it is also as good as random given e(X) (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983). So we can match or weight on a single score instead of many covariates.
Ways to use it:

Matching treated and untreated units with similar scores
Inverse probability weighting (IPW): weight untreated units by e(X) / (1 - e(X)) to estimate the ATT
Doubly robust estimators combine a propensity model with an outcome regression; consistent if either model is right





Diagnostics: Overlap and Balance






WarningCheck, Then Estimate




Overlap: plot the propensity score distributions for treated and untreated units; trim units outside the common range
Balance: after matching or weighting, compare covariates using standardized mean differences (difference in means divided by the pooled standard deviation). A common rule of thumb is below 0.1
Variance ratios near 1 for continuous covariates
Do not judge balance with p-values: they shrink with sample size and say nothing about bias
Balance on observables is necessary, not sufficient: it tells us nothing about unobservables

Specification tests did not reliably flag which estimates were wrong

The lesson: without a design, controlling for observables can leave large biases, and the data may not tell you so.




Case Study 1: The Debate That Followed






TipCan Propensity Scores Do Better?




Dehejia and Wahba (1999) showed that propensity score methods, with careful attention to overlap (dropping comparison units unlike any participant) and to pre-program earnings, came much closer to the experimental benchmark
Smith and Todd (2005) found that this success was sensitive to the sample and specification, and that difference-in-differences matching performed more reliably
Synthesis: matching helps when you have the right covariates (especially lagged outcomes) and enforce overlap; it cannot rescue a comparison group drawn from a different population





Case Study 1: What to Copy






TipPractices to Reuse




Benchmark against an experiment when you can. It is the only direct test of whether an observational method works in your setting.
Draw comparison units from the same population, and drop those with no comparable treated unit.
Condition on past outcomes (earnings before the program); demographics alone are not enough.





Case Study 1: Discussion Questions


Why does replacing the experimental control group with a national survey sample create such large differences in earnings?
Why are pre-program earnings so important as covariates in job-training evaluations?
What does “specification tests did not flag the problem” imply for applied work?
Why might matching on changes in earnings (DiD matching) be more robust than matching on levels?








NoteSuggested Answers (click to expand)






The national surveys sample the wider population: older, more often employed, and with much higher earnings than the disadvantaged people the program enrolled. Those differences dwarf the program’s effect.
Past earnings are the strongest predictor of future earnings, and people often enter training after an earnings drop. Without earnings history, comparisons confuse this dip and recovery with the program’s effect.
Passing standard specification tests does not show an estimate is right. Applied work needs a design argument, benchmarks where possible, and sensitivity analysis.
Differencing removes fixed differences in earning ability that matching on observed characteristics misses, so only differences in earnings growth remain.

title: Regression and Matching
section: Case Study 2: Social Media and Customer Value
text:
Case Study 2: Social Media and Customer Value

Case Study 2: Does Joining a Brand’s Social Media Page Change Customers?






NoteRishika, Kumar, Janakiraman & Bezawada (2013), Information Systems Research (Rishika et al. 2013)



Question: Do customers who join a retailer’s social media page (becoming a Facebook “fan”) visit more often and become more profitable?
Setting: a wine retailer in the northeastern United States that launched a Facebook page.
Data: transaction records for each customer from January 2008 to March 2011, linked to social media participation. Participants were identified through a customer survey (sent to 5,000 customers) and matched to the firm’s records of page members: 394 participants with enough data.
The selection problem: customers choose to join. Loyal, frequent buyers are more likely to join, and would visit often anyway.




Case Study 2: The Design






TipPropensity Score Matching, Then Difference-in-Differences




Propensity score: a logit model of joining, using 82 weeks of transaction and demographic data from before the page launched
Optimal pair matching: each participant paired with a similar non-participant; 287 matched pairs
Diagnostics: overlap of propensity scores (histograms and a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test); covariate balance before and after matching; Rosenbaum sensitivity analysis for hidden bias
Difference-in-differences on the matched sample, with customer fixed effects: compare the change in monthly visits after joining for participants with the change for their matched non-participants





This is the “matching as a helper” idea: matching makes the comparison group similar on observables; the DiD and customer fixed effects then remove any remaining fixed differences.




Case Study 2: Results and Checks






TipMain Findings




Joining the page raises visit frequency by about 5.2% relative to matched non-participants
Profits per customer rise by a similar proportion (an estimated elasticity of about 5.6%)
Effects are larger when the page is more active, and for customers who are more loyal, buy premium products, and are less deal-sensitive









NoteRobustness




Estimates are positive and significant when the post-period is restricted to 3, 6, 9, 12, or 15 months, and converge towards the full-period estimate
Alternative matching methods give similar results
Placebo launch dates within the 18 months before the real launch give estimates indistinguishable from zero





Case Study 2: Threats






WarningWhat Matching Plus DiD Cannot Rule Out




Time-varying unobservables: a customer whose enthusiasm for wine is rising may both join the page and start visiting more; DiD removes fixed differences, not changing ones
Who is in the sample: participants were identified through a survey (about a quarter of the 5,000 customers surveyed responded), so the matched sample may not represent all page members
Single retailer and category: effects for a wine retailer may differ elsewhere





Case Study 2: What to Copy






TipPractices to Reuse




Draw controls from the same firm’s customers and match on long pre-period behaviour (82 weeks).
Follow matching with difference-in-differences to remove remaining fixed differences.
Add placebo launch dates and a Rosenbaum sensitivity analysis.





Case Study 2: Discussion Questions


Why match on 82 weeks of pre-launch behaviour rather than only on demographics?
What does the DiD step add after matching? What would remain if the authors had only compared matched customers after launch?
Describe a confounder that would survive both matching and DiD.
How would you design an experiment to answer the same question? What would it cost the retailer?








NoteSuggested Answers (click to expand)






Past buying shows loyalty, interest in wine, and how often a customer visits, which drive both joining the page and future visits. Demographics capture these only weakly.
DiD removes any remaining differences that are constant over time. A comparison of matched customers after launch only would still include differences that matching did not balance, such as unobserved loyalty.
A change that starts around the time of joining, such as a new interest in wine, higher income, or moving closer to a store, could raise both joining and visits.
Randomly invite customers to join the page, for example by email with a small incentive, and use the invitation as an instrument for joining. Costs include the incentives, reaching fewer customers through the page during the test, and a large sample because take-up would be low.

title: Regression and Matching
text:
Best Practices

Selection-on-Observables Checklist






TipBefore and After Estimating




Explain how treatment was chosen and why the observed covariates capture it
Use only pre-treatment covariates, including past outcomes where possible
Check overlap and trim units without comparable counterparts; say how the estimand changes
Report balance with standardized differences, before and after
Compare estimators (regression, matching, weighting, doubly robust); large disagreements signal problems
Run a sensitivity analysis for unobserved confounding
Where possible, combine with a design that uses another source of variation (DiD, an instrument, a cutoff)





Common Pitfalls






WarningMistakes to Avoid




Treating good balance on observables as evidence of no hidden bias
Controlling for post-treatment variables (mediators) or colliders
Ignoring lack of overlap and letting regression extrapolate
Searching over covariates and matching settings until the estimate is significant
Judging balance with p-values
Presenting an observables-only estimate as causal without sensitivity analysis





Summary


Regression, matching, and propensity scores share one assumption: no unmeasured confounders, plus overlap
They differ in how they use covariates: functional form (regression), similar units (matching), a single score (propensity), or weights
Check overlap and balance; quantify how strong hidden confounding would have to be
The LaLonde (1986) benchmark is the standing warning: observables-only estimates can be badly wrong
Matching is most credible as a helper to designs with another source of variation




Next Steps


Read: LaLonde (1986) Sections I–III; Rishika et al. (2013) Sections 3–6 and 8
Practice: In the simulation, drop loyalty from the matching model. How much bias appears, and does the balance table warn you?
Next Class: Putting it together: combining designs, accumulating evidence, and reporting (Chapter 12)
