title: Panel Data and Fixed Effects
text:
Case Study 5: Running the Checklist
The fixed-effects checklist from the end of this chapter, applied to this paper. Try each question before revealing the answer.

State the comparison the fixed effects impose. A hotter weekday against a cooler weekday in the same postcode, in the same month of the same year.
Why is the remaining variation as good as random? Which confounders could still vary within a postcode-month? Nobody chooses the day’s temperature, and within a postcode-month it is unrelated to the local economy, workforce, or industry mix. Rain and the day of the week do vary from day to day and relate to both heat and injuries, so the model controls for them.
Does the fixed-effect structure match that argument? Yes. Postcode × month-year fixed effects absorb anything specific to one place in one month: seasonal work, local booms and slumps, the size of the workforce, and changes to the compensation scheme over 35 years.

title: Panel Data and Fixed Effects
text:
Case Study 5: Running the Checklist (4–6)

At what level should standard errors be clustered? Temperature is measured for each postcode, so standard errors are clustered by postcode. Neighbouring postcodes share weather; standard errors that allow for this spatial correlation (Conley) barely change, in a check using OLS.
How much variation in treatment is left after the fixed effects? A lot. In Melbourne the hottest and coolest days in a month differ by about 19°C in summer and 10°C in winter.
Is the result robust to other fixed effects and controls? Yes. The main estimate is 0.24% more claims per 1°C; 0.20 with a PM2.5 control, 0.27 with calendar-date fixed effects, and 0.22 with separate postcode × month and month-year fixed effects. It is similar using only accepted claims, OLS, dry days only, and including weekends.

title: Panel Data and Fixed Effects
text:
Case Study 5: Running the Checklist (7–8)

Do placebo tests support the design? Partly. The paper checks past, not future, temperatures: yesterday’s heat adds 0.14% per 1°C, the day before has no effect (−0.01%), and last night’s minimum has no effect. A natural addition is a lead test: tomorrow’s temperature should not predict today’s claims.
Could selection into the data bias the result? Claims appear only if lodged, so heat could change reporting rather than injuries. The result holds using only claims the insurer accepted. Postcode-months with no claims drop out of the Poisson model because they carry no information. Workers may choose jobs by heat tolerance, which the authors argue makes the gap between manual and other occupations conservative.

title: Panel Data and Fixed Effects
text:
Case Study 5: Running the Checklist (9–10)

Whose effect is estimated, and over what horizon? Workers in Victoria’s compulsory scheme, which leaves out some groups such as federal government employees. It is the effect of one hot day on that day’s and the next day’s claims, net of responses such as working less on hot days, because the number of workers at risk is not observed.
Does it separate short-run weather effects from long-run climate effects? The estimates come from day-to-day weather. The authors translate them with a simple calculation: 1.5°C of warming would add about 0.38% to claims (about 156 claims and AU$40.3 million a year), assuming current adaptation stays the same. Heat effects for high-risk workers did not fall over 35 years, a sign that adaptation has been limited.

title: Panel Data and Fixed Effects
text:
Choosing Time-Varying Controls






Which X_{it} to Include



Only time-varying variables matter. Anything fixed within a unit is already absorbed by \alpha_i, so adding it changes nothing.
Include variables that change within units and affect both treatment and the outcome (time-varying confounders). Example: rain is related to both temperature and injury risk (Case Study 5).
Exclude anything the treatment can change. Hours worked respond to AI access, and pollution may respond to heat. Controlling for them removes part of the effect.
Watch for feedback. A control affected by past outcomes, or a lagged outcome, breaks strict exogeneity (Nickell bias).
Variables that only predict the outcome are optional. They can improve precision but do not remove bias.
Report results with and without debatable controls. Example: Case Study 5 reports 0.24% per 1°C without a pollution control and 0.20% with it.
